data.toolkit_usage: Introductory foundations-layer concept for community organizers and growers new to crypto; explicitly distinguishes "sustainability maintains, regeneration improves" and walks through three concrete problem/solution pairs (proving impact via Silvi, community-driven funding via Gitcoin quadratic funding, local value circulation via community tokens) before addressing energy-use and greenwashing objections.
adjacent_meanings: sustainability (doing less harm — explicitly distinguished as a lesser goal than regeneration)
DeFi (decentralized finance generally, of which ReFi is framed as a values-driven subset)
important_distinctions: sustainability-maintains-vs-regeneration-improves — the article's central conceptual hinge distinguishing ReFi from ordinary sustainability framing.
tokenizing-is-not-automatically-good — a carbon token (or any tokenized "nature asset") is only as honest as the underlying project; tokenization is a wrapper, not a verification of quality.
tensions: pricing-nature-vs-commodifying-nature — putting a number on carbon, water, or biodiversity is presented as ReFi's headline move, but the article itself flags this is "exactly where greenwashing hides."
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing ReFi to "carbon tokens" or "crypto for climate" erases the article's broader claim that it is fundamentally about redirecting money toward people doing regenerative work (soil, community, local circulation), not only about pricing ecological assets.

data.title: Quadratic funding formula and the breadth-over-wealth design goal
data.short_description: For each project, take the square root of every individual donation, sum those roots, then square the total — that squared number is the project's share of a shared matching pool. The design goal: the number of distinct backers matters more than the size of any single donation.
source_traditions: "Liberal Radicalism: A Flexible Design for Philanthropic Matching Funds," a 2018 paper by Vitalik Buterin, Zoë Hitzig, and Glen Weyl
data.toolkit_usage: Walked through with a worked example in the article (100 people giving $1 each outweighs one person giving $100, 10,000 vs. 100 matching weight) to make the "breadth beats whales" design goal concrete for organizers deciding whether to run a round.
adjacent_meanings: Deep Funding, MACI private voting, Conviction Voting, Retroactive Funding, and peer-reviewed Hypercerts — the five other mechanisms GG24 ran alongside QF in the same cycle, per the article's "plural toolkit" framing.
important_distinctions: Democratic communities systematically underfund shared goods because no single person captures the full benefit — QF is designed to correct for that specific market failure, not to replace grants generally.
tensions: Rewarding breadth of support vs. vulnerability to sybil attacks (one person spinning up many wallets to fake a crowd).
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing QF to "more donors equals more match" without the sybil-defense caveats (proof of personhood, cluster-matching corrections) that make a round's match trustworthy in practice.

data.title: DAO treasury diversification
data.short_description: Holding a DAO's treasury across multiple asset types — especially stablecoins (USDC, DAI) alongside the native governance token — rather than concentrating value in one volatile, illiquid asset, in order to maintain operational continuity through market cycles.
source_traditions: traditional corporate/nonprofit treasury and reserve-fund management
DeFi lending and market-making mechanisms (Aave, Gnosis Auction, OTC desks)
data.toolkit_usage: Practical heuristic given: maintain 2-3 years of operating expenses in stablecoins as a survival buffer; diversify via organic stablecoin revenue, strategic token sales (OTC, batch auctions, bonding curves), strategic partnerships (discounted token swaps with lock-ups), or borrowing against native tokens.
adjacent_meanings: portfolio diversification (traditional finance) — same risk-reduction logic applied to a DAO's own governance token
important_distinctions: treasury size (paper wealth in governance tokens) vs. treasury liquidity (actual spendable/stable value) — the article's central paradox
diversification method choice (revenue vs. sale vs. partnership vs. borrowing) carries different risk/governance trade-offs, not interchangeable tactics
tensions: diversifying by selling native tokens can itself crash the token's price (the liquidity problem it's trying to solve)
borrowing against tokens avoids sales but introduces liquidation risk if token prices drop
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "diversify into stablecoins" as a universal prescription without weighing a specific DAO's values, risk tolerance, and governance structure — the article frames treasury management as inseparable from governance (who holds power), not a purely technical finance decision.

data.title: Native token concentration risk
data.short_description: The risk a DAO carries when most of its treasury value sits in its own governance token: thin order books (illiquidity), extreme volatility, and operational continuity breaking down precisely when the community most needs stability (bear markets).
source_traditions: crypto-market microstructure (order-book liquidity, slippage)
DAO/protocol treasury commentary
data.toolkit_usage: Named as the article's core paradox: DAOs holding "$15 billion" across the top 50 treasuries appear wealthy on paper while actual financial flexibility is severely limited by this concentration.
adjacent_meanings: home-bias / concentration risk (traditional finance analogue — over-exposure to a single, correlated asset)
important_distinctions: governance power (what the token measures) vs. spendable value (what the token can reliably realize in a sale) — the token does both jobs poorly when treated as the treasury's main asset
tensions: the token that best represents community ownership/governance is often the worst asset to actually spend from
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing this to "sell the token" ignores that forced or large token sales are exactly what triggers the illiquidity/slippage problem being described — the risk and its naive fix are in tension.

data.title: Quadratic Funding (QF)
data.short_description: Crowdfunding with a matching pool, where the match grows with the number of distinct backers rather than the dollar amount they give — "a vote you cast with a small donation."
source_traditions: Constrained Liberal Radicalism algorithm — "Liberal Radicalism," a 2018 paper by Vitalik Buterin, Zoë Hitzig, and E. Glen Weyl
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the prospective-funding mechanism a local node is most likely to use before it has a track record; Gitcoin Grants and Giveth run the largest QF rounds. Framed as a turnout exercise for organizers, not a grant application — outcomes are mostly decided by contributor-list size before a round even opens.
adjacent_meanings: direct grants (application-based, no matching-pool mechanics)
streaming QF (Gitcoin/Geo Web via Superfluid — real-time flow-rate matching)
conviction voting (1Hive — continuous token-weighted staking, no round cadence)
important_distinctions: QF is prospective (pays before the work), distinct from retroactive funding (RetroPGF/Retro Funding) and hypercerts, which pay after impact is shown.
tensions: Breadth-of-participation design goal vs. Sybil attacks (fake identities) and collusion (coordinated real users) — the article's stated "pitfall you most need to hear."
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating a QF round as free money rather than what the article insists it is: a turnout mechanism that rewards community-building work done long before the round opens.

data.title: Retroactive Public Goods Funding (RetroPGF / Retro Funding)
data.short_description: Funding that flips prospective funding's timing: instead of pitching a plan, a project ships work first, and a later round looks back and pays for what proved useful. The Optimism Collective runs the largest version.
source_traditions: Optimism Collective (850M OP reserved for public goods, 20% of supply)
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned as suiting nodes that already produce visible, attributable work rather than brand-new ones; hypercerts are presented as the evidentiary record that lets a retro round know what a node actually did.
adjacent_meanings: hypercerts (the structured impact record retro rounds are read against)
quadratic funding (the prospective counterpart in the article's "two families" framing)
important_distinctions: Retrospective (pays after impact is shown) vs. prospective (pays before the work happens) — the article's organizing distinction for the whole funding landscape.
tensions: "No proposal-writing theatre" relief vs. the risk of funding yourself out of pocket first and hoping a future round notices you.
data.risks_of_flattening: Assuming retro funding suits any node, when the article is explicit it rewards track records and therefore suits established nodes, not brand-new ones.

data.title: Phishing (crypto)
data.short_description: Impersonating a trusted service to steal login details or private keys/seed phrases — via fake emails, typosquatted websites, DMs offering "help," or malicious browser extensions.
source_traditions: general information-security phishing terminology, applied to crypto wallets/exchanges
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the first scam pattern in the article's field guide; the "golden rule" defense given is that no legitimate service ever asks for a seed phrase or private key.
adjacent_meanings: typosquatting
important_distinctions: phishing-vs-rug-pull — phishing steals credentials/keys from a victim; a rug pull is a project's own team absconding with pooled funds
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating all phishing as identical hides real variation in vector (email vs. malicious browser extension vs. DM) that requires different specific defenses.

data.title: Rug pull
data.short_description: A project's creators take investors' pooled funds and abandon the project, often after building tokenomics that quietly blocks holders from selling.
source_traditions: crypto/DeFi token-launch culture
data.toolkit_usage: Illustrated in the article with the SQUID token (2021) case: price spiked from cents to $2,800+, then developers drained funds and the sell-blocking code trapped 40,000+ buyers.
important_distinctions: anonymous-team-vs-rug-pull — the article stresses an anonymous team isn't automatically a scam; trust should come from open code and independent audits, not team visibility alone
data.risks_of_flattening: Not every failed/abandoned crypto project is a deliberate rug pull; conflating negligence, failure, and intentional fraud under one label can mislabel honest failures as scams.

data.title: Pig butchering (romance scam)
data.short_description: A long-con scam that builds a genuine-feeling romantic or personal relationship before introducing a crypto "opportunity" — the name refers to "fattening up" a victim with affection and small wins before draining their funds.
source_traditions: romance-scam fraud pattern, adapted to crypto investment fraud
data.toolkit_usage: Presented per Chainalysis research as among the most financially damaging scam categories; article gives a behavioral pattern (dating-app or "wrong number" contact, weeks of warm conversation, fake trading app, pressure to reinvest, then silence) and defenses (video call test, treat romance+investing overlap as a red flag).
adjacent_meanings: investment-scam
data.risks_of_flattening: Article's defenses (ask for a video call, watch for a romance/investing overlap) don't address increasingly convincing AI-generated video/voice, which the article itself flags as an emerging gap.

data.title: Taxonomy (knowledge organization)
data.short_description: A hierarchy of categories used to file and find things — each item sits under a broader category. The formal (SKOS) version gives each concept one preferred label and any number of alternate labels (synonyms), with broader/narrower/related relations.
source_traditions: library and information science
controlled-vocabulary / thesaurus practice
SKOS (W3C linked-data standard)
data.toolkit_usage: Recommended default for knowledge commons: build the taxonomy in SKOS first (prefLabel/altLabel/broader/narrower), reach for an ontology only when a specific recurring task needs machine reasoning.
adjacent_meanings: folksonomy (uncontrolled, user-generated tagging — taxonomy is controlled)
category tree / folder hierarchy (informal analogue)
important_distinctions: taxonomy classifies and enables navigation; it does not encode reasoning rules (that's ontology's job)
a taxonomy concept has ONE preferred label + alternates — this is what stops label drift (e.g. 'grants'/'funding'/'money')
tensions: simplicity/accessibility (non-technical teammates can read and extend it) vs. expressive limits (no inference)
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating every useful adjective or tag as if it were a taxonomy type causes the same "ontology sprawl" problem taxonomies are meant to avoid — the type/tag distinction has to be actively maintained, not assumed.

data.title: Ontology (knowledge organization)
data.short_description: Describes the kinds of things (classes) in a domain and the specific, named, typed relationships between them and their instances (individuals), in a form a computer can reason over — enabling inference (e.g. flagging a Grant missing a required Report) that a taxonomy cannot do.
source_traditions: knowledge engineering / semantic web (RDF, RDFS, OWL)
artificial intelligence (knowledge representation)
data.toolkit_usage: The Regen Toolkit's own ontology layer aims for "enough shared meaning that people, tools, and future AI workflows can work together without silently inventing incompatible categories" — not a perfect ontology before use. Positioned as the second step after a taxonomy, adopted only when a genuine need for machine-readable relationships and inference exists.
adjacent_meanings: knowledge graph (a populated instance of an ontology's classes + relationships)
controlled vocabulary (taxonomy's simpler cousin, often confused with ontology)
important_distinctions: class vs. individual — Grant (type) vs. this March seed grant (instance)
a type defines what something IS; a tag describes how something may be classified/filtered — confusing them creates ontology sprawl
tensions: expressive power (inference, structured queries) vs. maintenance cost (full-time modeling work if scope isn't disciplined)
data.risks_of_flattening: Building a full ontology before a task actually needs machine reasoning — most knowledge commons never need this step, and premature ontology work is the "opposite of outliving turnover" the article warns against.

data.title: Minimum Viable Node (MVN)
data.short_description: The smallest real version of a local initiative that actually does something for real people — the smallest loop of people coordinating value together that can be run with the people already on hand, before tokens, treasuries, or on-chain governance enter the picture.
source_traditions: lean-startup minimum viable product (MVP)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as the answer to three specific organizer fears — burnout, building something nobody wants, and central overreach — and operationalized in the article as three load-bearing parts: a one-sentence shared purpose, a way to track value, and five to ten people who reliably show up.
adjacent_meanings: minimum viable product (MVP), the lean-startup source concept
important_distinctions: "One is a plan. The other is a working node with a sample size of two." — the article's own distinction between writing a whitepaper for a community currency and actually lending a neighbour a drill in exchange for tracked time.
Autonomous yet connected — an MVN is explicitly not isolationist; the article distinguishes "belonging to a network" from "being captured by one."
tensions: Guarding against central overreach (keeping heavy machinery out) vs. tapping shared learning from networks like ReFi DAO and Greenpill so the node doesn't reinvent every wheel.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "minimum viable" as an excuse to skip the hard part (real conversations, an actual exchange with real people) rather than as a sequencing discipline that defers technology until human coordination is actually straining.

data.title: Source system
data.short_description: A living knowledge environment (wiki, repo, research database, forum, digital garden) — not a single document or a static link — that has a steward, receives ongoing additions, and offers a return path to credit and trace material back to its origin.
source_traditions: digital-garden practice (Maggie Appleton)
commons governance (Elinor Ostrom's design principles)
open-source repo/maintainer conventions
data.toolkit_usage: The Regen Knowledge Commons Toolkit's Resource Graph layer is explicitly framed as "not a link list" but the place the rest of the toolkit stays grounded in reality; the three-question test (Who tends this? Is new material still added? Can I trace and credit it?) determines whether a dependency is a source system or a rotting link.
adjacent_meanings: link list / resources page (a flat, unowned, unmaintained set of URLs — explicitly NOT a source system)
Resource Graph vs. Ecosystem Atlas (storage-with-lineage vs. the interpretive lens layered on top of it)
important_distinctions: a source system has three required properties: steward, ongoing additions, return path to credit — a source lacking any one of these is a link, not a system
inclusion does not mean endorsement — adding a source system as a reference is not the project vouching for its content
tensions: openness to add broadly vs. the discipline of marking maturity honestly so raw inclusions don't silently become 'true'
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating any URL you cite as a "source system" without a steward or return path — this collapses the distinction the whole concept exists to preserve, and lets link rot back in under a new name.

data.title: Provenance (vs. lineage)
data.short_description: The recorded origin and history of a piece of knowledge — where it came from, who made it, and how it changed — distinguished from "lineage," which is the path data took through systems. Provenance answers "why do we believe this, and who said it first?"
source_traditions: data-engineering (data lineage vs. provenance distinction)
archival/records science (chain of custody)
data.toolkit_usage: Directly maps to this framework's own `provenance` mixin (schemas/provenance.yaml: origin, surfaced_by, adapted_from, transformation, authorship) — the mechanism that keeps "inclusion does not mean endorsement" honest by making origin traceable on every object.
adjacent_meanings: data lineage (the technical path through systems — a related but distinct concept per the Snowflake source cited)
important_distinctions: lineage = the path data took through systems; provenance = the historical record of origin, custody, and trust
tensions: provenance is the highest-leverage habit for a long-lived commons, but it is also the part contributors most often skip because it feels like overhead in the moment
data.risks_of_flattening: Losing provenance lets claims decay into folklore — repeated by everyone, backed by no one — which is exactly the failure mode a knowledge commons is trying to avoid by recording origin every time.

data.title: Outputs vs. Outcomes vs. Impact
data.short_description: The core distinction the impact-measurement field rests on: outputs are countable activity ("we ran 12 workshops"), outcomes are what actually changed for people or ecosystems as a result ("30 farmers adopted a regenerative practice"), and impact is the difference the work made versus what would have happened anyway (if the trees would have been planted regardless, impact is zero even with 400 outputs).
source_traditions: impact evaluation / M&E (monitoring & evaluation)
theory of change methodology
MRV (measurement, reporting, verification) for ecological projects
data.toolkit_usage: Central diagnostic frame for local-node builders in the article: most nodes count outputs because they're "easy and seductive," but funders and the node's own future self care about outcomes and impact; the article uses it to argue for lightweight before/after surveys and follow-ups rather than a research budget.
adjacent_meanings: vanity metrics (activity counted for its own sake, named as the failure mode this distinction guards against)
theory of change (the one-page map from activities to desired change, used to decide which two or three numbers are worth collecting)
important_distinctions: counting-activity-vs-demonstrating-change — "we ran 12 workshops" (output) tells no one anything on its own; "12 workshops, after which 30 farmers switched to cover-cropping, up from 4 the year before" (outcome) is a story with a spine.
outcome-vs-counterfactual-impact — an outcome can occur without the node's work being the cause of it; impact specifically nets out what would have happened anyway.
tensions: rigor-vs-burnout — the article explicitly warns against "becoming a spreadsheet bureaucracy"; the recommended discipline is a small number of weekly-checked metrics, not comprehensive measurement.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating any counted number as equally meaningful "measurement" erases the distinction the whole article is built on — a high output count can coexist with zero real impact, and the article frames that gap as where "good local initiatives quietly die."

data.title: Stablecoins
data.short_description: Cryptocurrencies pegged to a stable reference asset (typically the US dollar) so their value doesn't swing the way bitcoin's does, making them practical for organizations needing predictable budgets.
source_traditions: crypto/DeFi
traditional finance (currency-peg concept)
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned in this article as the practical, everyday-operations use case for nonprofits (vs. bitcoin/volatile-crypto donations for one-off crisis fundraising) — cross-border payments and predictable budgeting.
adjacent_meanings: crypto-donations
cross-border-payments
important_distinctions: stablecoins-vs-volatile-crypto — stablecoins are framed as suited to recurring operational use, not speculative holding
data.risks_of_flattening: The article doesn't distinguish stablecoin types (fiat-collateralized vs. algorithmic vs. crypto-collateralized) or their differing risk profiles — treating "stablecoin" as a single practical mechanism.

data.title: Blockchain
data.short_description: A digital record (ledger) that many computers (nodes) keep identical, synchronized copies of, organized into blocks that each carry a hash (fingerprint) of the previous block, making the history tamper-evident and removing the need for a single trusted keeper.
source_traditions: distributed systems / distributed ledger technology
cryptography (cryptographic hashing, consensus mechanisms)
digital currency (Bitcoin's original use case)
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced via a "village notebook" analogy for readers new to crypto; grounds the toolkit's later, more technical articles (proof of work/stake, wallets, decentralization) in a plain-language first encounter.
adjacent_meanings: distributed ledger (the general category; a blockchain is one specific structure — hash-chained blocks — within it)
database with replication (superficially similar copy-everywhere idea, but lacks the hash-chaining + consensus that make a blockchain tamper-evident without a trusted operator)
important_distinctions: immutable ≠ unchangeable-in-theory — rewriting settled history is possible in principle but requires redoing every subsequent block and persuading a majority of nodes simultaneously, which is what makes it impractical rather than impossible
trustless ≠ untrustworthy — it means no single keeper needs to be trusted because every node can verify every other node's records
tensions: permanence protects against tampering but also means mistakes (wrong entries, misdirected payments) usually can't be undone
public chains are often fully visible, so transparency and privacy pull against each other for sensitive community information
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "blockchain" as a single monolithic technology with one energy profile or one privacy model — proof-of-work vs. proof-of-stake chains differ by roughly three orders of magnitude in energy use, and public vs. permissioned chains differ sharply in visibility.

data.title: Proof of work vs. proof of stake
data.short_description: Two blockchain consensus mechanisms for agreeing what's true across nodes without a central authority. Proof of work secures the chain by burning computing power/electricity (Bitcoin); proof of stake secures it through deposited funds rather than raw computation (Ethereum since its 2022 "Merge," and Celo).
source_traditions: cryptography / distributed-consensus research
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article's "honest costs" section to correct a dated assumption: "blockchain wastes energy" is true of proof-of-work chains like Bitcoin but false of proof-of-stake chains, which is what most regenerative-economy projects (built on Ethereum, Celo) actually run on.
adjacent_meanings: mining (the proof-of-work process of competing to add the next block) vs. staking (the proof-of-stake process of depositing funds to earn the right to validate)
important_distinctions: energy use differs by roughly three orders of magnitude between the two mechanisms per the article's cited figures — they are not interchangeable when evaluating a project's environmental footprint
Ethereum's 2022 switch ("the Merge") changed only the consensus mechanism, not what the chain is used for — same network, different security method
tensions: proof-of-work's energy cost buys a very long, battle-tested security track record (Bitcoin); proof-of-stake trades some of that track record for far lower energy use
data.risks_of_flattening: Citing Bitcoin's energy use as if it applied to "blockchain" generally — the article explicitly warns this generalization is now false for Ethereum and Celo, the chains most regenerative projects actually use.

data.title: Local node (ReFi)
data.short_description: A place-based community that meets regularly to learn and apply regenerative-finance tools on the ground, rooted in a specific town or city with a long-term commitment to regeneration.
source_traditions: ReFi DAO local-node network
data.toolkit_usage: The organizing unit for the whole 90-day playbook; ReFi DAO is cited as coordinating the largest network of these nodes (100+ events across 58 cities).
adjacent_meanings: local-node-incubator
regen-coordination-hub
important_distinctions: local-node-vs-product-launch — the article stresses a node is a relationship that starts with people, not a treasury or token launch
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "local node" as a template to copy-paste (fixed structure, fixed timeline) rather than a relationship-first process that varies by city and community.

data.title: Quadratic funding
data.short_description: A matching-fund mechanism that weights the number of backers more heavily than the size of any single gift, so broad community support outweighs one large donor ("one whale").
source_traditions: Gitcoin Grants matching-round design
data.toolkit_usage: Explains why Gitcoin Grants is recommended as the main funding on-ramp for a local node once it has a track record — small, broad-based community donations get amplified by a matching pool.
adjacent_meanings: gitcoin-grants
gitcoin-passport
important_distinctions: quadratic-funding-vs-flat-matching — rewards breadth of small backers rather than simply matching whatever is donated 1:1
data.risks_of_flattening: The article doesn't cover known quadratic-funding attack vectors (e.g. collusion/Sybil attacks), which Gitcoin Passport is partly designed to mitigate — worth linking if a dedicated quadratic-funding page exists.

data.title: Review-maturity ladder (four-rung: Draft / Reviewed / Maintained / Deprecated)
data.short_description: A shippable per-page trust-state label for knowledge commons: Draft (written, unchecked, anyone can edit) -> Reviewed (a second person confirmed accuracy) -> Maintained (reviewed AND someone owns keeping it current, with a review date) -> Deprecated (kept for history, points to its replacement). Stored in page frontmatter (`status`, `reviewed_by`, `last_reviewed`) so it travels with the content.
source_traditions: Wikipedia content assessment (Stub -> Start -> C -> B -> GA -> FA)
Architecture Decision Records / MADR (Proposed -> Accepted -> Deprecated/Superseded)
Kubernetes feature gates (Alpha -> Beta -> Stable)
data.toolkit_usage: Crosswalks onto this toolkit's own K1 review-maturity model (schemas/review-maturity.yaml): Draft -> maturity "draft", Reviewed -> maturity "reviewed", Deprecated -> maturity "deprecated". "Maintained" has no exact K1 rung — it layers ownership + a recency check (last_reviewed expiry) on top of "reviewed" rather than being a distinct maturity value, which is itself a useful gap to flag for K1's crosswalk table.
adjacent_meanings: self-claimed state (Draft/Proposed/Alpha — 'I wrote this') vs. granted state (Reviewed/Accepted/Stable — 'someone else checked this')
important_distinctions: 'Maintained' is not just 'still reviewed' — it requires an owner AND a last_reviewed date, i.e. an active maintenance commitment, not a static label
review effort should scale with risk (low-stakes: one reader; high-stakes — money/legal/ecological/governance: two reviewers + an owner) rather than a single fixed bar for every page
tensions: frictionless draft tiers (encourage capture) vs. gated granted tiers (protect trust) — loosening either side breaks the mechanism
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "Reviewed" as a permanent badge rather than a maintenance commitment — the article's core warning is that reviewed pages silently rot once nobody re-checks them; conflating "was reviewed once" with "is still trustworthy" undoes the whole point of the ladder.

data.title: Bus factor
data.short_description: The number of people who would have to disappear before a project stalls — knowledge concentrated in one head has a bus factor of one, meaning a single departure breaks continuity.
source_traditions: software engineering / knowledge-management risk metrics
data.toolkit_usage: Motivates maturity labelling in the Regen Toolkit: when the one expert leaves, unreviewed drafts stay behind looking as authoritative as reviewed pages unless the trust-state was made legible in advance.
adjacent_meanings: key-person dependency / single point of failure (general risk-management framing)
important_distinctions: bus factor is about knowledge concentration risk, not about the quality of any single piece of writing — a well-written draft can still raise the bus factor if it is the only record of a decision
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing bus factor to "hire more people" rather than "make trust state and provenance legible" — the article's point is that labelling is a cheap mitigation that does not require more staff.

data.title: Decentralization
data.short_description: The distribution of power, control, and decision-making away from a single hub, existing on a spectrum (centralized → decentralized → distributed) rather than as a binary state.
source_traditions: network/distributed-systems architecture (computer science)
public-administration governance typology (deconcentration, delegation, devolution, privatization)
blockchain/crypto governance discourse
data.toolkit_usage: Anchor concept for Layer 1 (Foundations) — used to teach that "decentralized" is not a single yes/no property but a position on multiple independent axes (architecture and governance; technological and sociopolitical), and that the right position is context-dependent rather than an ideological default.
adjacent_meanings: subsidiarity
polycentric-governance
distributed-systems
important_distinctions: architecture-vs-governance — a system can be architecturally decentralized (nodes) while remaining politically centralized (who decides), or vice versa
technological-vs-sociopolitical-decentralization — infrastructure independence is separate from equitable distribution of actual power (e.g., token concentration)
deconcentration-vs-delegation-vs-devolution-vs-privatization — four governance forms of increasing (then differently-directed, in privatization's case) authority transfer
tensions: decentralization-as-tool-vs-decentralization-as-ideology — the article explicitly warns against treating maximal distribution as inherently superior ("a tool, not a religion")
data.risks_of_flattening: Collapsing "decentralized" into a single label hides that a system can score very differently on technical vs. sociopolitical decentralization — e.g., a blockchain with thousands of nodes but 50% of tokens in one wallet is technologically distributed yet sociopolitically centralized.

data.title: Self-Custody Crypto Wallets
data.short_description: An app that lets a person store, send, and receive digital assets directly, controlled by a public address (shareable, like an account number) and a secret seed phrase (12 or 24 words granting full access), without a bank as intermediary.
source_traditions: Bitcoin/Ethereum-era self-custody wallet design (public/private key pairs)
browser-extension and mobile wallet UX patterns (MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, Trust Wallet, Rainbow)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the entry point for a beginner-facing program: contrasts "bank account you don't control" with "wallet you fully control," then routes beginners to a specific first wallet based on their goal.
adjacent_meanings: custodial wallets (e.g., exchange-held funds) as the implicit contrast case, though not directly named in this article
hardware/cold wallets as a more security-hardened but higher-friction alternative (referenced only via the "related" article link, not explained here)
important_distinctions: public address (safe to share) vs secret/seed phrase (never share, full access)
self-custody (you hold the keys) vs custodial (a company holds them for you)
tensions: beginner-friendliness vs the real, unforgiving risk of an irrecoverable loss if the seed phrase is lost or leaked
data.risks_of_flattening: The guide's ranked "easiest for beginners" framing risks understating that all four wallets carry the same fundamental self-custody risk (irreversible loss on seed-phrase compromise) — ease-of-setup is not the same axis as security posture, and the article does not clearly distinguish the two.

data.title: Mempool (transaction waiting room)
data.short_description: The pool of unconfirmed transactions a blockchain node holds after a transaction is broadcast but before it is included in a block; higher fees generally earn priority inclusion in the next block.
source_traditions: bitcoin/ethereum node-software terminology
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced in how-transactions-work.md as step 3 ("Broadcasting") of the seven-step transaction journey, framed as a "waiting room" for not-yet-confirmed transactions.
adjacent_meanings: block
gas-fee-priority
important_distinctions: Being in the mempool is not the same as being confirmed — a transaction can sit in the mempool indefinitely (or be dropped) if fees are too low relative to network demand.
tensions: "Higher fees = priority seating" framing simplifies real fee-market dynamics (fee estimation, replace-by-fee, congestion spikes).
data.risks_of_flattening: The "bus with limited seats" analogy is a helpful beginner mental model but does not capture that mempool contents differ across nodes (each node's mempool is a local, not globally synchronized, view).

data.title: Three kinds of trust: competence, integrity, benevolence
data.short_description: A three-part model for the trust a community finance system needs: competence trust ("can you do what you say?"), integrity trust ("will you do what you said?", built through consistency), and benevolence trust ("do you care about me?", built by listening and helping without keeping score).
source_traditions: organizational-trust research (the competence/integrity/benevolence typology is a standard framing in trust literature, applied here to community finance specifically)
Francis Fukuyama's social-trust-and-cooperation thesis (cited elsewhere in the same article)
data.toolkit_usage: Used to argue that community finance needs all three at once: competence to manage funds, integrity to follow the rules, and benevolence so members believe the rules protect them rather than trap them. Each type is paired with a concrete building practice (e.g. "I am still learning this" earning more competence-trust than overclaiming).
adjacent_meanings: 'trust' used loosely as a single undifferentiated feeling, without the article's three-part decomposition
important_distinctions: competence trust is about ability, integrity trust is about kept promises, benevolence trust is about care for the other person's interests — the article treats these as separable and each independently buildable.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "trust" as one thing collapses the article's practical distinction between three different failure modes (incompetence, unreliability, self-interest) that require different remedies.

data.title: Gathering Formats for Community Building
data.short_description: A typology of gathering containers (informal, educational, decision-making, celebration) chosen deliberately to match a community's developmental stage, on the premise that the format shapes the outcome more than the topic does.
source_traditions: Priya Parker's The Art of Gathering (intentional gathering design)
agile retrospective practice — Norm Kerth's Project Retrospectives (2001) and its Prime Directive
sociocracy's consent-based decision-making (Sociocracy For All)
The World Café (Juanita Brown) and Open Space Technology (Harrison Owen) — participant-driven large-group formats
Liberating Structures — a menu of facilitation microstructures
data.toolkit_usage: Applied as a stage-matched menu (pre-formation, early formation, active operations, growth, renewal) for regen local-node organizers, with a sustainability constraint (weekly/monthly/quarterly rhythm) layered on top of the format choice.
adjacent_meanings: facilitation microstructures (Liberating Structures) as a lighter-weight adjacent toolkit to full gathering formats
consent-based decision-making as both an offline meeting practice and a rehearsal for on-chain governance tools (Snapshot, multisig)
important_distinctions: consent (no remaining objections — Does anyone object / Can you live with this) vs consensus (unanimous enthusiasm)
a retrospective (structured look-back on a project/period) vs a town hall (forward-looking proposal decision)
informal relationship-building gatherings (foundation layer) vs formal decision-making gatherings (built on top of that foundation)
tensions: the guide's own warning against turning a relationship-building meal into a decision-making meeting ("while we're all here, let's just quickly...")
predictability/rhythm vs the temptation to run an ambitious, high-effort calendar
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting a five-stage node lifecycle (pre-formation to renewal) as a clean linear progression risks flattening the reality that real communities cycle between stages non-linearly (e.g., renewal needs can arise mid-"active operations"); the guide does gesture at this by listing renewal as its own recurring stage rather than a one-time end point.

data.title: Smart Contract
data.short_description: A small program that lives on a blockchain network and executes automatically when its conditions are met — no salesperson, no negotiation, no third party enforcing the rules.
source_traditions: Ethereum developer documentation (ethereum.org)
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced via a vending-machine metaphor (pick item → see price → insert payment → machine verifies → item dispensed) to make the concept concrete for a non-technical audience, then applied to two regen scenarios: transparent community-garden fundraising (funds released only when members vote yes) and automatic crop insurance (payout triggered by external weather data via an oracle).
adjacent_meanings: DAO (a group that uses smart contracts to govern collective decisions)
oracle (a service that feeds real-world data to a smart contract)
important_distinctions: A smart contract enforces rules already agreed and coded — it does not decide the rules or verify real-world facts on its own; the crop-insurance example still depends on trusted weather data reaching the contract.
tensions: "The code does what it was programmed to do" is reassuring but also the limit: a bug or a bad initial rule is enforced just as faithfully as a good one.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing "smart contract" to just "automatic payment" erases the point the article is making — that the interesting part is removing a trusted middleman for a *class* of coordination problems (fundraising, voting, conditional payouts), not any single payment.

data.title: Digital Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (dMRV)
data.short_description: Using phones/computers to measure what happened (e.g. trees planted), report that information, and verify it is true — the "digital" version of traditional MRV (Measurement, Reporting, Verification) used in environmental/carbon programs.
source_traditions: traditional MRV frameworks used in carbon markets and environmental programs (implied by the article's "many carbon markets... now require verified impact data")
participatory/community-based monitoring practice
mobile data-collection tooling (KoboToolbox, ODK) developed for humanitarian/development-sector fieldwork
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced in this article as an accessible, low-barrier practice for grassroots regenerative-project practitioners (tree planting, water conservation, grazing-land recovery), explicitly framed as something achievable with a basic smartphone rather than expensive equipment.
adjacent_meanings: dMRV as a formal carbon-credit-issuance requirement (heavier-weight, standards-body usage, referenced but not detailed in this beginner article)
dMRV as informal community impact-storytelling (this article's actual framing — "you become the storytellers of your own impact")
important_distinctions: measurement-vs-reporting-vs-verification — the article is careful to define these as three distinct steps, not synonyms: counting/recording, sharing the information, and proving it is true respectively.

automated-vs-human-verification — the article names both satellite imagery (automated) and human verifiers as valid verification paths, often used together (e.g. the grazing-land example uses both community observation and satellite confirmation).
tensions: simple-community-level-practice vs formal-carbon-market-requirements — the article bridges a low-barrier practice to a high-stakes use case (carbon market access) without fully addressing the gap between informal photo-logging and the rigor formal carbon registries require.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "took some photos with a phone" as equivalent to formal, registry-grade dMRV flattens a real rigor gap; the article's own framing (start simple, build the habit, connect with practitioner networks) reads as a beginner on-ramp toward more rigorous dMRV, not a claim that phone photos alone satisfy carbon-market verification standards.

data.title: Institutional Memory (for community nodes)
data.short_description: Durable, documented knowledge (decisions, processes, history) that survives personnel changes, so a community "becomes more than the sum of its current members" and doesn't lose knowledge every time someone leaves.
source_traditions: organizational-memory theory (broader management/knowledge-management field)
the Greenpill Local Regen Guide (named directly in the article as emphasizing that communities need to "remember what they have learned")
open-source project documentation culture (GitHub/GitBook practices)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as this article's central justification for documentation practice — framed specifically for Local Node communities (per ReFi DAO's Local Nodes model) rather than generic corporate knowledge management, with East Africa-specific tool-accessibility framing (basic smartphones, data/WiFi access).
adjacent_meanings: institutional memory as formal records-management practice (broader, more bureaucratic usage)
institutional memory as informal oral tradition passed between members (the implicit "before" state this article is trying to move nodes away from)
important_distinctions: documentation-vs-institutional-memory — documentation is the mechanism; institutional memory is the outcome. The article is explicit that undocumented knowledge "walks out the door when people leave," making documentation the necessary but not sufficient condition (it must also be maintained, per the article's "Maintaining Documentation Over Time" section).
tensions: documentation-effort-now vs benefit-realized-later — institutional memory's value is often invisible until a key person leaves or a dispute needs resolving, making it easy to deprioritize versus urgent day-to-day work.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "we have a wiki" as equivalent to having institutional memory flattens the article's explicit warning that outdated, unowned documentation "can actually cause harm" — the memory has to stay current and owned, not merely exist.

data.title: One job per event (educational / social / working / celebration)
data.short_description: A design constraint for community events: give each gathering exactly one of four jobs — educational (teach one thing), social (build relationships, no agenda), working (make concrete progress together), or celebration (mark a win, thank contributors) — rather than trying to do all of them in one evening.
data.toolkit_usage: Structures the article's five-phase event-planning process; "define the job" is phase one, and the article argues social and working events are the most underrated for a young node (education attracts strangers, relationships and shared output make them stay).
adjacent_meanings: Priya Parker–style intentional gathering design (purpose-first event framing, referenced by name in a sibling article on gathering patterns rather than this one)
important_distinctions: "The single biggest mistake is asking one event to do everything" — the article explicitly contrasts this against combining teaching, relationship-deepening, decision-making, and celebration in one event.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a general event-facilitation heuristic, not attributed to a specific tradition or community.

data.title: Local Node (regen network chapter)
data.short_description: A small, place-based chapter of a wider regenerative network that runs its own projects and coordination — the article's central unit of analysis for where founding pitfalls occur.
data.toolkit_usage: Used throughout common-pitfalls.md as the thing being founded/stewarded; contrasted against "the wider network" (e.g. Greenpill Network, Regen Coordination Hub) it connects to without being absorbed by.
adjacent_meanings: chapter (Greenpill's term for the same unit)
DAO (a local node may or may not formalize as one)
important_distinctions: a local node is autonomous-yet-connected, distinct from both full isolation and full absorption into a parent network
tensions: autonomy vs shared-learning
technology-first vs relationships-first founding
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "local node" as synonymous with "DAO" erases that most founding failures in the article are social/organizational, not technical.

data.title: Flat vs Hierarchical Organizational Structure
data.short_description: A contrast between pyramid-shaped organizations (departments, managers, executives, decisions flowing top-down) and flat, peer-coordinated structures where contributors take on roles by interest and capability rather than job title.
source_traditions: 20th-century theory of the firm (organizational hierarchy as a response to coordination-cost problems)
cooperative and associational governance (East African cooperatives cited in the article as a comparison point)
DAO/blockchain-native peer coordination
data.toolkit_usage: Used in this article as the structural half of the DAO-vs-traditional-firm comparison, paired with the decision-making and capital-formation dimensions, and connected to the observation that traditional companies are geographically limited while DAOs are not.
adjacent_meanings: flatness as an absence of formal titles (this article's framing)
flatness as an absence of any power differential (a stronger, contested claim the article does not make)
important_distinctions: flat-structure-vs-actual-power-distribution — the article itself cautions elsewhere (token concentration) that a flat org chart does not guarantee flat power; formal hierarchy and informal concentration are different things.

even-democratic-traditional-orgs-can-drift — the article notes that "even organizations founded on democratic principles can drift toward concentrated control over time," applying this critique to cooperatives, not only corporations.
tensions: flexibility-and-self-direction (flat) vs need-for-self-direction-without- management-support — flatness "creates flexibility but also requires self-direction," per the article.
data.risks_of_flattening: Assuming "flat" automatically means "equal" erases the article's own later caution about token concentration recreating centralized control inside a nominally flat structure.

data.title: Review boundary (consequence-based content tiering)
data.short_description: A written rule sorting knowledge-commons content into tiers by how much damage a wrong or misleading entry does if unchallenged (ephemeral/ personal → working/shared → canonical/load-bearing), with the human review gate applied only where consequence is high.
source_traditions: SuperBenefit Knowledge Garden's raw-notes/working-docs/refined-artifacts tiering
Elinor Ostrom's commons-governance design principles (clear boundaries, locally-made rules)
Git/pull-request code-review practice
data.toolkit_usage: The organizing idea of human-review-boundaries.md — proposed as the mechanism that lets a knowledge commons stay both open to contribution and trustworthy for load-bearing claims.
adjacent_meanings: review-and-maturity-k1-state-model
source-system-stewardship
important_distinctions: Sort by "the claim the content makes," not by length or authorship — a two-line recorded decision is load-bearing (canonical); a forty-page brainstorm is ephemeral.
A review boundary must be legible (written down, findable by a stranger) — an unwritten habit in one steward's head is not a boundary.
tensions: Cheap-to-pass reviewer checklists vs. the risk that a shrunk review becomes a rubber stamp.
data.risks_of_flattening: Framing this as a settled three-tier model risks obscuring that the right number and definition of tiers is genuinely team-specific — the article itself says the first boundary drawn "will be wrong" and must be revisited.

data.title: Community Readiness Model (nine-stage readiness assessment)
data.short_description: A nine-stage framework (from "no awareness" through "preplanning," "preparation," "initiation," to "community ownership") for assessing how ready a community actually is to take on a new initiative, developed for public health work and applied here to launching a local ReFi node.
source_traditions: Tri-Ethnic Center for Prevention Research, Colorado State University (public health readiness research)
adrienne maree brown's "emergent strategy" (complex systems developing through experimentation and relationship, not master plans)
data.toolkit_usage: Used in is-community-ready.md to set an honest launch threshold ("stage 5, preparation": leadership emerged, active planning, people mobilizing) below which a node is being pushed onto a community that hasn't decided it wants one.
adjacent_meanings: local-node-refi
emergent-strategy
important_distinctions: "Interested" is distinguished from "ready" — the article insists on 5-7 people who are *already showing up*, not people who might join.
Readiness is a stage on a spectrum, not a binary yes/no gate.
tensions: Wanting to talk a community out of premature launch vs. not gatekeeping genuine grassroots energy that's simply framed informally ("Web3 is interesting" vs. a felt shared problem).
data.risks_of_flattening: A model built for public-health behavior change is applied here to financial-system adoption without validating that the same nine stages transfer cleanly; the article itself only claims it "travels well," not that it was validated for this context.

data.title: Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake
data.short_description: The two dominant consensus mechanisms blockchains use to agree on the record book, with very different energy footprints — the article uses this distinction to give a precise (not hand-wavy) answer to "is crypto bad for the environment."
data.toolkit_usage: Used in common-concerns.md to explain why Bitcoin (proof of work, ~140-175 TWh/year per Cambridge CBECI) and Ethereum/Celo (proof of stake, ~99.95% less energy after Ethereum's 2022 "Merge") cannot be answered with one blanket environmental verdict.
adjacent_meanings: mining (the proof-of-work compute race)
staking (the proof-of-stake deposit-and-follow-rules model)
important_distinctions: the network/consensus method, not 'crypto' as a category, determines energy footprint
tensions: security-via-energy-expenditure (PoW) vs security-via-economic-stake (PoS)
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "crypto" as a single monolithic energy story erases the real, large difference between individual networks' designs.

data.title: Cryptocurrency, Blockchain, and Decentralisation
data.short_description: Money that exists only as digital records, moved directly between people via a shared, tamper-resistant ledger (blockchain) copied across many computers, with no single bank, company, or government running the system (decentralisation).
source_traditions: Bitcoin (2009), the first cryptocurrency, as the article's origin point
mutual-credit / community-currency traditions (the article's explicit "digital version of mutual credit" framing for the Sarafu Network)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the plain-language on-ramp article for readers with no prior crypto exposure, translating blockchain/decentralisation into a "shared lending notebook" analogy drawn from seed-library practice.
adjacent_meanings: a coin (native money of its own chain, e.g. Bitcoin, ether) vs a token (built atop an existing chain for a specific purpose)
proof of work vs proof of stake as different ways a blockchain achieves that shared, tamper-resistant record
important_distinctions: owning cryptocurrency means owning a key that moves a record, not owning a physical thing (the article's core reframing)
community-set rules (what a token represents) vs blockchain-provided honesty (the ledger just keeps the count straight)
tensions: the article's own honest framing (you almost certainly don't need crypto) vs four specific cases where it is presented as genuinely useful
data.risks_of_flattening: Framing decentralisation via the "farmers' market without a central boss" analogy risks understating the real infrastructure, expertise, and governance that blockchains still require (node operators, protocol developers, validator/miner economics) — the article simplifies for a first-time audience rather than engaging this.

data.title: NFT as verifiable ownership record (beyond the art/collectible use case)
data.short_description: An NFT (non-fungible token) is a blockchain record asserting unique-item ownership. The article's core reframe: the underlying capability isn't "digital art" — it's permanent, tamper-resistant, instantly-verifiable proof of ownership or credential, which generalizes to gaming assets, credentials, property, supply-chain provenance, tickets, and music rights.
source_traditions: Ethereum NFT standard (ethereum.org NFT explainer, cited in article references)
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article as the unifying concept behind six otherwise-unrelated application domains (gaming, credentials, real estate, supply chains, ticketing, music).
adjacent_meanings: Digital collectible / profile-picture NFT (the "hype" use case the article explicitly sets aside)
Verifiable credential / on-chain attestation (overlapping but distinct — see onchain-attestations entry)
Fractional ownership token (property/asset divided into tradeable shares)
important_distinctions: "An NFT is a blockchain record of ownership for a unique digital item" — the article is explicit that the ownership-record function, not the image/media attached to it, is what generalizes beyond art.

NFT credentials vs. on-chain attestations: the article treats blockchain diplomas/certifications as an NFT use case, while a sibling article (onchain-attestations) treats attestations as a related but separate primitive — worth reconciling in ontology review.
tensions: Player/creator value capture (gaming, music) vs. platform/marketplace capture — the article raises this without resolving it.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged as high-risk; article is general-audience education, not a claim about a specific community or person.

data.title: Distributed Leadership
data.short_description: Leadership where multiple people hold leadership responsibilities and power flows contextually, rather than concentrating in one founder or "heroic leader."
source_traditions: organizing/community-organizing training traditions (cited: "Organizing for America training materials") cooperative leadership development practice

East African / Somaliland relational-authority traditions (clan elders, women's group leaders, mosque committee members, trading network coordinators) named explicitly as a cultural foundation to build on rather than replace
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned as the resolution to the article's "leadership paradox" — not less leadership, but a different kind, distributed across roles and people so no single point of failure exists.
adjacent_meanings: the "founder trap" (single-founder model this concept is defined against)
shared/rotating leadership (a specific structural technique, see role rotation)
important_distinctions: distributed leadership ≠ no leadership — the article is explicit that "too little leadership and nothing gets done"; the goal is distribution, not absence
tensions: the article imports Western organizing-training language ("Organizing for America") for a technique it then explicitly grounds in existing East African/Somaliland relational authority — worth watching whether the framing privileges the imported vocabulary over the local one
data.risks_of_flattening: "Distributed leadership" as a slogan can mask real power concentration if roles are distributed on paper but one person retains informal veto — the article's own "Mistake 4: Concentrating Power" section names this risk directly.

data.title: Nested Leadership / Leadership Pathway
data.short_description: A layered leadership structure (core team, active members, general members) matched to a five-stage individual pathway (Observer, Contributor, Emerging Leader, Established Leader, Elder) that lets people move between commitment levels in both directions.
source_traditions: cooperative/nonprofit board-and-membership tiering practice
apprenticeship / mentorship models of skill progression
data.toolkit_usage: Offered as one of three distribution structures (with role rotation and federated structure) and paired with the five-stage pathway so a community can see both its current leadership layers and each individual's likely trajectory through them.
adjacent_meanings: role rotation (a technique for developing many leaders, not a tiering structure)
federated structure (domain-based, not commitment-based, division of leadership)
important_distinctions: nested leadership tiers (core/active/general, by commitment) ≠ pathway stages (Observer→Elder, by development) — the article presents both as complementary but they are two different axes (structural layer vs. individual growth)
tensions: the article states "not everyone will move through all stages, and that is fine" — in tension with the pathway's implicit ladder framing, which could read as prescribing advancement as the default good outcome
data.risks_of_flattening: A five-stage naming (Observer/Contributor/Emerging/Established/Elder) risks becoming a status hierarchy in practice even when the article's intent is descriptive, not a rank to climb — communities adopting this language should watch for that drift.

data.title: Claim-Evidence Discipline
data.short_description: Keeping the assertion, the source for it, the interpretation, and the uncertainty as distinct, separately reviewable things, so a reviewer can verify a page's factual claims rather than just admiring its prose.
source_traditions: the Regen Toolkit / Regen Knowledge Commons's own claim-evidence discipline (named directly in the article as "the Regen docs call this claim-evidence discipline")
Wikipedia's Good Article citation and verifiability standards
academic citation practice (claims requiring inline, checkable sources)
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned in this article as the discipline that makes a commons trustworthy over time, operationalized via a reviewer "spot-check" — pulling a sample of citations and confirming each source actually supports the sentence it's attached to, mirroring Wikipedia's Good Article process.
adjacent_meanings: claim-evidence separation as a formal knowledge-schema pattern (this toolkit's own claim-evidence schema/object type)
claim-evidence separation as an informal editorial habit (this article's practical framing — "pull three citations and verify")
important_distinctions: well-written-vs-reviewed — the article's central distinction: prose quality and factual accuracy are separate axes, and claim-evidence discipline is specifically how you check the second one.
full-citation-audit-vs-spot-check — the article recommends a sampling spot-check (a few citations, not every one) as the practical, sustainable version of full verification.
tensions: reviewer-time-cost vs thoroughness — a full citation audit of every claim would be prohibitively slow for small teams; the spot-check is an explicit trade-off the article endorses rather than treats as a compromise.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "it has a citation" as equivalent to "it has been verified" flattens the article's whole point — a citation that doesn't actually support its attached sentence is exactly the failure mode the spot-check step exists to catch.

data.title: Seed Phrase (BIP39 / HD Derivation)
data.short_description: A 12- or 24-word mnemonic, generated per the BIP39 standard from a random number and a fixed 2,048-word list, that acts as the master backup for a wallet's private keys and addresses across every BIP39-compatible chain and wallet app.
source_traditions: BIP39 (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39) — the cross-wallet standard defining the wordlist and phrase-generation/checksum rules.
Hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet derivation — the design that lets one phrase regenerate every private key and address beneath it.
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article as the foundational self-custody concept: back up the phrase once, and it can rebuild every key/address on every chain that follows the standard.
adjacent_meanings: Secret Recovery Phrase (MetaMask's term)
mnemonic phrase
important_distinctions: Seed phrase vs private key vs address: the article is explicit that the chain runs phrase -> private keys -> addresses; the phrase is the single backup point for all of them, not a stand-in for a private key.
12-word (128-bit entropy) vs 24-word (256-bit entropy) phrases — both considered unguessable; 24 words framed as a preference for larger treasuries/long-term holdings, not a security requirement.
tensions: One phrase controlling many chains is simultaneously the feature (no per-chain backups) and the risk (single point of compromise for everything at once).
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "seed phrase" as interchangeable with "password" undersells that there is no reset mechanism at all — the article stresses this is a categorical difference from conventional account recovery.

data.title: Peer-to-peer (P2P) crypto exchange with escrow
data.short_description: A way to buy crypto directly from another person rather than a company: the platform locks the seller's crypto in escrow, the buyer pays the seller directly (bank transfer, PayPal, etc.), and escrow releases the crypto only after the buyer confirms payment.
source_traditions: classifieds-marketplace-model (Craigslist-style listings)
escrow practice from traditional high-value in-person transactions
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in how-to-get-crypto.md as "Way 2" of acquiring crypto, for people who would rather not hand ID to a centralized exchange.
adjacent_meanings: centralized-exchange
non-custodial-wallet
important_distinctions: The platform's escrow is the safety mechanism — a seller asking to be paid "directly to skip the fee" bypasses escrow entirely and is explicitly flagged in the source article as the scam pattern to walk away from.
tensions: Privacy/no-ID-check appeal vs. reduced recourse if a counterparty defrauds outside the escrow flow.
data.risks_of_flattening: Naming specific platforms (LocalCoinSwap, Bisq) risks staleness — the source article itself notes that Paxful, "the platform most older guides still recommend," wound down by 1 November 2025.

data.title: ROSCA (Rotating Savings and Credit Association)
data.short_description: A savings arrangement where members pool money on a recurring basis and take turns receiving the full pot; used in the article to explain and legitimate the "member contributions" funding model for regen nodes.
source_traditions: Pre-crypto community savings-circle traditions, described in the article as having "worked in communities worldwide for generations, long before crypto" (e.g. tandas, susus, chit funds, hui — not individually named in the source article)
data.toolkit_usage: Cited as the real-world precedent that makes a node's small recurring member-contribution model ("give what you can," $0-20/month) feel familiar and legitimate rather than a crypto-native invention.
adjacent_meanings: Cooperative membership dues (a related but distinct, non-rotating funding pattern)
Crypto-native "streaming" contributions (e.g. Superfluid-based recurring donations described elsewhere on the site) — same cadence idea, different mechanism
important_distinctions: A ROSCA rotates the full pooled amount to one member at a time; a node's "member contributions" model described in this article does not rotate payouts to members — it pools dues to fund the node itself. The article invokes ROSCA as a legitimating analogy, not an exact structural match.
tensions: Using ROSCA as a precedent risks implying more structural similarity to the node's funding model than actually exists (see distinction above).
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "ROSCA" as a single, universal pattern flattens real regional and cultural variation (tandas, susus, chit funds, hui, etc. differ in rules around trust, default risk, and payout order) that the source article does not get into.

data.title: Quadratic Funding (QF)
data.short_description: A matching system where the number of people who back a project matters more than how much each one gives — the match is calculated by taking the square root of every contribution, summing those roots, then squaring the total, so a hundred people giving $5 pulls far more matching money than one person giving $500.
source_traditions: Gitcoin (the platform most associated with running QF rounds at scale, per the article)
data.toolkit_usage: Used to explain why, for a local node in a QF round, "the job isn't only to impress a panel — it's to turn out a lot of real people," reframing grant-proposal-writing as a community-organizing task rather than a persuasive-writing task.
adjacent_meanings: prospective grants (a grant category QF rounds typically fall under)
retroactive public goods funding (the alternative grant category, distinct from QF)
important_distinctions: Breadth of support vs. depth of support — QF is explicitly designed to compress the influence of a few large donors relative to many small ones.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating QF as just "a matching pool" misses the article's actual point — the mechanism structurally rewards community-organizing effort (turning out donors), not just proposal quality.

data.title: Onboarding as trellis, not funnel
data.short_description: A reframe of member onboarding: a marketing "funnel" treats newcomers as throughput to be converted; a "trellis" is a pre-built structure (a known first-week path, a buddy, a graduation sequence) that's already in place before a newcomer arrives, so integration doesn't depend on the steward's personal, one-off effort each time.
data.toolkit_usage: Framing device for the whole article: every subsequent recommendation (buddy system, first-week structure, role graduation) is presented as a plank of "the trellis."
adjacent_meanings: Marketing/sales funnel (the framing explicitly rejected as a model for community work)
ReFi DAO's Seed / Sapling / Canopy node-maturity model (a parallel growth metaphor cited in the same article)
important_distinctions: "A funnel treats people as throughput. A community is a garden" — the article is explicit that the metaphor shift is meant to change steward behavior, not just language.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a general community-management framing device, not a claim about a specific person or tradition.

data.title: Seed / Sapling / Canopy local-node maturity model
data.short_description: A three-stage growth model for local (place-based) regenerative-finance nodes: a Seed node is still building its core team; a Sapling has active engagement and real projects; a Canopy node is mature enough to "provide shelter and support" to other nodes. New members are framed as "seedlings" that the onboarding system helps grow.
source_traditions: ReFi DAO Local Node Incubator, Beta Cohort Retrospective
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article both as a description of node-level maturity and as a template readers are told to "map your node against" in the closing exercise.
adjacent_meanings: Deployment-readiness ladders (L0 idea → L6 field-informed pattern) used elsewhere in the toolkit's own K1 state model
important_distinctions: This is a node-level maturity model (about the whole local chapter), distinct from individual member-onboarding stages (observe → first contribution → real role) described in the same article.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — sourced to a named program retrospective, not attributed to an unnamed community or tradition.

provenance.surfaced_by: ReFi DAO Local Node Incubator, Beta Cohort Retrospective

data.title: Blockchain Trilemma
data.short_description: The observation that every blockchain must balance three competing priorities — scalability (can it handle growing transaction volumes?), security (how protected against attacks?), and decentralization (how widely distributed is network control?) — and that optimizing for one typically means compromising on another.
source_traditions: Widely used framing in Ethereum-ecosystem developer discourse; cited in the article via ethereum.org's chain-comparison material.
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the article's core decision lens: Ethereum L1 is positioned as prioritizing security/decentralization at the cost of scalability, Solana as prioritizing scalability at some cost to decentralization, and Layer 2s as a middle path that inherits Ethereum's security while improving scalability.
adjacent_meanings: EVM compatibility (a technical-portability property distinct from the trilemma tradeoffs)
important_distinctions: No single "best" chain — the article insists the right choice is use-case-dependent, not an objective ranking across the trilemma's three axes.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing the trilemma to "pick two" oversimplifies — the article shows real chains (Layer 2s, Polkadot/Cosmos) attempting partial mitigations (inherited security, interoperability) rather than a strict binary tradeoff.

data.title: Smart Contract
data.short_description: A program that lives at an address on a blockchain, self-executing its coded conditions with no company, government, or individual able to alter it once deployed.
source_traditions: Term coined by cryptographer Nick Szabo in 1994, decades before the technology existed to run one.
First implemented practically with Ethereum's 2015 launch, the first blockchain able to run general-purpose smart-contract programs.
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced via the market-stall analogy (two traders, a machine that releases payment automatically once delivery conditions are met) to ground an abstract concept in a concrete regional trade scenario.
adjacent_meanings: self-executing agreement
on-chain program
important_distinctions: Smart contract vs traditional contract: traditional contracts need lawyers/courts to enforce terms; a smart contract's code enforces the terms automatically.
Smart contract vs oracle: the contract's logic is the closed, deterministic part; the oracle is the separate service that feeds it real-world data.
tensions: Immutability protects against secret rule changes but also means bugs are permanent — "code is law" cuts both ways.
data.risks_of_flattening: Framing smart contracts as simply "automatic enforcement" risks eliding that most real-world regenerative use cases (verified conservation practice, verified shipment) depend entirely on the accuracy of an external oracle feed, not the contract logic itself.

data.title: Blockchain Oracle
data.short_description: A service that feeds external, real-world data (weather, shipment arrival, prices) into a blockchain so smart contracts — which are closed systems by design — can respond to real-world events.
source_traditions: Framed in the article as the answer to smart contracts' fundamental limitation: a blockchain cannot natively observe anything outside itself.
data.toolkit_usage: Used to explain why smart-contract failures in practice are often oracle failures (bad or manipulated data feeds), not contract-logic failures — directly relevant to regenerative-monitoring and supply-chain use cases.
adjacent_meanings: data feed
real-world bridge
important_distinctions: Oracle (external data provider) vs smart contract (the on-chain logic that consumes that data) — two separate trust surfaces.
tensions: Oracles reintroduce a trust/centralization point into an otherwise "trustless" system, which the article flags as "worth knowing before you trust a contract with real value."
data.risks_of_flattening: Discussing smart contracts without naming the oracle dependency risks implying blockchain systems are fully autonomous verifiers of physical reality, when they in fact inherit the reliability of whatever oracle feeds them.

data.title: Multisig (multi-signature wallet)
data.short_description: A wallet that requires a threshold number of designated signers (e.g. 3 of 5) to approve a transaction before it executes, so no single person can move community funds alone.
source_traditions: Bitcoin/Ethereum multisig smart-contract wallet design (Gnosis Safe/Safe as the dominant implementation)
traditional co-signer/dual-control practice in conventional finance and treasury management
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the foundational treasury-security primitive for any community holding funds — recommended even before any legal wrapper or formal governance exists (cross-referenced in local-node-model.md and local-nodes-and-daos.md, both ingested in this same batch).
adjacent_meanings: social recovery (a guardian-based alternative for individual wallets, not multi-party community funds)
timelock (a complementary delay mechanism, not a substitute for a signing threshold)
important_distinctions: multisig ≠ social recovery — multisig is for ongoing, legitimate multi-person access (community treasuries); social recovery is for an individual regaining access to their own single-owner wallet
threshold ≠ number of signers — "the threshold should be more than half the signers, but less than all of them," e.g. 3-of-5, not simply "have 5 signers"
tensions: the article's own "Common Mistakes" section flags a threshold set too low (2-of-3) as vulnerable, in tension with its earlier framing of 2-of-3 as "useful for small teams of 3 people" — the right threshold is genuinely context-dependent, not a single universal rule
data.risks_of_flattening: "3-of-5 is a sensible starting point" (repeated across this and sibling articles) can calcify into a default nobody re-examines — the article's own reasoning (geographic spread, role diversity, technical capacity of signers) matters more than the specific numbers and can vary a great deal by community size and risk.

data.title: DAO (Decentralised Autonomous Organisation)
data.short_description: A group that agrees its rules up front, writes them where everyone can see, and decides by votes anyone can verify — described in the article as "a far scarier name than the thing deserves."
source_traditions: Framed via the analogy of a seed-saving collective with its bylaws pinned to a noticeboard that can't be quietly edited and whose vote count can't be fudged.
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced to make transparent, verifiable group decision-making concrete for a non-technical audience, paired with Snapshot as the free tool to actually see the pattern in action.
adjacent_meanings: self-custody (holding funds directly rather than through a company)
token (a membership/voting marker, distinct from a speculative asset)
important_distinctions: Transparent process is not the same as good outcomes — the article is explicit that "a transparent vote on a bad idea is still a bad idea"; DAOs remove a specific suspicion (did the count really happen honestly?), not a group's culture problems.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing a DAO to "the jargon-y crypto version of a bylaws document" misses the article's actual selling point — verifiable, un-editable process, not novelty for its own sake.

data.title: Regenerative Finance (ReFi)
data.short_description: Takes DeFi's smart-contract machinery (no-gatekeeper lending, funding, exchange) and points it at ecological and social repair rather than pure financial return. The article's framing: DeFi asks "how do we make money?"; ReFi asks "how do we use money to heal soil, water, forests, and communities?"
source_traditions: DeFi (decentralized finance) — ReFi is explicitly framed as DeFi's tools redirected, not a separate technology stack
data.toolkit_usage: Central concept of the article; illustrated through three named real projects (Regen Network ecocredits, Gitcoin quadratic funding, Grassroots Economics Sarafu) rather than defined abstractly.
adjacent_meanings: TradFi (traditional finance — the centralized baseline ReFi/DeFi are contrasted against)
Quadratic funding (a specific ReFi-adjacent mechanism, not synonymous with ReFi as a whole)
