important_distinctions: "ReFi is young, and parts of it are still messy. But unlike TradFi and DeFi, regeneration is the point, not a side effect someone hopes for" — the article distinguishes ReFi from DeFi by stated intent/purpose, not by underlying technology.
tensions: "Decentralised is a spectrum, not a switch" — the article flags that many DeFi/ReFi apps still depend on a small founding team or one company's servers, complicating any clean centralized/decentralized binary.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — the article explicitly acknowledges ReFi's youth and messiness rather than overclaiming maturity.

data.title: Eight Forms of Capital
data.short_description: A framework naming eight forms of capital, financial, social, cultural, material, living, spiritual, experiential, and intellectual, used to argue that sending money alone doesn't grow the deep local roots that make regeneration last.
source_traditions: Ethan Roland and Gregory Landua (credited in the article as the framework's coiners)
data.toolkit_usage: Used to justify why a local node's "unglamorous translation work" (relationships, language, cultural context) matters beyond just moving funding — the node is framed as what grows the seven non-financial forms of capital.
adjacent_meanings: subsidiarity (the governance principle that assigns this work to the local level)
important_distinctions: Financial capital vs. the other seven — the article's point is specifically that Greenpill-style regen communities lean on this framework to avoid conflating "funded" with "regenerating."
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating the eight forms of capital as a checklist to tick off risks missing the article's actual point — that these forms are built through sustained local relationship-work, not through a program or a grant line item.

data.title: Building in public (as a community practice)
data.short_description: Sharing progress, failures, and learnings openly as you build rather than only announcing finished results — for local nodes, this means posting updates, sharing decisions, and being transparent about challenges as they happen.
source_traditions: indie-hacker / startup "build in public" culture (originating outside web3, adopted broadly by crypto-native builders)
web3/DAO transparency norms
data.toolkit_usage: Applied in the article specifically to local regen nodes: the "journey IS the content," and public commitments and shared struggles are framed as tools for accountability and trust, not just marketing.
adjacent_meanings: marketing/growth-hacking use of "build in public" (purely promotional cadence, without the accountability/trust framing this article emphasizes)
important_distinctions: the article distinguishes vague positivity ("Things are going great!") from specific, falsifiable updates ("We held our first event with 12 attendees"), naming specificity as a best practice in its own right.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing "building in public" to a content/marketing tactic misses the article's framing of it as an accountability and trust mechanism — public commitments are described as "harder to abandon," which is a governance effect, not just a communications one.

data.title: Onchain Donation Transparency
data.short_description: Publishing blockchain-verifiable proof of how donated crypto funds are used — e.g. a nonprofit publishing its wallet address so donors can trace fund flows directly, without relying solely on the organization's own reporting.
source_traditions: traditional nonprofit financial-transparency/annual-reporting practice
blockchain's public-ledger property (any transaction is traceable by design)
crypto-philanthropy platforms and communities (the article's cited source, CryptoAltruists Web3 Impact Toolkit)
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned in this article as a differentiator crypto donors specifically value, tied to the donor-motivation category "transparency" and offered as a concrete stewardship action nonprofits can take (publish a wallet address, share transaction IDs in thank-yous).
adjacent_meanings: onchain transparency as a technical property of any public blockchain (baseline, not donor-facing)
onchain transparency as a deliberate donor-relations practice (this article's framing — actively surfacing that traceability to donors)
important_distinctions: technically-traceable-vs-actively-communicated — a transaction being technically traceable on a public ledger is different from a nonprofit actively publishing and explaining that trace to donors; the article's recommendation is specifically about the latter, more deliberate practice.
tensions: donor-trust-benefit vs organizational-financial-privacy — publishing a wallet address exposes an organization's full transaction history (including amounts and counterparties) publicly and permanently, a trade-off this short article does not explore in depth.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting onchain transparency as a purely additive trust-building feature flattens the real trade-off (permanent public exposure of an organization's full financial activity) that the article's brevity does not surface.

data.title: Crypto donation platform selection checklist
data.short_description: The article's five-factor evaluation framework for choosing among crypto donation platforms — fees, supported cryptocurrencies, instant stablecoin conversion, integration with existing donor-management systems, and setup support.
data.toolkit_usage: Given directly in crypto-donation-platforms.md as "What to Look For" ahead of the getting-started steps (create account, verify 501(c)(3) status, customize page, publish, promote).
adjacent_meanings: vendor-selection-checklist (a generic org-tooling pattern this specializes for crypto)
important_distinctions: these are user-facing selection criteria, not the compliance/KYC criteria covered in the sibling compliance-legal.md article
tensions: low-fees vs full-feature-set-and-support
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting five bullet factors as sufficient understates real diligence needs (e.g. platform security history, insurance/custody model) not mentioned in the source article.

data.title: ReFi (Regenerative Finance)
data.short_description: Using web3 tools (tokens, DAOs, on-chain markets) to fund and coordinate environmental and social projects, such as carbon credits or conservation efforts.
source_traditions: regenerative economics / regenerative agriculture
DeFi (decentralized finance) tooling and mechanics
impact investing and carbon-market finance
data.toolkit_usage: Listed in the glossary's "R" section as one of ~80 beginner terms; the toolkit's own scope and name ("Regen Web3 Toolkit") is built directly on this term.
adjacent_meanings: regenerative agriculture (no web3/finance component)
carbon markets / voluntary carbon credits (may or may not use web3 rails)
important_distinctions: ReFi ≠ DeFi — DeFi is the financial-mechanics layer (lending, trading, staking); ReFi is a values/purpose layer that may or may not use DeFi primitives to fund ecological/social outcomes
tensions: "ReFi" is used both narrowly (on-chain carbon/biodiversity finance) and broadly (any web3-enabled community/mutual-aid economics) across the toolkit's own articles — this glossary entry gives only the broad, one-line version
data.risks_of_flattening: A one-sentence glossary definition ("using web3 tools to fund environmental and social projects") can read as if ReFi is inherently regenerative by virtue of using blockchain — the toolkit's own frame- language discipline (see docs/CSIS.md) cautions against exactly this conflation of "on-chain" with "regenerative."

data.title: Tokenomics
data.short_description: The economics of a cryptocurrency or token system — how many tokens exist, how they are distributed, and what incentives are built in.
source_traditions: mechanism design / game theory
traditional monetary economics (supply, inflation)
token engineering (post-2018 DeFi practice)
data.toolkit_usage: Defined in the glossary's "T" section alongside Token, Transaction Fee, and Treasury; underlies design choices covered elsewhere in the toolkit (e.g. local-currency design questions of unit, backing, and issuance).
adjacent_meanings: token design (the mechanics of a single token's rules)
monetary policy (the macro discipline tokenomics borrows from)
important_distinctions: Tokenomics ≠ Token — a token is the asset; tokenomics is the designed system of incentives, supply, and distribution around it
tensions: the glossary treats tokenomics as a neutral, technical discipline; elsewhere in web3 discourse "tokenomics" is often used to paper over extractive incentive design (Frame 1 language flagged in docs/CSIS.md)
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing tokenomics to "supply, distribution, incentives" omits the value judgments embedded in any incentive design — who benefits from a given distribution schedule is a governance question, not just an economics one.

data.title: Double-spend problem and the pre-Bitcoin proof-of-work lineage
data.short_description: The problem of preventing someone from spending the same unit of digital money twice without a trusted central bank to check balances — the central puzzle Bitcoin's 2008 whitepaper solved by having every participant keep a shared, proof-of-work-verified record of all transactions.
source_traditions: David Chaum's ecash (1983) — privacy-preserving digital money, still needed a central authority
Adam Back's hashcash (1997) — introduced proof-of-work (computers prove they expended energy)
Wei Dai's b-money (1998) — distributed ledger where everyone tracks everyone else's money, couldn't work without a central server
Nick Szabo's bit gold (1998) — digital tokens with real scarcity via proof-of-work, never launched
Hal Finney's RPOW (2004) — proved proof-of-work tokens could transfer between people
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article as the throughline connecting five prior attempts at digital cash to Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 whitepaper, which the article frames as solving the double-spend problem "without a bank" by having "everyone... keep a shared record of all transactions, verified through proof-of-work."
adjacent_meanings: byzantine fault tolerance (the general distributed-systems problem of reaching agreement despite unreliable/adversarial participants)
important_distinctions: each pioneer solved a piece (privacy, proof-of-work, distributed tracking, scarcity, transferability) but none combined all of them into a working, launched system before Bitcoin
data.risks_of_flattening: Crediting Bitcoin's whitepaper as a single point of invention erases the 30-year lineage of prior attempts the article itself documents — the innovation was combination and shipping, not any one novel primitive.

data.title: Liquid Delegation
data.short_description: A delegation model where members can delegate, re-delegate, or revoke their voting power at any time, and delegation can be transitive — Alice delegates to Bob, who delegates to Carol, so Alice's vote flows through Bob to Carol.
source_traditions: liquid democracy theory (named directly in the article's own sources list)
representative-vs-direct-democracy debates
DAO governance-tooling implementations of transitive delegation
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in this article as the most flexible of four delegation types (full, topic-based, liquid, time-limited), traded off against full delegation's simplicity and topic-based delegation's expertise-matching.
adjacent_meanings: liquid democracy as a national/political voting-reform proposal (broader usage, not DAO-specific)
liquid delegation as implemented in specific on-chain governance tooling (this article's DAO-specific framing)
important_distinctions: liquid-vs-full-delegation — full delegation is a single, static grant of all voting power to one delegate; liquid delegation allows continuous re-delegation and transitive chains.
liquid-vs-topic-based-delegation — topic-based splits delegation by subject area (finance, technical, community); liquid is about revocability and transitivity, and the two dimensions can combine.
tensions: flexibility-and-responsiveness vs complex-power-chains — the article names "can create complex power chains, requires sophisticated tooling" as liquid delegation's direct con.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating liquid delegation as strictly "more democratic" than full delegation flattens the article's own caution that transitive chains can obscure where power actually concentrates, making accountability harder to track even as flexibility increases.

data.title: Quadratic Voting
data.short_description: A voting mechanism where a member can cast multiple votes on an issue, but each additional vote costs exponentially more (tokens burned), creating diminishing returns that counter simple wealth-weighted dominance.
source_traditions: mechanism design / public-choice economics
Glen Weyl and Eric Posner's "Radical Markets" work (per the article's cited "Essays in Power" reference)
DAO governance experimentation (e.g. CityDAO)
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in this article as the second of five DAO governance models — positioned as the direct response to token-weighted voting's whale-dominance problem, at the cost of added conceptual and implementation complexity.
adjacent_meanings: quadratic voting as a governance mechanism (this article's usage)
quadratic funding as a related-but-distinct matching-funds mechanism (not covered in this article)
important_distinctions: quadratic-voting-vs-token-weighted-voting — quadratic voting still requires holding tokens to vote, it changes the cost curve of casting additional votes rather than removing the token requirement entirely.
tensions: fairer-representation vs harder-to-understand — the article names "requires user familiarity with the underlying mathematics" as a direct con.
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing quadratic voting only as "fairer" flattens that it is still a token-gated mechanism — it changes who wins among token holders, not whether non-token-holders get a voice.

data.title: DAO Voting Mechanisms
data.short_description: The family of mechanisms DAOs use to turn proposals into decisions — ranging from simple token-weighted quorum voting to quadratic voting, time-weighted conviction voting, prediction-market-based holographic consensus, small-group multi-sig approval, and gasless off-chain signature voting.
source_traditions: traditional deliberative-assembly quorum rules (the article's own "general assembly" analogy)
Gitcoin's quadratic funding mechanism design
Giveth's conviction voting implementation
prediction-market mechanism design (holographic consensus)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as a comparison menu for DAO operators, explicitly concluding that most mature DAOs layer multiple mechanisms rather than picking one.
adjacent_meanings: quorum voting as practiced in non-blockchain cooperative boards and community associations (the article notes Somaliland/East-Africa cooperative boards face the same low-active-participation dynamic, without naming a specific case or source)
important_distinctions: on-chain quorum/token voting (simple, plutocratic) vs quadratic voting (cost rises with the square of votes cast, dampening wealth dominance)
conviction voting (time-weighted, cannot be swung last-minute) vs holographic consensus (prediction-market-based proposal triage)
full-community voting vs multi-sig (small trusted group, fast but centralized)
tensions: decentralization ideal vs the practical need for fast multi-sig decisions on routine/emergency matters
manipulation-resistance (conviction voting, quadratic voting) vs added complexity and slower decisions
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting these six mechanisms as a tidy toolkit risks understating that each embeds different values about whose voice counts more (wealth, time-commitment, prediction-market savvy, or trusted-group membership) — the article does gesture at this ("depends on your community's values") but doesn't work through any single mechanism's failure modes in depth.

data.title: Digital Garden (seedling / budding / evergreen)
data.short_description: A living, linked collection of notes tended over time rather than published once, using openly-marked growth stages so readers can tell a rough sketch from a settled, maintained answer.
source_traditions: Mike Caulfield's 2015 talk "The Garden and the Stream," which contrasted the chronological "stream" of feeds/chat with the slowly-cultivated "garden" of linked, revisited knowledge
Maggie Appleton's digital-garden writing, which popularized the seedling (🌱) / budding (🌿) / evergreen (🌳) growth-stage convention
data.toolkit_usage: Used in this article as the organizing metaphor for community knowledge commons, paired with a concrete stack recommendation (Obsidian + Quartz + GitHub) and a named "gardener" role responsible for tending.
adjacent_meanings: wiki (typically filled once, less emphasis on revisiting/pruning)
document dump / shared drive ("a compost heap nobody turns")
important_distinctions: Garden ≠ document dump — the difference is three habits (linking over filing, openly-marked growth stages, active tending), not which tool is used
Stream ≠ garden — chat/feeds are chronological and ephemeral; a garden is linked and revisited
tensions: "growth stage" maturity marking (seedling/budding/evergreen) is a different vocabulary from this toolkit's own K1 maturity axis (raw/draft/candidate/reviewed/...) — both solve the same problem (letting readers trust the right things) but do not map 1:1
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating the seedling/budding/evergreen convention as just a labeling scheme misses its actual function: it is a permission structure that lets contributors publish before perfect, which is the harder cultural change than the labels themselves.

data.title: Verifiable Credentials vs Soulbound Tokens
data.short_description: Two credential formats doing the same underlying job (issuer-signed, independently verifiable proof of achievement) via different technical means — VCs as an open cross-platform data format, SBTs as non-transferable NFTs bound to the earning wallet.
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced together in credentials-certifications.md as "the most common standard right now" (VCs) and an alternative format readers might encounter (SBTs), both contrasted against a paper certificate that can be lost, copied, or is hard to verify remotely.
adjacent_meanings: open-badges (an older, still-active credentialing standard named alongside VCs/SBTs)
important_distinctions: an SBT's non-transferability is the point — it represents something about the holder, not something ownable/sellable, unlike a regular NFT
a VC is a data-format standard that can live on-chain or off-chain; an SBT is specifically an on-chain non-transferable token
tensions: non-transferability-proves-authenticity vs no-way-to-correct-or-revoke-a-mistaken-issuance-without-issuer-cooperation
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting VCs and SBTs as interchangeable "both do the same job" glosses over real differences in revocability, privacy (SBTs are visibly on-chain by default; VCs can be selectively disclosed), and infrastructure maturity.

data.title: Social Token
data.short_description: A community-specific token representing membership, access, or reputation, whose value derives primarily from its social context rather than a stand-alone utility function.
source_traditions: Community-building practice (per article frontmatter source)
data.toolkit_usage: Split into three types for local-node use: creator tokens (audience access/governance over a creator's direction), community tokens (membership, earned or purchased, used for governance/access/identity), and reputation tokens (non-transferable, contribution-history record — "a resume on-chain").
adjacent_meanings: creator token
community token
reputation token
important_distinctions: Social token vs utility token: a utility token's value comes from a defined function; a social token's value comes from the social context it exists in.
Reputation tokens are explicitly non-transferable, distinguishing them from tradeable creator/community tokens.
tensions: Community tokens can be "earned through contribution or purchased" — two very different legitimacy models for the same token type, unresolved in the source.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "social token" as one category flattens real differences in transferability, governance weight, and regulatory exposure between creator, community, and reputation tokens.

data.title: Web3 as addition, not replacement, to existing mission-driven work
data.short_description: A framing that positions web3 tooling as analogous to "your website" — a tool that supports existing work (community relationships, program delivery, physical presence) without replacing it. The recommended adoption pattern: identify a specific current pain point (fundraising, transparency, coordination, or community building), then try one small web3-native intervention rather than a wholesale rebuild.
data.toolkit_usage: The organizing idea of the whole article; every subsequent recommendation (pick one pain point, start small, keep what works) follows directly from this framing.
adjacent_meanings: "Tool, not strategy" adoption framing common in general digital-transformation guidance (not named in the article, but the same underlying pattern)
important_distinctions: "The goal is impact, not technology for its own sake" — the article is explicit that web3 adoption is instrumental to mission, not a goal in itself.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a general adoption-strategy framing, not attributed to a specific community or tradition. Note: this article is short (~380 words) and generic, with no named organizations, tools beyond a passing mention of Snapshot/POAP, or case studies — the concept-lineage here captures the article's full argument rather than a deeper tradition.

data.title: Community momentum flywheel and rhythm model
data.short_description: A self-reinforcing cycle (ship → celebrate → invite → onboard → empower → contribute → acknowledge → repeat) paired with predictable rhythms at weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual cadences, that keeps a local node's energy from fading after its initial launch excitement.
source_traditions: Greenpill Local Regen Guide (cited generically in the article's frontmatter sources)
general community-building and DAO-governance literature (cited generically, not by specific title)
East African community traditions the article names as existing precedent (saving circles, inter-clan coordination, post-jumu'ah community meals)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as a structural fix for the observation that "many nodes launch with enthusiasm, then fade... the culprit is rarely a lack of care, it's a lack of structure." The article explicitly asks organizers to channel existing community rhythms into regen finance work "in ways that feel natural, not foreign," rather than importing an unfamiliar cadence.
adjacent_meanings: generic "community engagement" growth-hacking frameworks (funnel-style, not necessarily rooted in local relational practice)
important_distinctions: the article treats "momentum" as distinct from "activity": momentum is meaningful, self-reinforcing activity, not just frequency of events.

"dips" (attendance drops, energy decreases) are explicitly named as normal and often seasonal (harvest season, exams, Ramadan), not a sign of failure — a distinction the article asks organizers to plan for rather than panic over.
tensions: the article's own claim that this rhythm model builds on "existing traditions rather than inventing new ones" is asserted at a general "East African contexts" level rather than sourced to a specific named community or community-authored account.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating this as a generic, portable "growth loop" framework risks stripping out the article's own framing that the model is meant to channel practices (saving circles, communal meals, rotational leadership) that specific communities already hold — presenting it as culturally neutral would misrepresent the source.

data.title: dMRV (Digital Measurement, Reporting, and Verification)
data.short_description: A system for turning real-world actions (e.g. planting a tree) into unchangeable, verifiable proof by recording photos, location, and other data on the blockchain — used to attract funding, demonstrate accountability, and prove contributions.
source_traditions: Named directly in the article as the term for programs like Silvi that prove tree planting and pay contributors for verified impact.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the third of three Ethereum use cases relevant to "Sarreya" program participants: photograph a planted tree, record its location, and submit through an app, creating permanent, verifiable proof of the contribution.
adjacent_meanings: oracle (dMRV data must ultimately be trusted/fed onto the chain by someone)
important_distinctions: dMRV proves that specific reported data was submitted and recorded immutably; it does not, on its own, independently verify the underlying real-world claim (e.g. that the tree survives) — this distinction is not made explicit in this particular article, unlike the more cautious framing given in "What Web3 Can and Can't Do."
tensions: This article presents dMRV/on-chain impact proof relatively uncritically compared to the toolkit's own "what-web3-can-cant-do" article, which names MRV/carbon claims as a high-risk area requiring oracles and human trust, not just recording data on-chain.
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing on-chain impact records as simply "permanent proof of your contribution" risks overstating what dMRV can guarantee — permanence of the record is not the same as verification of the underlying real-world fact.

data.title: Dimensions of inclusion (economic, technical, temporal, social, accessibility)
data.short_description: A five-dimension checklist for whether a community finance system actually welcomes diverse participants: can people with limited money, limited technical skill, limited time, different social backgrounds, and disabilities all participate?
source_traditions: community-organizing / accessibility-design practice
data.toolkit_usage: The organizing structure of inclusive-practices.md, used to walk through concrete design choices (sliding-scale fees, low-tech options, flexible meeting times, culturally appropriate spaces, physical/cognitive accessibility) dimension by dimension.
adjacent_meanings: accessibility-as-afterthought-anti-pattern
inclusion-as-tokenism-anti-pattern
important_distinctions: "Inclusion as tokenism" (diverse faces, unchanged power structures) is explicitly distinguished from true inclusion, defined as sharing power.
"Measuring participation" (headcounts) is distinguished from "measuring belonging" (do people feel valued, do they influence decisions, do they stay).
tensions: Designing multiple on-ramps and flexible formats for every dimension vs. the real coordination overhead of maintaining many parallel paths.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting the five dimensions as a checklist risks treating inclusion as a box to check rather than, as the article itself insists, "an ongoing practice" with "no destination where you have arrived."

data.title: Informal community savings mechanisms (chamas, iqqub, hawala)
data.short_description: Community-run informal savings and value-transfer systems named in inclusive-practices.md as long-standing alternatives to formal banking in East Africa and the Horn of Africa — Kenyan chamas (savings/investment groups), Ethiopian/Eritrean iqqub (rotating savings associations), and hawala (informal value-transfer networks).
source_traditions: East African and Horn of Africa community finance traditions
data.toolkit_usage: Cited in inclusive-practices.md's "Why Inclusion Matters" section as evidence that community-designed financial systems can serve people banks refuse, and as the bar a new community finance system should meet rather than replicate banking's exclusions.
adjacent_meanings: rotating-savings-and-credit-association-ROSCA
dimensions-of-inclusion-economic-technical-temporal-social-accessibility
important_distinctions: These are named as a category ("chamas in Kenya," "iqqub in Ethiopia and Eritrea," "hawala networks") without naming specific groups, operators, or communities — a general reference to known practice-types, not a documented case study.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article attributes these mechanisms to whole countries/regions in passing, secondary-source language, without naming a specific community, operator, or citation. Treating this as settled ethnographic/economic fact rather than a broad-strokes reference risks flattening genuinely diverse, locally-specific practices into a single toolkit talking point. See accompanying public-use-boundary.

data.title: Stablecoin
data.short_description: A crypto token engineered to hold a steady value, almost always pegged to one US dollar, via one of three backing designs: fiat-backed, crypto-backed (overcollateralised), or algorithmic.
source_traditions: Fiat-backed model: USDC (Circle) and USDT (Tether) — company-held dollar/short-term-bond reserves.
Crypto-backed model: DAI/Sky (rebranded from MakerDAO) and Liquity's BOLD — overcollateralised, transparent smart-contract-held reserves.
Algorithmic model: Terra (UST) and early Frax — code-only peg mechanisms with no real backing.
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced via a "seed that doesn't change variety in storage" analogy to explain why a stable-value token is practically useful for cross-border community payments and grant receipt.
adjacent_meanings: digital dollar
peg
important_distinctions: Fiat-backed (auditable, freezable) vs crypto-backed (transparent on-chain, overcollateralised, harder to freeze) vs algorithmic (unbacked, historically prone to collapse).
"Stable" means "usually," not "guaranteed" — small wobbles are normal; real depegs have happened even to fiat-backed coins (USDC, March 2023).
tensions: Regulated fiat-backed coins offer legal/audit assurance (reinforced by the 2025 GENIUS Act) but concentrate freeze power in one company; decentralised crypto-backed coins remove that single point of control but are harder for a newcomer to independently verify.
data.risks_of_flattening: Calling any of the three designs simply "stablecoins" without distinguishing backing mechanism flattens a real risk spectrum — from audited fiat reserves to a fully algorithmic peg, the latter of which (Terra/UST) collapsed to near zero in 2022.

data.title: Coordination-without-central-control tools (DAOs, quadratic voting, futarchy)
data.short_description: A family of decision-making mechanisms the article groups together as web3 alternatives to hierarchical organization: DAOs (community-vote governed orgs), quadratic voting (dampens wealth-weighted dominance), and futarchy (deciding via prediction markets).
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced together in coordination-transparency.md as evidence that "groups can make decisions together, even if they've never met," framed as the non-monetary appeal of web3 for regens.
adjacent_meanings: quadratic-funding (a related but distinct mechanism for allocating money, not votes)
important_distinctions: quadratic voting (decision weight) is distinct from quadratic funding (matching-fund allocation), though both use the same square-root mathematical dampening idea
futarchy (bet-driven decisions) is a much less-adopted, more experimental mechanism than DAOs or quadratic voting
tensions: decision-quality-in-theory vs low-real-world-adoption-of-futarchy-specifically
data.risks_of_flattening: Grouping DAOs, quadratic voting, and futarchy as equally mature options obscures that futarchy remains largely theoretical/experimental compared to the other two, which the source article does not distinguish.

data.title: Retroactive (public goods) funding
data.short_description: A funding model where contributors get paid for work they already did, even if funding wasn't arranged upfront, rather than the traditional grant-application-before-work pattern.
data.toolkit_usage: Listed in coordination-transparency.md under "New Economic Models / Credentialing" alongside POAPs and Gitcoin's peer-reviewed public-goods funding as an example of value capture becoming possible for people/ communities who previously could not access it upfront.
adjacent_meanings: grant-funding (the traditional, apply-before-you-build model this contrasts with)
poap (proof-of-attendance token, a related but distinct credentialing primitive named in the same section)
important_distinctions: retroactive funding rewards proven-useful past work; traditional grants fund proposed future work
tensions: rewards-what-already-proved-useful vs risk-of-underfunding-untested-new-ideas
data.risks_of_flattening: The article names the concept without specifying who judges "usefulness" retroactively or what mechanism (e.g. Optimism's RetroPGF rounds) actually implements it — worth expanding with a concrete implementation record later.

data.title: Legal Wrapper
data.short_description: A registered entity (co-op, nonprofit, LLC, or DAO-specific structure) that sits "around" a community group so the entity, not individual members, holds money, signs contracts, and absorbs liability.
source_traditions: traditional corporate/nonprofit/cooperative law
emerging DAO-specific legal-personality statutes (Wyoming DUNA, DAO LLC)
default general-partnership liability law (the "do-nothing" baseline)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as risk-matched, not aspiration-matched — "match the structure to the risk, not to how serious you want to look," with a five-step decision path from "stay informal" to "Wyoming DUNA" to "offshore, only for large cross-border treasuries."
adjacent_meanings: unincorporated association (the default, zero-protection starting state)
fiscal sponsorship/fiscal host (a lighter-weight alternative that defers full incorporation)
important_distinctions: Legal Wrapper ≠ DAO — a DAO-specific wrapper (DUNA, DAO LLC) is one *kind* of legal wrapper suited to groups already voting on-chain or holding a multisig treasury; a co-op or nonprofit wrapper requires no on-chain governance at all
general partnership (default, unlimited personal liability) ≠ any registered wrapper (liability sits with the entity)
tensions: cost/complexity scales enormously across wrapper types — from "$0, stay informal" to Cayman Islands setup (~US$2,250 plus thousands/year in ongoing fees) — and the article explicitly warns against "over-wrapping," i.e. choosing based on aspiration rather than actual risk
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting a single "decision path" checklist can read as more settled law than it is — DAO-specific wrappers (DUNA, DAO LLC) are recent (Wyoming DUNA effective July 2024) and largely untested in court; their liability-shield claims rest on statute and early adoption (e.g. Uniswap's DUNI), not extensive case law.

data.title: Oracle (blockchain)
data.short_description: A service that feeds outside (off-chain) data to a blockchain, so a smart contract can react to real-world information it otherwise has no way to observe.
source_traditions: ethereum.org developer documentation on oracles
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced to explain the limit of "a blockchain cannot verify the real world for you" — oracles are presented as a partial bridge, not a solution, since "someone still has to be trusted to report the truth in the first place."
adjacent_meanings: dMRV (digital measurement, reporting, and verification — an applied use of oracle-fed data for impact claims)
important_distinctions: An oracle moves the trust problem, it does not remove it — the chain only knows what the oracle told it, so oracle data quality/trustworthiness becomes the new bottleneck.
tensions: The article's own cautionary example (Toucan/Verra) shows that even with good-faith tokenization, the underlying real-world/regulatory truth can diverge from the on-chain record in ways an oracle alone does not prevent.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting oracles as a full solution to "blockchain can't see the real world" understates the article's own point — oracles bridge the gap but still depend on trusted reporting.

data.title: Anatomy of a good DAO proposal
data.short_description: A seven-part structure for a governance proposal: (1) a clear, specific title, (2) a 2-3 sentence summary of what's proposed/costs/outcome, (3) background/context explaining the need and evidence, (4) a specification of exact deliverables/timeline/responsible parties, (5) a detailed budget breakdown, (6) measurable success criteria, and (7) a risks section with mitigations.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the complete template structure the article recommends DAO members follow, paired with a "before you propose" stage (informal temperature check, coalition-building, preemptive objection-handling).
adjacent_meanings: Grant-application templates (title/summary/budget/timeline structures used in traditional funding contexts — not named in the article but structurally similar)
important_distinctions: The article distinguishes the *proposal document* structure from the *pre-proposal process* (temperature check, coalition-building) — framing proposal failure as usually a process failure ("proposal is unclear, poorly scoped, or doesn't address community concerns") rather than an idea-quality failure.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a generic governance-process template, not attributed to a specific tradition or community.

data.title: Centralization vs decentralization spectrum
data.short_description: Centralized systems put one authority in charge of a resource or decision (a bank, a single telecom's mobile-money network, a handful of large farms); decentralized systems spread control across many independent parts that collaborate toward shared goals (cooperatives, rotating savings circles, seed banks, Bitcoin). Most real systems are hybrids somewhere on a spectrum between the two poles.
source_traditions: Bankless Academy's "Foundations of Decentralization" course
permaculture design principles (resilience through diversity)
food-systems resilience research (PMC 2022 study)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as a foundations-layer bridge concept: reframes "decentralization" for an audience of gardeners and permaculturists by mapping it onto systems they already run (community gardens, seed swaps, cooperatives) before connecting it to blockchain/crypto examples like Bitcoin.
adjacent_meanings: technical/architectural decentralization (node count, consensus mechanism)
economic decentralization (distributed ownership of value/tokens)
important_distinctions: the spectrum framing: most effective organizations are hybrids (e.g. a steering committee providing coordination while individual members make their own decisions), not purely one pole or the other
single point of failure is the article's named weakness of centralization; distributed resilience (the whole continues if one node fails) is its named strength for decentralization
tensions: the article's cited 2022 study found decentralization improves supply-chain resilience but centralization can better address labor shortages — used to argue "decentralization is not always the answer," not a categorical claim of superiority either way.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating decentralization as an unqualified good (or centralization as an unqualified failure mode) erases the article's explicit both-sided framing and its closing line: "neither is inherently better. The question is which approach fits the problem you are trying to solve."

data.title: Grassroots Web3 Adoption Pattern
data.short_description: A recurring on-ramp pattern observed across illustrative regenerative-practitioner adoption stories: start small, find at least one person who understands the tech, keep learning through mistakes, and stay focused on mission rather than the technology itself.
source_traditions: Distilled in the article from three composite/illustrative stories sourced from "ReFi DAO Local ReFi Toolkit" and "Reimagining Power."
data.toolkit_usage: Used as reassurance content: "you don't need a computer science degree, a huge budget, or to understand everything" to begin using web3 tools for regenerative work.
adjacent_meanings: web3 onboarding pattern
first-90-days pattern
important_distinctions: Distinguishes "finding one ally who understands the tech" from "becoming a crypto expert yourself" — the pattern explicitly does not require individual technical mastery.
data.risks_of_flattening: The pattern is drawn from a small number of illustrative (possibly composite) stories, not a systematic study of adoption outcomes — presenting it as a proven universal path risks overstating its evidentiary base.

data.title: Stakeholder education before crypto adoption
data.short_description: The practice of educating board/staff/donors on what crypto is and how donations would work before an org formally adopts crypto donations, so the eventual decision is informed rather than reactive.
data.toolkit_usage: Framed in communicating-stakeholders.md as the mandatory first step, ahead of even a board vote — "not in depth, just enough to make an informed decision."
adjacent_meanings: change-management (general org practice of preparing stakeholders for a new capability)
important_distinctions: education-before-adoption differs from marketing-after-adoption (the later donor-communication step)
tensions: thoroughness-of-education vs board's-limited-attention-and-time
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating this as a one-time presentation rather than an ongoing readiness practice risks a board that nods along without real understanding of risk.

data.title: Token allowances (dApp spending permissions)
data.short_description: The permission a user grants a smart contract to access/spend their tokens when using a dApp; the article's core security advice is to limit the allowance to the immediate trade size rather than the full balance.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as a "Security Essentials" item in creating-buying-earning.md, alongside seed-phrase custody and starting-small advice.
adjacent_meanings: seed-phrase-custody (the other named security essential in the same article)
important_distinctions: an allowance is a revocable smart-contract permission, distinct from a seed phrase, which is full wallet control
tensions: convenience-of-unlimited-approval vs exposure-if-that-contract-is-later-exploited
data.risks_of_flattening: The article gives the rule ("limit allowances") without explaining how to check or revoke existing allowances (e.g. via a token-approval checker tool) — a practical gap for a true beginner guide.

data.title: DAO alternatives (cooperatives, sociocracy, lightweight voting tools)
data.short_description: Non-DAO structures offered in is-dao-right.md as fits when a full DAO feels like too much: legal cooperatives with shared ownership, consensus-based decision-making (including sociocracy, used by many permaculture groups), and simple voting tools (Google Forms, Loomio, or paper ballots) for low-tech communities.
source_traditions: cooperative-movement legal structures
sociocracy / consensus-based-facilitation practice
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as "A Note on Alternatives" in is-dao-right.md, positioned as the answer when a community's discussion-guide questions point away from a DAO (need for speed/legal protection/low-tech simplicity).
adjacent_meanings: dao-decentralized-autonomous-organization
legal-structures-for-community-organizations
important_distinctions: A cooperative offers legal recognition a DAO typically lacks; sociocracy offers a decision-making process, not a legal or financial-custody structure — the article treats these as answering different needs, not as interchangeable DAO substitutes.
data.risks_of_flattening: Naming "sociocracy" and "cooperatives" as a pair risks implying they are equivalent options; a cooperative is a legal/ownership structure while sociocracy is a decision-making method that could run inside a cooperative, a DAO, or neither.

data.title: Zero-knowledge proof (selective disclosure)
data.short_description: A cryptographic method letting someone prove a statement about themselves (e.g. "I am over 18") is true without revealing the underlying data (e.g. an exact birthdate or ID document) that makes it true.
source_traditions: cryptography (zero-knowledge proof research)
privacy-preserving-computation
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in identity-verification.md as the mechanism that lets a web3 verification system ask yes/no questions ("are you over 18?", "do you live in Somaliland?") and get an answer without collecting the underlying document.
adjacent_meanings: verifiable-credential-wallet-held-attestation
onchain-attestation
important_distinctions: Proving "yes, over 18" is not the same as disclosing a birthdate — the article is explicit that this is the "clever part" distinguishing web3 verification from showing an ID card.
tensions: Selective-disclosure privacy benefits vs. the practical reality that the issuing credential system still had to verify the underlying fact at some point.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article's "prove you have a key without showing the key" analogy is a simplification; it does not capture the specific cryptographic guarantees or failure modes of any particular ZK-proof scheme.

data.title: Verifiable credential (wallet-held attestation)
data.short_description: A digital credential issued into a user's wallet once a verification system confirms an attribute or requirement is met; the holder chooses when to present it and when to keep it hidden.
source_traditions: decentralized-identity / self-sovereign-identity movement
data.toolkit_usage: Described in identity-verification.md's "A Credential Is Created" step as what a wallet holds after a zero-knowledge verification succeeds, and as the thing a person can "show when you need to prove something, and hide when you don't."
adjacent_meanings: zero-knowledge-proof-selective-disclosure
onchain-attestation
important_distinctions: Holding a credential is not the same as broadcasting it — the article stresses user-controlled disclosure as the differentiator from regular-internet data collection.
tensions: Building a portable reputation across platforms (the article's stated benefit) vs. the risk that a credential becomes a new form of cross-platform tracking if not designed carefully.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article does not name a specific credential standard or issuer, so "verifiable credential" here reflects the article's general conceptual framing rather than a specific technical implementation.

data.title: Gas Fee (EIP-1559 Base Fee + Tip Model)
data.short_description: The cost of processing a transaction on a blockchain, expressed as Gas Used × (Base Fee + Tip). Since Ethereum's EIP-1559 upgrade (2021), the base fee auto-adjusts with network demand and is burned; the tip (priority fee) is an optional extra to jump the queue.
source_traditions: Ethereum protocol economics (EIP-1559, 2021)
Pre-EIP-1559 first-price auction gas markets (the older model this replaced)
data.toolkit_usage: Explained here as foundational vocabulary (gas, gas price/gwei, gas fee, gas limit) every newcomer needs before transacting, with Layer 2 networks positioned as the practical fee-reduction path.
adjacent_meanings: Bitcoin transaction fees (a simpler, non-EIP-1559 fee-market model not discussed in this article)
Layer 2 gas fees (same base concept, much lower absolute cost, per the article)
important_distinctions: Base fee (burned, algorithmically set) vs. priority fee/tip (paid to the validator, user-set) — conflating the two obscures why "network busy" and "I set a high tip" are different levers on cost.
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing gas simply as "gasoline for your car" is a useful first analogy but risks obscuring that gas price is a live auction/algorithmic market, not a fixed unit price the way fuel is.

data.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
data.short_description: An AI answers only from documents you give it instead of its general training, and returns citations back to the exact passage it drew from.
source_traditions: information-retrieval + language-model synthesis (NLP research)
data.toolkit_usage: Named in the article as "the single most useful pattern for a knowledge commons, because answers come with receipts." Google NotebookLM is given as the accessible entry point: load your governance docs and meeting summaries, then a new member can ask "how do we make spending decisions?" and get a sourced answer instead of pinging a person on Discord.
adjacent_meanings: general-purpose chat with an LLM's training-data knowledge (no grounding, no citations)
fine-tuning (baking documents into model weights, a different technique with different risks)
important_distinctions: "when it cites nothing, the knowledge is not there" — the article frames an uncited answer as a documentation gap to fill, not a failure of the tool.
tensions: grounded-but-cloud-hosted (NotebookLM, convenient, but files live on Google's servers) vs local-and-private (Smart Connections on Obsidian, slower to adopt, fully offline).
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating RAG as "AI search" flattens the distinction the article leans on: the discipline of the format (a system that literally cannot answer beyond what's uploaded) is what makes it trustworthy for governance questions, not any general capability of the underlying model.

data.title: Decentralized Trust (from institutions to code)
data.short_description: The shift from trusting institutional intermediaries (banks, platforms) to trusting verifiable, distributed systems — open-source code, consensus mechanisms, and cryptography — as the basis for coordinating value and information.
source_traditions: Web2 platform/institutional trust model (the article's explicit contrast case)
blockchain consensus mechanism design (Proof of Work / Proof of Stake)
community-reputation-based trust (article names Somali and East African community/clan-network traditions as a loose historical analogue, unattributed to a specific source)
data.toolkit_usage: Used to frame blockchain not as "trustless" but as trust-relocated — a reframing device for explaining decentralization's value proposition.
adjacent_meanings: trust as reputation/community-standing (pre-digital, e.g. the article's Somali/East African community-trust aside)
trust as cryptographic verifiability (the article's main thesis)
important_distinctions: trustless (a common but, the article implies, imprecise marketing term) vs trust-relocated (to code/math/consensus)
transparency (visibility) vs accountability (consequences) — related but not identical
tensions: verifiability-in-principle (anyone *can* inspect open-source code) vs verifiability-in-practice (most users lack the expertise to actually audit it)
data.risks_of_flattening: Naming "Somali and East African traditions" as a general parallel to decentralized trust risks flattening distinct community practices into a single undifferentiated analogy; the article does not cite a specific community, elder, or documented practice, so this lineage note should be treated as an unverified generalization pending a real source.

data.title: Stewardship Roles (Knowledge Commons)
data.short_description: Five named jobs — Editor, Curator, Facilitator, Maintainer, Onboarder — that together cover the tending a knowledge commons needs to survive turnover: publish-worthiness, routing/composting, conflict-hosting, upkeep, and onboarding legibility.
source_traditions: Regen Toolkit's cross-cutting principle of "living systems health" (energy, trust, contribution flow, maintenance capacity).
GitHub's graduated permission model (triage vs maintainer), cited via Ben Balter's open-source-governance guide, as prior art for handing out roles without handing out full write access.
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as "a verb before it is a title" — the article stresses one person can hold several roles on a small team, but each role must be named, not assumed.
adjacent_meanings: open-source maintainer roles
governance role
important_distinctions: Editor (claim-evidence discipline: what's true enough to publish) is distinct from Curator (what belongs and where — routing, pruning, composting).
Facilitator (hosts disagreement) is distinct from Maintainer (keeps the technical lights on) — conflict-work and ops-work are different jobs even though both are often invisible.
tensions: A role you cannot hand off is called out in the article as "not a role, it is a hostage situation" — naming a role is necessary but not sufficient; the handoff must be documented while the holder is still present.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "stewardship" as one generic job flattens five genuinely different failure modes (unreviewed claims, junk-drawer sprawl, unresolved conflict, technical rot, and un-onboardable contributors) that each need a differently-shaped intervention.

data.title: Contributor Absence Factor (Bus Factor)
data.short_description: A metric defined as "the smallest number of contributors responsible for 50% of total contributions" — sort contributors by volume, add them up until crossing 50% of total contributions, and count how many it took.
source_traditions: CHAOSS project (Community Health Analytics in Open Source Software), a Linux Foundation effort — formerly called the "Bus Factor."
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as a computable-by-hand (about ten minutes, from a commit log or wiki revision history) fragility check, meant to be run on a calendar rather than discovered during a burnout crisis.
adjacent_meanings: Bus Factor (the metric's older, more informal name)
important_distinctions: The number itself ("1 or 2") is a diagnostic trigger, not the point — the article stresses the real value is turning "who does half the work here?" into a scheduled question rather than a crisis discovery.
data.risks_of_flattening: Renaming "Bus Factor" to "Contributor Absence Factor" is itself a deliberate reframing (removing a morbid metaphor) — using only one name risks losing the metric's more widely recognized prior identity for people searching under the older term.

data.title: Internal capacity
data.short_description: A community's ability to do things independently, without relying on external experts, consultants, or hired help — the skills, knowledge, and systems that live within the members themselves, spanning technical, governance, communication, and financial domains.
source_traditions: community organizing / capacity-building practice (general)
web3-specific operational skills (wallet, smart contract, treasury, security)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed in the article as the alternative to permanent dependence on external experts — the five-step build process (identify gaps, map existing skills, create learning pathways, practice with low stakes, document everything) is presented as how a node closes the gap over time.
adjacent_meanings: 'capacity building' in international-development discourse (a broader, often institution-to-institution framing)
important_distinctions: the article separates "what can you do now" from "what can't you do" as the diagnostic starting point, rather than assuming capacity gaps are obvious.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating capacity-building as a one-time training event rather than an ongoing five-step cycle (gap → skill map → pathway → low-stakes practice → documentation) loses the article's framing of it as continuous infrastructure work, not a single workshop.

data.title: On-chain attestation as a vouching record
data.short_description: A digital certificate/proof-record model with three steps: (1) a trusted party — teacher, mentor, organization, or system — "vouches for you" by making a statement, (2) the statement is written to a blockchain where it "cannot be changed, deleted, or faked," (3) anyone can verify it without contacting the original issuer. The article frames this as "trust without needing a middleman."
data.toolkit_usage: Central mechanism explained in the article as the basis for all four use cases it lists (skills, reputation, impact, opportunity access).
adjacent_meanings: NFT-based credentials (nfts-beyond-art.md treats blockchain diplomas as an NFT use case — same underlying idea, different framing/schema)
Verifiable credentials (W3C-style digital credential standards; not named in this article but the closest formal analogue)
important_distinctions: An attestation is a claim someone else makes about you, not a possession you mint yourself — distinct from an NFT you buy or create, even though both live "on-chain."

"Trust without needing a middleman" describes verification, not the original vouching step — the attestation is only as trustworthy as the issuer who created it; the underlying trust is relocated, not removed.
tensions: The article's framing implies attestations are inherently more trustworthy than paper certificates, but the trustworthiness of any attestation still depends entirely on who is allowed to issue one — a point the source text doesn't address.
data.risks_of_flattening: None regarding a cultural tradition; but see accompanying public-use- boundary regarding the article's specific, named, vulnerable audience.

data.title: Cosmo-Local Coordination
data.short_description: Global standards and infrastructure combined with local implementation and governance — communities share knowledge, tools, and resources globally while adapting implementation to their own ecological, cultural, and economic context.
source_traditions: the regenerative-economics / ReFi movement (article names it as "emerging from the regenerative movement")
open-source / commons-based peer production (global standard, local instance pattern)
local currency and community seed-library practice
data.toolkit_usage: Used as this article's central framing device: bridges the abstract decentralization/resilience argument to concrete regenerative practice — local currency systems, community seed libraries, and Local ReFi Nodes are all given as cosmo-local examples.
adjacent_meanings: cosmo-localism as a general design philosophy (broader movement usage, not confined to this article)
glocal (older, adjacent business/globalization term for a similar global-local balance, not used by this article)
important_distinctions: cosmo-local-vs-purely-local — the article is explicit that "you cannot build regenerative economies in isolation"; cosmo-local requires both the global sharing layer and local autonomy, not local action alone.

cosmo-local-vs-purely-global — equally, a single global standard imposed without local adaptation is not cosmo-local by this article's definition ("you cannot regenerate a dryland watershed in Somaliland the same way you would regenerate a highland forest in Ethiopia").
tensions: shared-global-infrastructure vs risk-of-external-capture — the article's broader principles list warns that "dependence on a single external power breeds capture," a live tension with the "global standards" half of cosmo-local.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing cosmo-local to "think globally, act locally" flattens the article's more specific claim that it requires actual shared infrastructure/tooling connecting nodes (e.g. a Local ReFi Nodes network), not just a mindset.

data.title: Anti-Fragility (in decentralized systems)
data.short_description: A property beyond mere robustness — systems that don't just survive stress but actually strengthen under pressure, developing stronger bonds, better protocols, and deeper trust through each disruption.
source_traditions: Nassim Nicholas Taleb's "Antifragile" framework (concept not attributed by name in this article, but the definition given matches Taleb's usage)
decentralized-network resilience theory
community-organizing / mutual-aid practice under crisis
data.toolkit_usage: Used in this article as the fourth of four mechanisms (with redundancy, fault tolerance, adaptive capacity) linking decentralization to resilience — positioned as the strongest claim: not just "survives" but "strengthens."
adjacent_meanings: anti-fragility as an individual/organizational trait (broader usage)
anti-fragility as a systems-engineering property (this article's framing, applied to community coordination systems)
important_distinctions: resilience-vs-anti-fragility — the article treats these as a graduated scale: redundancy and fault tolerance produce resilience (surviving), while anti-fragility is a stronger claim (thriving because of stress), and it should not be assumed automatically from mere decentralization.
tensions: the-article-asserts-rather-than-demonstrates — "communities that navigate challenges together... often develop stronger bonds" is a plausible but unevidenced generalization within this piece.
data.risks_of_flattening: Assuming any decentralized system is automatically anti-fragile flattens the distinction the article itself draws between the four mechanisms — redundancy and fault tolerance are the load-bearing, well-evidenced claims; anti-fragility is presented as an aspiration, not a guarantee.

data.title: Regenerative Finance (ReFi)
data.short_description: Tools and projects built to create economies that restore ecosystems and communities rather than deplete them; the article quotes Ethereum's own explainer describing ReFi as systems that "create value for participants while simultaneously benefiting ecosystems and communities."
source_traditions: Web3 / crypto-native regenerative-economics movement (ReFi DAO, Greenpill Network)
Ethereum Foundation's own ReFi explainer (ethereum.org/refi)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the umbrella "corner" of the crypto space this guide points newcomers toward, deliberately distinguished ("closer to compost than to a casino") from purely speculative crypto culture.
adjacent_meanings: Impact investing / ESG finance (non-crypto analogue, not discussed in article)
Regenerative agriculture / permaculture economics (the article's bridging analogy)
important_distinctions: ReFi (a values/mission orientation within web3) vs. crypto broadly (which includes purely speculative or extractive projects the article explicitly warns readers away from).
tensions: The "closer to compost than to a casino" framing is aspirational branding as much as description; the article does not examine whether self-labeled ReFi projects consistently deliver on that framing.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting ReFi DAO and Greenpill as *the* two front doors risks implying ReFi is smaller/more centralized than the many overlapping, loosely connected circles the article itself says exist ("no single crypto community").

data.title: Decentralized Finance (DeFi)
data.short_description: Financial services (swaps, lending, stablecoins) built on public blockchains that operate without traditional intermediaries like banks; anyone with a wallet can access them directly.
source_traditions: Ethereum smart-contract protocol design (Uniswap, Aave, Compound, MakerDAO)
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced in this article as one of four pillars of the Ethereum ecosystem (alongside Layer 2s, NFTs, and DAOs), framed for regenerative communities as a lens on "community-controlled finance" running on transparent, auditable code rather than closed corporate infrastructure.
adjacent_meanings: Traditional finance (TradFi) intermediated by banks/brokers
Community currencies / local exchange systems (non-blockchain analogues)
important_distinctions: DeFi is permissionless access to financial primitives (swap, lend, borrow), not a guarantee of safety or fairness — it removes an intermediary, it does not remove risk.
tensions: The article's own caution ("smart contracts can have bugs... the space has seen significant losses from hacks and fraud") sits alongside its framing of DeFi as an opportunity for community finance; the two need to be held together, not resolved into pure optimism.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting DeFi purely as "transparent, auditable" risks understating that audits are imperfect and that transparency does not equal safety for a first-time, low-resource user.

data.title: No single point of failure (organizational crypto custody)
data.short_description: "The most critical rule for organizational crypto security: no single individual should have full control over the organization's funds." Operationalized via multi-sig wallets (multiple keys required to authorize any transaction) and layered role-based access control (view-only operations staff, capped-limit managers, approval-authority executives, unlimited-approval board), plus a hot/cold wallet split so a compromised operational wallet never exposes treasury reserves.
data.toolkit_usage: The article's stated "core rule," from which every subsequent recommendation (multi-sig, layered access, cold storage, policy framework) is derived.
adjacent_meanings: Corporate dual-signature bank accounts (the article's own analogy — "a corporate bank account that needs two signatures")

Personal wallet recovery planning (a related but distinct concern — see the sibling recovery-planning.md article in this batch, which covers individual/organizational recovery methods including the same Safe multi-sig tool)
important_distinctions: Multi-sig is framed as both security (preventing single-actor theft or collusion) and de facto recovery redundancy (if one signer's device is compromised, attackers still cannot act alone) — the article treats these as one continuous property, not two separate features.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a technical governance/custody framework, not attributed to a specific community or tradition.

data.title: Local / Community Currency
data.short_description: A currency circulating within a defined community (not a national fiat currency) designed to keep value local, recognize labour that national markets undervalue, and enable exchange when mainstream money is scarce.
source_traditions: time-banking / timebank movement (one unit = one hour of labour, e.g. Ithaca Hours since 1991)
UK transition-town local-currency movement (Brixton Pound, and similar "Totnes Pound"-style projects, value-based and pegged)

informal rotating-savings traditions predating any formal currency design — chamas and ROSCAs across Kenya, Tanzania, and wider East Africa; susu rotating savings — named explicitly as proof communities already run mutual financial systems
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as a design decision-tree (unit → backing → issuance → rules) rather than a single template, with an explicit recommendation to start with a time-based, labour-backed, member-issued design and paper or a shared spreadsheet before considering blockchain.
adjacent_meanings: timebank (a specific time-based subtype of local currency)
mobile money (a different tool — moves national currency digitally, does not create a local unit)
important_distinctions: Local currency ≠ mobile money — mobile money moves the same national currency faster; a local currency creates a new unit that only circulates within the community
time-based ≠ value-based unit — time-based ties value to an hour of anyone's labour (equality-oriented); value-based pegs to national currency (familiar, but inherits its instability)
tensions: the article's most-cited examples (Ithaca Hours, Brixton Pound, BerkShares) are all Global North projects, while the target audience is explicitly East African/Somaliland — the article itself acknowledges this and reframes the practice as building on chamas/ ROSCAs/susu rather than importing the Global North template wholesale
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting "time-based, labour-backed, member-issued, paper-ledger" as the universally-right starting design flattens real variation in what already works locally (e.g. established chama/ROSCA cash-rotation norms) — the article's own advice to "build on practices already common" should be weighed against its own most-detailed prescriptive default.

data.title: Impact DAO
data.short_description: A DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) whose shared mission is specifically to create positive change — restoring ecosystems, funding local projects, or building alternative economic systems — rather than a DAO organized around, e.g., a protocol, an investment fund, or a social club.
source_traditions: General DAO organizing model (blockchain-coordinated, code-encoded rules)
Regenerative Finance (ReFi) movement
data.toolkit_usage: Used in this article as the umbrella term for ReFi DAO, Greenpill, and Klima DAO, positioned as the web3-native analogue to existing cooperative/commons organizing (permaculture design courses, seed swaps, tool libraries) that a non-crypto-native reader already recognizes.
adjacent_meanings: "DAO" generally (any blockchain-coordinated group; not all DAOs are impact-oriented — see investment DAOs, protocol-governance DAOs)
Cooperative / commons organizing (non-blockchain analogue named explicitly in the article)
important_distinctions: Impact DAO vs. DAO broadly: the "impact" qualifier is a stated mission orientation, not a technical or legal distinction — nothing in the tooling enforces that a self-labeled Impact DAO actually delivers impact.
tensions: The article's own closing line ("Impact DAOs are not a magic solution... some will succeed, others will fail") sits in tension with the earlier framing of DAOs as trust-built-into-the-system; worth holding both.
data.risks_of_flattening: Equating "no central boss" with genuine equity of voice risks flattening real participation and accountability challenges that DAOs face (named only briefly, in the related ethereum-ecosystem article, not here).

data.title: Hybrid web3 adoption (selective tool use by function)
data.short_description: Using web3 tools only where they add clear value (e.g. treasury management, governance voting) while keeping traditional tools where they don't (communication, scheduling, document management), rather than treating "web3 vs. not" as an all-or-nothing choice.
source_traditions: pragmatic-tool-selection / "right tool for the job" practice
data.toolkit_usage: The recommended default in is-web3-right.md's "The Hybrid Approach" section, positioned as what "most communities" actually benefit from.
adjacent_meanings: is-a-dao-right-for-your-community
important_distinctions: Being honest about whether web3 "serves your community or your curiosity" — the article frames both as valid but insists they not be confused with each other.
tensions: Simplicity of an all-traditional or all-web3 stack vs. the coordination overhead of maintaining a mixed toolset.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article's "when web3 adds value" / "when it doesn't" lists are presented as fairly clean-cut, but in practice the line (e.g. "under 10 and high-trust") is a rule of thumb, not a hard threshold the article substantiates with evidence.

data.title: Layer 2 (Ethereum scaling)
data.short_description: A secondary network built on top of a main blockchain (here, Ethereum) that processes transactions separately and cheaply while still relying on the base chain's security for final settlement.
source_traditions: Ethereum scaling research (rollup-centric roadmap)
Optimistic Rollup design (fraud-proof / challenge-window model)
Zero-Knowledge Rollup design (validity-proof model)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed for regen projects as the affordability unlock for on-chain micro-transactions, carbon-credit tracking, and community token systems — the difference between "sustainable" and "unsustainable" fee costs at scale.
adjacent_meanings: sidechain (independent security model, not inheriting L1 security directly)
Layer 1 / Ethereum Mainnet (the base chain being scaled)
important_distinctions: Optimistic Rollup ≠ ZK Rollup — Optimistic assumes validity and allows a ~7-day fraud-challenge window; ZK Rollups submit a mathematical proof of correctness verified immediately, no waiting period
Layer 2 ≠ independent blockchain — a genuine L2 inherits Ethereum's security guarantees; assets are not held by a company that could fail
tensions: the article frames ZK Rollups as "still maturing" and Optimistic Rollups as "more accessible... for now" — a claim that is time-bound and likely to shift as ZK tooling matures
data.risks_of_flattening: "Layer 2s are as secure as Ethereum" is true of the cryptographic settlement guarantee but glosses over operational risk: each L2 still has its own sequencer/team/infrastructure, which is a real (if smaller) trust surface the article itself flags in its "Note on Security."

data.title: Self-Custody (Non-Custodial Wallets)
data.short_description: Holding your own private keys/seed phrase directly, with no intermediary able to sign, freeze, or recover a transaction on your behalf — control and responsibility sit entirely with the key holder.
source_traditions: cryptography / public-private key systems
Bitcoin/Ethereum wallet design
the "not your keys, not your crypto" community ethos
data.toolkit_usage: Positioned in this article as the higher-responsibility, higher-control counterpart to custodial (exchange-held) wallets, and connected to mobile money precedents (M-Pesa, Eva, Telesom ZAAD) already familiar to East African audiences as a bridge concept.
adjacent_meanings: self-custody as a security practice (key management)
self-custody as a political/ideological stance (censorship resistance, anti-intermediary)
self-custody as a treasury design choice (multisig for community funds)
important_distinctions: seed-phrase-vs-private-key — the article notes the seed phrase is the human-manageable form; the wallet derives keys from it, generated and kept on-device.
custodial-recovery-vs-non-custodial-no-recovery — losing a seed phrase in a non-custodial wallet means permanent loss of funds, unlike a custodial account's password-reset path.
tensions: full-ownership vs total-personal-responsibility — the article is explicit that greater control comes with zero safety net for user error.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "non-custodial" as simply "safer" flattens the article's actual point: it shifts risk from counterparty/exchange failure to individual operational-security failure (malware, lost phrase) — neither is strictly safer, they are different risk profiles.

data.title: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) vs. Local Node
data.short_description: A DAO is a legal-and-technical form (membership, money, and decisions encoded onto a blockchain with verifiable votes); a local node is a community concept (people in a place organized around shared purpose). A node becomes DAO-shaped only when the cost of informality exceeds the cost of the tooling.
source_traditions: SuperBenefit's "minimum viable coordination" framing (just enough structure to enable collaboration while preserving autonomy)
ReFi DAO and Greenpill Network's hybrid, tool-optional network model
data.toolkit_usage: Used to reframe "should we become a DAO?" as "which of three concrete problems (treasury custody, verifiable decisions, roles surviving turnover) do we actually have?" — formalize only the piece that answers a live problem, not the whole stack pre-emptively.
adjacent_meanings: legal wrapper (a DAO-specific wrapper like a Wyoming DUNA is one path to legal personality for an on-chain-governed node, not the same as "becoming a DAO" informally)
working group / council (organizational models a node can adopt without any on-chain component at all)
important_distinctions: DAO ≠ local node — conflating the two is named directly as "two things people constantly merge"; a node can run for years as "a Signal group, a shared calendar, and a monthly meal" without ever becoming DAO-shaped
formalizing a treasury (multisig) ≠ formalizing decisions (voting) ≠ formalizing roles (onchain permissions) — three separable problems, not one bundled "become a DAO" step
tensions: the article frames a healthy network (ReFi DAO, Greenpill) as making a node "more sovereign, not less," while naming central overreach (a network steering or taking custody of a node's funds/decisions) as a real failure mode requiring structural, not just cultural, defense
data.risks_of_flattening: "Minimum viable coordination" can be used to justify never adding structure a group genuinely needs, just as easily as it guards against over-building — the article's own guardrail ("add structure in response to a problem you can name") requires the same honest self-assessment in either direction.

data.title: Layered custody (hot/cold/multisig by purpose)
data.short_description: A three-tier custody framework for an organization's crypto holdings: day-to-day operational funds in a hot wallet, reserves/grants in hardware cold storage, and any large organizational transaction gated behind a multi-signature wallet requiring three-or-more approvers.
source_traditions: personal-finance cash-in-pocket-vs-savings-account analogy
corporate treasury segregation-of-duties practice
crypto-native multisig treasury management
data.toolkit_usage: Recommended in hot-vs-cold.md as the default treasury pattern for a regenerative organization holding crypto, rather than choosing hot OR cold exclusively.
adjacent_meanings: custodial-vs-noncustodial-wallets
multi-signature-wallet
important_distinctions: "Hot vs. cold" is a storage-location choice; "multisig" is a decision-authority choice — the article treats them as complementary, not alternatives (a multisig wallet can itself be hot or cold).
tensions: convenience-of-single-signer-access-vs-accountability-of-multisig-approval
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting this as a universal best practice risks understating the real operational cost of multisig for very small or resource-constrained groups (coordination overhead among 3+ signers, key-loss risk multiplied across signers).

data.title: Subsidiarity
data.short_description: The design principle that decisions should sit at the most local level able to make them well — a local node is not a branch office taking orders from a DAO, it's the level where the real call gets made, plugged into a global network for what it can't generate alone.
source_traditions: Ethereum Localism (advanced by Greenpill Network and Gitcoin co-founder Kevin Owocki) — frames the chain as infrastructure for local autonomy, not a remote authority.
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article to directly answer the fear "will some central org swallow my project?" — the network (e.g. the Localism Fund, stewarded by Regen Coordination and OpenCivics) funds and shares tools but doesn't run the node's treasury or pick its projects.
adjacent_meanings: local node (the organizational unit subsidiarity is applied to)
important_distinctions: subsidiarity vs. isolation — a node practicing subsidiarity still plugs into the wider network for funding, tooling, and solidarity; it is not the same as operating standalone.
tensions: Node autonomy vs. network funding dependence — networks fund nodes specifically to avoid extraction, but any funding relationship carries some influence risk the article does not fully resolve.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating subsidiarity as simply "local control" ignores its relational half — the principle explicitly includes staying "plugged into the wider network," not full independence.

data.title: Archive / Compost / Deprecate / Remove (the four moves)
