data.short_description: The four ways a knowledge commons can handle a document that has stopped being true: archive (preserve as a labeled historical record), compost (harvest the still-good parts into living pages, then retire the husk), deprecate (mark obsolete with a warning banner pointing to a replacement), and remove (delete outright — treated as rare).
source_traditions: the Regen Knowledge Commons Toolkit's Evolution Layer (cross-cutting principle
software documentation practice (Read the Docs, Grafana Writers' Toolkit deprecation conventions)
Wikipedia page-history and talk-page archiving conventions
evergreen-notes / digital-garden practice (Andy Matuschak, Maggie Appleton)
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in the article as the antidote to teams that "only know two verbs: keep and delete." Maps directly onto the Toolkit's own Evolution Layer principle, which the article quotes as existing to keep a living commons from "both stagnation and reactive overcorrection."
adjacent_meanings: 'deprecate' in software release management (a feature slated for removal, with a version-numbered timeline)
'archive' in general records-management (cold storage, not necessarily discoverable)
important_distinctions: archive preserves the whole page as history; compost breaks the page down and reuses only its good parts elsewhere
deprecate leaves the page live with a warning; remove is deletion and is the rare, last-resort move
tensions: compost is the only one of the four that requires judgment (what's worth keeping) rather than being near-mechanical, which the article argues is exactly why it's the least-practiced move.
data.risks_of_flattening: Collapsing all four moves into "cleanup" or "archiving" erases the distinct trust properties each preserves — a deprecated page still resolves and keeps links alive, an archived page is explicitly historical and excluded from default search, and a composted page's value survives in a different, living location. Treating them as interchangeable re-creates the keep-or-delete trap the framework exists to escape.

data.title: Evergreen notes / seedling-budding-evergreen maturity taxonomy
data.short_description: A practice of writing notes that "evolve, contribute, and accumulate over time, across projects" (Andy Matuschak's definition), paired with a visible maturity label — seedling, budding, evergreen — so a reader can tell at a glance whether they're looking at a rough sketch or a settled idea (Maggie Appleton's digital-garden taxonomy).
source_traditions: Andy Matuschak's "Evergreen notes" essay
Maggie Appleton's digital-garden maturity taxonomy ("Growing the Evergreens")
Quartz (static-site generator) frontmatter maturity/publish flags
data.toolkit_usage: Cited in the article as the ethic behind composting: a dying page may contain a few paragraphs that were never about the deprecated content at all (working agreements, a good rationale, hard-won gotchas), and composting means lifting those into pages that carry the same growth- state signal so readers can trust what they're reading.
adjacent_meanings: the Toolkit's own K1 maturity axis (raw/held/draft/candidate/source-linked/reviewed/...), a different, more granular ladder for a different purpose (trust/review state, not editorial roughness)
important_distinctions: "seedling/budding/evergreen" signals *editorial* maturity (how settled the writing is); it is not the same axis as the Toolkit's K1 maturity/public_use/lifecycle_state model, though both aim to make trust visible rather than assumed.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating maturity labeling as decoration rather than a load-bearing trust signal misses the article's point: the label is what lets a reader tell a rough sketch from a settled idea without asking anyone.

data.title: Elinor Ostrom's Eight Principles for Governing Commons
data.short_description: Eight design principles (clear boundaries, locally-fit rules, participatory decision-making, self-monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict-resolution mechanisms, recognized right to organize, nested governance) that Nobel-winning research found in communities that successfully self-govern shared resources without privatization or top-down state control.
source_traditions: Elinor Ostrom's commons-governance research (Nobel Prize in Economics)
data.toolkit_usage: Applied in cooperative-commons.md as a practical checklist for both physical cooperatives (savings circles, coffee cooperatives) and digital commons/DAOs — the article frames them as guidelines to work through deliberately, not abstract theory.
adjacent_meanings: commons-governance (the broader field Ostrom's work founded)
important_distinctions: principles apply equally to physical and digital/on-chain commons per the article's framing
tensions: self-governance-legitimacy vs the-work-of-actually-running-graduated-sanctions-and-monitoring
data.risks_of_flattening: Listing the eight principles as a checklist can obscure that Ostrom's original research emphasized they interact and depend on context — no single principle guarantees success in isolation.

data.title: Cooperative types (worker / consumer / savings-and-loan / multi-stakeholder)
data.short_description: Four cooperative models the article distinguishes as building blocks for thinking about what might work locally — owned/controlled by workers, by consumers pooling purchasing power, by savers/lenders (credit unions), or jointly by multiple stakeholder groups.
data.toolkit_usage: Used as a taxonomy readers can map onto existing informal practice (savings circles, burial societies) before deciding what to formalize.
adjacent_meanings: credit-union (the savings-and-loan cooperative form, "one of the most widespread cooperative forms in Africa" per article)
community-supported-agriculture (named as the consumer-cooperative example)
important_distinctions: a cooperative differs from a company in that the people who do the work/use the service own and govern it, rather than outside investors capturing profits
tensions: single-stakeholder-simplicity vs multi-stakeholder-representativeness
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting these as four clean categories understates that real-world cooperatives (e.g. Somaliland's informal savings circles) often blend features and predate formal legal typologies.

data.title: Knowledge Commons
data.short_description: A shared pool of knowledge that a group creates, governs, and maintains together — owned by the group rather than any one person, and structured to keep being useful as people come and go. The "commons" part refers specifically to governance, not just shared access.
source_traditions: Elinor Ostrom, "Governing the Commons" (1990) — eight design principles for how communities manage shared resources (fisheries, forests, irrigation) without privatizing or collapsing them: clear boundaries, locally-fit rules, participation of those affected, monitoring, graduated sanctions, accessible conflict resolution, right to self-organize, and nested governance for larger systems.

Hess & Ostrom, "Understanding Knowledge as a Commons" (MIT Press, 2007) — extends the commons frame to information itself, treating knowledge as vulnerable to the same enclosure/neglect/pollution risks as a physical commons.
data.toolkit_usage: Used to argue that a wiki alone is not a commons — a commons additionally needs rules about who edits, who reviews, and what happens when something is wrong. Applied practically as: write down decisions (not just procedures), assign a steward without centralizing the work, and make contribution legible/low-friction.
adjacent_meanings: wiki (shared editable pages, without necessarily any governance layer)
digital garden (a commons that explicitly admits its unfinished state)
important_distinctions: wiki vs. commons — a wiki with no agreement about how it's tended is "just a slower mess"; the commons label requires the governance layer (Ostrom's monitoring, self-organization, conflict resolution), not merely shared-edit access.

process docs vs. historical docs — the article (citing the Regen Toolkit's own documentation guidance) distinguishes "how to do X" from "why we decided X, what we tried that failed"; the latter is what typically walks out the door with departing people and is what a commons must deliberately capture.
tensions: Open license as governance decision vs. "legal boilerplate" — the article frames choosing CC BY-SA / CC BY 4.0 up front as cheap insurance against future re-enclosure, not a paperwork afterthought.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "knowledge commons" as simply a synonym for "shared wiki" erases Ostrom's core contribution — that a commons is defined by its governance structure (rules, monitoring, self-organization, conflict resolution), not by mere technical shared-access.

data.title: Digital Garden
data.short_description: A knowledge base deliberately grown over time rather than published once and frozen — notes are planted rough, tended, and linked to each other, with their maturity shown openly.
source_traditions: Maggie Appleton, "digital-gardeners" (curated resource collection on GitHub)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as "a knowledge commons that admits it's unfinished" — the right posture for a knowledge base meant to outlive team turnover, since waiting for pages to be "perfect" is the enemy of a living knowledge base. The article's practical instruction: mark a page "rough draft" and publish it rather than withholding it.
adjacent_meanings: knowledge commons (the governance layer a digital garden may or may not have)
wiki (a digital garden is typically personal/small-team rather than mass-collaborative)
important_distinctions: "rough and published" vs. "polished and withheld" — a flagged half-answer is treated as strictly better than a missing one.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "digital garden" as just an aesthetic/tooling choice (Obsidian + Quartz) misses the article's point that it is a posture toward maturity and honesty about a note's completeness, independent of which tool renders it.

data.title: ERC-20 (Fungible Token Standard)
data.short_description: The most widely used Ethereum token standard, covering fungible tokens where every unit is interchangeable with every other unit, with a shared interface for balances, transfers, and delegated spending.
source_traditions: Ethereum Improvement Proposal 20 (ERC-20), per ethereum.org documentation.
data.toolkit_usage: Named in the article as the standard behind community currencies, governance tokens, loyalty/reward systems, and stablecoins like USDC.
adjacent_meanings: fungible token
important_distinctions: ERC-20 vs ERC-721: every ERC-20 unit is identical to every other unit, unlike ERC-721's one-of-a-kind tokens.
tensions: ERC-20 tokens sent to an incompatible smart-contract address can become permanently stuck — a well-known standard-level footgun the article quantifies (see accompanying claim-evidence).
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing ERC-20 only through its "SIM card" interoperability analogy risks omitting the real-world failure mode (irrecoverable loss on incompatible-address sends) that the article itself flags as a named limitation.

data.title: ERC-721 (Non-Fungible Token Standard)
data.short_description: An Ethereum token standard, launched in 2018, in which every token is unique and individually identified within its contract — used for digital art/collectibles, event tickets, ownership certificates, and impact tokens like carbon-removal or biodiversity credits.
source_traditions: Ethereum Improvement Proposal 721 (ERC-721), per ethereum.org documentation.
data.toolkit_usage: Named in the article as the standard for representing specific-verifiable-action impact credits (e.g. carbon removal, biodiversity), land/credential ownership certificates, and event tickets.
adjacent_meanings: non-fungible token (NFT)
important_distinctions: ERC-721 vs ERC-20: uniqueness (each token has its own ID) vs interchangeability.
ERC-721's "safe transfer" function only sends tokens to addresses capable of handling them — a safeguard the article contrasts with ERC-20's lack of that protection.
data.risks_of_flattening: Grouping all "impact tokens" under ERC-721 risks obscuring that ERC-1155 can represent similar unique/semi-fungible impact assets within a single contract, which the article covers separately.

data.title: ERC-1155 (Multi-Token Standard)
data.short_description: An Ethereum token standard that handles both fungible and non-fungible tokens within a single smart contract, supporting batch transfers, lower deployment costs, and semi-fungible tokens (e.g. an event ticket that later becomes a collectible).
source_traditions: Ethereum Improvement Proposal 1155 (ERC-1155), per ethereum.org documentation.
data.toolkit_usage: Named in the article as the fit for communities managing multiple asset types at once — e.g. fungible carbon-credit tokens and non-fungible land-stewardship certificates under one contract.
adjacent_meanings: multi-token standard
semi-fungible token
important_distinctions: ERC-1155 vs deploying separate ERC-20 and ERC-721 contracts: one contract manages both fungible and non-fungible assets, batching transfers and reducing gas costs.
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing ERC-1155 only as "the flexible one" risks understating that the tradeoff for that flexibility is added contract complexity compared to a single-purpose ERC-20 or ERC-721 deployment.

data.title: Type vs. Tag (metadata discipline)
data.short_description: A type says what something *is* (a document has exactly one type, e.g. guide, meeting note, decision, person); a tag says how something might be classified or filtered (a document can have many tags, e.g. governance, solar, draft). Confusing the two creates ontology sprawl.
source_traditions: the Regen Web3 Toolkit's own internal ontology principle 11 ("type / tag discipline")
folksonomy research on collaborative/uncontrolled tagging
library/information-science controlled-vocabulary practice
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as "the one distinction to get right" before designing any metadata schema — the article states plainly that this toolkit's own architecture "makes this its eleventh cross-cutting principle" and warns that confusing tags with types creates ontology sprawl.
adjacent_meanings: controlled vocabulary (the fix once type/tag is separated — a fixed set of approved tag values)
folksonomy (uncontrolled, emergent tagging — the failure mode this distinction guards against)
important_distinctions: type ≠ tag — one type per document (routes it) vs. many tags per document (classifies/filters it); this is the article's central claim
tensions: light vocabulary control (recommended) vs. unmoderated folksonomy tagging — research cited ("Folksonomy," Wikipedia) shows unmoderated tags drift into inconsistency, but heavy-handed control kills contribution; the article does not fully resolve where the line sits, only that some control beats none
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting type/tag discipline as a simple binary rule undersells how hard the "what is the type" question can get for genuinely hybrid documents (e.g. a meeting note that is also a decision record) — the article's own examples are the clean cases, not the ambiguous ones a real commons will hit.

data.title: Token-Based Coordination Mechanisms
data.short_description: The set of mechanisms (signaling, voting, reputation, incentives/penalties) by which token-holding groups align on priorities and manage shared resources without a single central decision-maker.
source_traditions: DAO governance tooling (Snapshot signaling, Tally on-chain voting)
reputation-based contribution tracking (Colony)
quadratic funding mechanism design (Gitcoin)
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article to frame tokens as a governance/coordination layer for regenerative communities, distinct from tokens as speculative assets.
adjacent_meanings: token-weighted voting (plutocratic variant)
reputation/non-transferable Soulbound Tokens (SBTs) as an alternative to wealth-based influence
important_distinctions: signaling (non-binding temperature check) vs voting (binding decision)
on-chain voting (permanent record, gas cost) vs off-chain voting (lighter weight, e.g. Snapshot)
token-wealth-based influence vs contribution/reputation-based influence
tensions: decentralized framing vs multisig-concentrated real power
rewarding participation vs penalizing inactivity without excluding low-capacity members
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "tokens for coordination" as a single solved pattern risks hiding that most implementations still concentrate power in early/wealthy holders or small multisig groups — the article names this explicitly as a recurring, unsolved problem across "thousands of DAOs."

data.title: Chain-selection tradeoffs (speed, sovereignty, shared security, accessibility)
data.short_description: A framework for choosing among non-Ethereum blockchain ecosystems along four axes: raw transaction speed/cost (Solana), full chain sovereignty via custom application-specific chains (Cosmos), shared/borrowed security without running your own validator set (Polkadot parachains, Avalanche subnets), and accessibility/usability for non-technical users (Near).
data.toolkit_usage: Structures the whole article — each ecosystem section maps to one point on this tradeoff space, and the closing "Choosing Where to Build" section makes the framework explicit as a four-question decision guide.

adjacent_meanings.EVM-compatibility (a separate axis: whether existing Ethereum tooling/skills transfer directly)

adjacent_meanings: Layer-2 scaling (a different approach to the speed/cost tradeoff, built on top of Ethereum rather than a separate L1 — referenced in the article's `related` frontmatter but not discussed in the body)
important_distinctions: "You don't need to pick a favourite" — the article frames ecosystem choice as context-dependent rather than a single best-chain ranking.

Cosmos (build-your-own-chain) is distinguished from Polkadot/Avalanche (borrow shared security for a custom chain) — both let a project have "its own chain," but with very different infrastructure commitments.
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — general technical/ecosystem comparison, not attributed to a specific community or tradition.

data.title: Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization
data.short_description: Representing ownership of an off-chain asset (real estate, gold, bonds, art, carbon credits) as an on-chain token, enabling fractional ownership and blockchain-based trading of a claim on that asset.
source_traditions: securitization / fractional ownership finance (traditional REITs, bond markets)
blockchain token-standard infrastructure (ERC-20/ERC-721-style ownership tokens)
data.toolkit_usage: Used in the article as a beginner on-ramp: tokenization framed as "a digital deed" that trades like crypto but derives its value from a real underlying asset.
adjacent_meanings: carbon credit tokenization (ecological asset variant, overlaps with what-are-tokens.md)
tokenized government treasuries (described in article as a fast-growing RWA category)
important_distinctions: owning the token vs owning the underlying asset (custody remains a real-world, off-chain problem)
token price vs oracle-reported real-world value (the two can diverge)
tensions: promise of borderless trading vs assets still bound by national law
promise of "less fraud" via public records vs unresolved custody trust (someone must still physically hold the asset)
data.risks_of_flattening: The article presents tokenization benefits (liquidity, access, cost, speed) as largely settled while listing challenges more thinly; a fuller treatment would need more scrutiny of who verifies the oracle price and who is legally accountable when a custodian fails.

data.title: Hypercert (ERC-1155 impact-claim token)
data.short_description: A digital token, built on the ERC-1155 multi-token standard on Ethereum, that captures who did what work, where, and during what timeframe, sold prospectively (before work, to raise capital) or retrospectively (after impact, to claim funding for completed work), and that can be split or merged so funders can support exactly the slice of impact they care about.
source_traditions: Hypercerts Foundation protocol design
ERC-1155 multi-token standard (Ethereum)
data.toolkit_usage: The core mechanism described in impact-certificates-hypercerts.md for making retroactive-funding claims verifiable, permanent, and transferable.
adjacent_meanings: retroactive-public-goods-funding
quadratic-funding
important_distinctions: A hypercert is a claim of work done, not a certified/audited proof — the article names "Evaluators" as the separate role that assesses impact claims and builds reputation for doing so, distinct from the creator and funder roles.
tensions: Split/merge flexibility for funders vs. the risk of double-counting or overlapping claims across split certificates if not tracked carefully.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article states hypercerts are "Built on the AT Protocol," which appears to be a factual error (AT Protocol is the Bluesky/social-web protocol; hypercerts are ERC-1155 tokens on Ethereum per the same article's "How It Works" section) — flagged separately as a signal rather than repeated here as fact.

data.title: Typing vs Tagging
data.short_description: Two distinct classification jobs that get confused when treated as one: typing answers "what kind of thing is this?" (a small, stable set — guide, tool, case study, meeting note); tagging answers "what is this about, and how might I want to filter it?" (a large, growing set of topics, domains, audiences).
source_traditions: library/information science cataloguing (type vs subject heading)
the Regen Toolkit's own ontology layer
data.toolkit_usage: Framed in the article as the reason AI classification projects go wrong: asking a model one mushy question ("classify this") instead of two clear ones (what kind, what about). The article quotes the Toolkit's ontology layer directly: "A type defines what something is. A tag describes how something may be classified, interpreted, filtered, or used. Confusing tags with types creates ontology sprawl."
adjacent_meanings: categorization (used loosely to mean either typing or tagging)
taxonomy (the overall system of types + tags together)
important_distinctions: type set is small and stable; tag set is large and grows over time
keeping type and tag in separate schema fields makes the AI's job easier because each question has one clear answer
tensions: teams often reach for one all-purpose "category" field, which the article argues quietly recreates the sprawl problem it was meant to solve.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "classification" as a single undifferentiated task erases the distinction the article treats as load-bearing — a taxonomy that mixes types and tags in one field cannot be constrained to a stable enum, because the tag half is supposed to keep growing.

data.title: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) — Core Parts
data.short_description: A group that manages shared money and makes decisions together through code-enforced rules rather than a bank, lawyer, or board of directors — reducible to four parts: treasury, proposals, voting, and smart contracts.
source_traditions: traditional community savings circles / ROSCAs (the article's explicit analogy)
Ethereum smart-contract infrastructure (the "vending machine" mechanism behind automatic execution)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the plain-language entry point before naming specific DAO tooling (Snapshot, Safe, Aragon) and real regen-space DAO examples.
adjacent_meanings: a DAO's treasury as the digital-native version of a shared community bank account
Local Nodes (ReFi DAO) as a DAO-adjacent, place-based organizing pattern rather than a single monolithic DAO
important_distinctions: decentralized (no single boss decides) vs autonomous (rules run automatically as code) — the article treats these as separate properties, not synonyms
off-chain signaling (Snapshot, gasless but not self-executing) vs on-chain execution (Safe/Aragon, enforced by code)
tensions: a DAO "encodes trust so it can't be lost, manipulated, or forgotten" vs the article's own caveat that it won't fix a group that doesn't already trust each other
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing every DAO to "four core parts" risks flattening real differences in how treasuries are actually secured (single multisig vs layered governance), how proposals are vetted before a vote, and how much of the "autonomous" execution is genuinely code-enforced versus still requiring a trusted human signer (as the article itself notes for Snapshot).

data.title: Community-Member Attraction Funnel (Awareness → Interest → Visit → Join)
data.short_description: A four-stage funnel model applied to community building: people discover a node (Awareness, via content/events/referrals), learn more (Interest, via website/docs/conversation), attend (Visit), then commit (Join, becoming members who contribute and stay).
source_traditions: Marketing / growth-funnel frameworks (AIDA and its descendants), applied here to community organizing rather than sales
data.toolkit_usage: Used in this article as the structuring device for a local node's member-attraction strategy, paired with content marketing, community presence, events, and one-on-one outreach as the levers that move people through each stage.
adjacent_meanings: Sales/marketing conversion funnels (the direct source of the metaphor)
Organic community formation (mycelial-network framing used elsewhere on the site, e.g. find-your-community.md, which resists funnel language)
important_distinctions: A member-attraction funnel (this article) vs. organic, listen-first community discovery (find-your-community.md's guidance to "eavesdrop, not join") — the same site holds both framings without reconciling them.
tensions: Funnel/marketing language treats community growth as a conversion process to be optimized, which can pull toward extractive growth-hacking instincts even when the stated goal (authenticity, belonging, purpose) is explicitly anti-extractive.
data.risks_of_flattening: Reducing "who joins and stays" to funnel stages risks flattening the slower, relational, trust-building process the site elsewhere insists on (see find-your-community.md's "slow is safe").

data.title: Peer-Vouched Verification (DeVouch Model)
data.short_description: A decentralized alternative to a single-authority "verified" stamp: trusted verifiers across the ecosystem issue on-chain vouches (worth 1, 3, or 30 points by tier) for a project, replacing one central office's approval decision.
source_traditions: Giveth's project-verification system, decentralized into DeVouch
Web-of-trust / social-vouching models generally (not named in the source article)
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in this article as the mechanic that lets a local node earn donor-facing rewards (GIVpower boost at 3 points, GIVbacks eligibility at 30 points) "decided by your peers, not a gate."
adjacent_meanings: Centralized platform verification (e.g. a single company's "verified" badge)
KYC-based identity verification (a different trust problem — identity, not project legitimacy)
important_distinctions: Peer-vouched verification establishes project legitimacy/reputation; it is not the same as Sybil-resistant identity verification (see governance-mechanism-design.md's treatment of proof-of-humanity tools like Gitcoin Passport/BrightID, a related but distinct problem).
tensions: "Decided by your peers, not a gate" is still a gate — access to GIVpower/GIVbacks depends on which verifiers choose to vouch, which concentrates influence in whoever already has standing in "reputable organizations in the Ethereum ecosystem."
data.risks_of_flattening: Framing this purely as decentralization-of-trust risks obscuring that new/unconnected local nodes without existing Ethereum-ecosystem relationships may find it just as hard to get vouched as to get centrally verified.

data.title: Decentralized MRV (dMRV) for Tree Planting
data.short_description: Using a smartphone (photo + geolocation), AI verification, community review, and blockchain recording to monitor, report, and verify individual tree-planting actions, replacing traditional institution-mediated MRV with a phone-and-protocol pipeline.
source_traditions: Framed in the article through Silvi Protocol's specific implementation: photo/geo capture -> AI check -> community review -> automated stablecoin payout.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the mechanism that lets individual planters "prove" impact directly to funders/donors without an intermediary institution.
adjacent_meanings: impact verification
reforestation MRV
important_distinctions: AI + community "verification" via photo and geopin is a lighter-weight process than field-audited/scientific dMRV used in formal carbon-credit programs; the article does not distinguish these rigor levels.
tensions: The article's framing ("It's transparent... your impact is real and provable") asserts verification confidence that a single promotional source cannot independently substantiate.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting phone-photo + AI + peer-review verification as equivalent to "real and provable" impact risks flattening the real methodological differences between lightweight community MRV and audited ecological verification used for compliance-grade carbon/biodiversity credits.

data.title: Optimistic governance (covenant-challenge pattern)
data.short_description: A governance pattern where proposals execute by default ("act first") and can be challenged if they violate a written covenant, pausing the proposal for adjudication — scales because only contested proposals need review.
source_traditions: 1Hive Gardens (conviction voting + Celeste dispute resolution)
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in conflict-resolution.md as the healthy way to put tooling behind a node's social conflict process: anyone can flag a proposal as violating the community's covenant, sending it to Celeste, where randomly selected token-holders rule on the challenge.
adjacent_meanings: optimistic rollups (same "assume valid, allow challenge" pattern applied to blockchain scaling, not governance)
important_distinctions: optimistic governance (community proposal disputes) is distinct from optimistic rollups (L2 scaling), despite the shared 'optimistic' naming
tensions: low overhead for the common case vs. relying on someone noticing and flagging a bad proposal in time
data.risks_of_flattening: Framing this as a pure tooling fix risks skipping the article's own caution that mechanism only works once the social process (a written, agreed covenant) already exists.

data.title: Fungible vs Non-Fungible Tokens (FT/NFT)
data.short_description: The foundational token distinction: fungible tokens are mutually interchangeable units of equal value (like currency), while non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are each unique and not interchangeable one-to-one with another of the same type.
source_traditions: Ethereum ERC token-standard ecosystem (ERC-20 fungible, ERC-721 non-fungible, ERC-1155 hybrid)
mobile-money systems (M-Pesa) as a pre-crypto fungibility analogue named directly in the article
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the entry-level conceptual split before introducing asset-tokenization use cases (carbon credits, land stewardship rights, cooperative membership) for regenerative communities.
adjacent_meanings: semi-fungible tokens (ERC-1155's hybrid capability, mentioned but not elaborated)
tokens as access keys (the article's opening theme-park-pass framing, broader than the FT/NFT split itself)
important_distinctions: a coin (native to its own blockchain) vs a token (built atop someone else's blockchain) — named as the article's first clarifying distinction
fungible tokens (1:1 interchangeable, e.g. stablecoins) vs NFTs (unique identifier + characteristics, e.g. digital art/collectibles)
tensions: tokens-as-tools-for-real-value (the article's stated conclusion) vs tokens-as-speculation/volatility (named as a real, unresolved concern)
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "carbon credits could be tokenized" and "land stewardship rights could be represented as tokens" as roughly equivalent, low-friction use cases risks flattening the very different legal, ecological- verification, and governance complexity each one actually requires; the article states these as possibilities without engaging that complexity.

data.title: Social recovery and multi-sig as distributed wallet-recovery methods
data.short_description: Two distinct ways to remove a single point of failure from crypto wallet access. Social recovery designates 3-5 trusted "guardians" who can collectively help restore access to a lost wallet (typically with a threshold approval and a time-lock window for the owner to cancel unauthorized attempts). Multi-signature (multi-sig) requires multiple private keys to authorize any transaction in the first place (e.g. 2-of-3, 3-of-5, 4-of-7), functioning as both ongoing security and de facto recovery redundancy.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as two of five recovery methods in the article (alongside seed- phrase backups, Shamir Secret Sharing, and inheritance planning), and recommended as the core organizational/DAO-level practice.
adjacent_meanings: Shamir Secret Sharing (splits a single seed into reconstructable shares — a related but mathematically distinct approach to removing single points of failure)
Multi-sig as security (the article notes multi-sig is "not just recovery planning, it is ongoing security")
important_distinctions: Social recovery restores access to an existing wallet after loss; multi-sig prevents any single actor (including an attacker) from moving funds unilaterally in the first place — the article treats them as complementary, not interchangeable.
"Secret sharing done wrong": the article explicitly distinguishes ad hoc seed-phrase splitting (which weakens security) from proper Shamir Secret Sharing (a specific cryptographic scheme).
data.risks_of_flattening: None flagged — a technical security framework, not attributed to a specific community or tradition.

data.title: Self-custody (non-custodial wallet)
data.definition: A wallet where the user holds the private keys directly rather than a company custodying them — full control and full responsibility, contrasted with a bank that can freeze, reverse, or recover funds.

data.title: Node founding-team roles: convener, builder/doer, treasurer-ops
data.short_description: A minimal role model for a local node's founding team, filling jobs rather than titles — the convener (runs meetings, holds the calendar), the builder/doer (ships events/workshops/on-chain actions), and the treasurer/ops (holds the multisig, tracks grants, keeps the spreadsheet).
source_traditions: ReFi Medellín and ReFi Cartagena's real named team structures (cited as worked examples)
BanklessDAO's contributor playbook (specialize, delegate decisions)
Other Internet's "Web3 Work" research on DAO contributor burnout
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the antidote to "you don't need a CEO, you need a few jobs covered." The article's explicit rule: one person can hold two of the three roles at the start, but no one should hold all three for long, and ownership should be named out loud even informally.
adjacent_meanings: conventional startup C-suite roles (CEO/COO/CFO) — the article explicitly rejects this framing ("you do not need a CEO")
important_distinctions: role clarity (naming who owns what) is treated as the cheapest burnout-prevention tool available, distinct from skill level or technical expertise.
tensions: fast bootstrapping (one person covering multiple roles early) vs. burnout risk and single-point-of-failure risk if that concentration persists.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "founding team" as a headcount question rather than a coverage question misses the article's core claim: two people who trust each other and cover the three roles beats ten who attended one call.

data.title: Quadratic Voting
data.short_description: A voting mechanism where the cost of each additional vote a member casts on a proposal increases quadratically (1 vote = 1 credit, 2 votes = 4 credits, 3 votes = 9 credits), balancing intensity of preference against breadth of support.
source_traditions: Mechanism design theory (credited generally to Glen Weyl / Vitalik Buterin's "quadratic" family of mechanisms, not individually cited in this article)
data.toolkit_usage: Recommended in this article for allocating resources across multiple competing options (e.g. treasury allocation, which projects to fund), and named as a whale-resistance safeguard against wealthy members dominating decisions.
adjacent_meanings: Quadratic funding (a matching-pool allocation formula for donations, not a voting mechanism — see the funding-gatherings and funding-your-node articles' treatment)
Token-weighted voting (the plutocratic mechanism quadratic voting is designed to counterbalance)
important_distinctions: Quadratic voting (governance decisions, personal credit budget) vs. quadratic funding (donation-matching, sponsor-funded pool) — same underlying quadratic-cost math, applied to structurally different problems; conflating them is a common error.
tensions: The article names its own risk directly: "complex to understand, requires credits system" — a mechanism designed for fairness can fail in practice if members don't understand how to use it.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting quadratic voting as simply "the mechanism for fair resource allocation" risks understating its real implementation burden (a credits system, voter education, and Sybil-resistant identity to prevent vote-splitting across fake accounts).

data.title: Conviction Voting
data.short_description: A continuous-funding governance mechanism where members stake tokens on proposals they support; the longer tokens stay staked, the more "conviction" builds, and a proposal passes once conviction exceeds a threshold.
source_traditions: DAO/commons-funding governance patterns (associated in the wider ecosystem with 1Hive/Gardens-style implementations, not named in this article)
data.toolkit_usage: Recommended in this article for continuous funding allocation without discrete voting rounds, positioned alongside quadratic voting as a treasury-allocation mechanism.
adjacent_meanings: Discrete/periodic voting rounds (the model conviction voting replaces)
Token-weighted voting (conviction voting still weights by stake, but adds a time dimension)
important_distinctions: Conviction voting encodes preference *intensity over time* (how long you've stayed committed), whereas quadratic voting encodes preference intensity *at a point in time* (how many credits you spend); the two solve different governance problems and the article recommends them for different situations.
tensions: The article names its own risk: "slow for urgent decisions, complex to implement" — a mechanism built for continuous, patient allocation is a poor fit exactly when a DAO needs to move fast.
data.risks_of_flattening: Describing conviction voting only by its formal mechanic risks understating that it structurally favors well-resourced, patient stakeholders who can afford to leave tokens locked, over cash-constrained members who need liquidity.

data.title: Crypto Donation Onboarding (Nonprofit)
data.short_description: The workflow a nonprofit follows to start accepting crypto donations: choose a donation platform, verify 501(c)(3)/equivalent nonprofit status, configure the account, embed a donate button/widget, and test before going live.
source_traditions: CryptoAltruists Web3 Impact Toolkit (per article frontmatter sources)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed in the article as a low-effort ("about an hour") operational add-on once nonprofit documents are ready, paired with automatic tax-receipt generation for donors.
adjacent_meanings: crypto donation platform onboarding
nonprofit crypto acceptance
important_distinctions: Choosing which cryptocurrencies to accept (e.g. start with Bitcoin and Ethereum) is separate from choosing the platform itself.
data.risks_of_flattening: The "about an hour" framing risks understating the real bottleneck the article itself names: gathering nonprofit verification documents, which is often the slower, org-dependent step.

data.title: KYC/AML handling on crypto-donation platforms
data.short_description: The article's framing that money-laundering/compliance concerns are largely offloaded by a nonprofit onto its chosen donation platform, which verifies donor identity (KYC), screens transactions, and keeps records.
data.toolkit_usage: Used to reassure nonprofit boards that "you're not on your own" for compliance — the platform, not the org, does the heavy lifting.
adjacent_meanings: custodial-vs-noncustodial (most nonprofits use a platform that manages the wallet for them)
important_distinctions: org-level compliance vs platform-level compliance — the article claims the burden sits mostly with the platform
tensions: convenience-of-outsourcing-compliance vs org's-own-fiduciary-responsibility-to-verify-the-platform-is-reputable
data.risks_of_flattening: "Reputable platforms handle it" is a generalization; not every platform's KYC/AML program is equivalent, and the article does not name specific compliance certifications to check for.

data.title: Consent-based Governance (sociocracy)
data.short_description: A decision-making mode where proposals pass unless someone raises a reasoned objection ("can anyone live with it?"), rather than requiring unanimous enthusiasm or a simple majority vote.
source_traditions: sociocracy (the article names this explicitly as "the core of sociocracy")
ReFi DAO's Steward Council as a real-world worked example (first stewards election moving decision-making from founders to elected stewards)
data.toolkit_usage: Named as the mechanism that makes the article's third governance model (the Council) legitimate and fast — a small elected/rotating council handles day-to-day decisions, big calls still go to the whole community.
adjacent_meanings: simple-majority voting (faster to explain, riskier for minorities — the article contrasts these directly)
full consensus (unanimous enthusiasm — the article frames this as "far safer... but far... slower to chase")
important_distinctions: consent ≠ consensus — consent asks "can anyone live with it?" (objection-based, faster); consensus asks "does everyone love this?" (unanimity-based, slower)
tensions: the article recommends term limits/rotation as the guardrail against "power concentrating and the council drifting out of touch" — an acknowledgment that consent-based councils are not self-correcting by design alone
data.risks_of_flattening: Calling a structure "consent-based" does not guarantee it functions that way in practice — the article's own two guardrails (term limits, a written line on what the council can decide alone) suggest the label needs enforced structure behind it, not just adoption of the vocabulary.

data.title: Capital Gains (Crypto, US)
data.short_description: Under US tax treatment, crypto is property; capital gains/losses are calculated from cost basis (what you paid, including fees), and taxed differently depending on holding period: short-term (held ≤1 year, taxed as ordinary income) vs long-term (held >1 year, taxed at 0/15/20%).
source_traditions: US Internal Revenue Service property-taxation framework, as applied to crypto.
data.toolkit_usage: Presented as the foundational concept the rest of the article's taxable/non-taxable event tables and DeFi/NFT tables build on.
adjacent_meanings: cost basis
short-term vs long-term holding
important_distinctions: Taxable events (selling, trading crypto-for-crypto, spending crypto, mining/staking income, airdrops, hard-fork receipts) vs non-taxable events (buying with USD, wallet-to-wallet transfers, charitable donations, gifts under $15,000).
Ordinary income treatment (mining/staking/airdrops) vs capital gains/loss treatment (sales/trades) — two different tax categories for different crypto activities.
tensions: The article notes NFT "collectible" status (28% rate) is contested because NFTs are not physical, unlike the traditional collectibles the 28% rate was designed for.
data.risks_of_flattening: This is explicitly US-specific guidance; presenting "crypto tax rules" without a jurisdiction qualifier risks readers outside the US applying US-specific thresholds (e.g. the $15,000 gift-tax figure) and forms (Form 8949, 1099-DA) to a jurisdiction where they don't apply.

data.title: Quadratic Funding
data.short_description: A matching-fund formula that rewards the *number* of contributors to a project rather than just the total dollar amount, so many small donations can out-earn one large donation; used by Gitcoin Grants rounds.
source_traditions: Mechanism design / public-goods funding theory (Buterin, Hitzig, Weyl)
Gitcoin Grants rounds (crypto-native implementation)
data.toolkit_usage: Introduced here as the mechanism behind Gitcoin Grants' web3-native funding tier for gatherings, illustrated with "100 people giving $1 can out-earn one person giving $100."
adjacent_meanings: Traditional matching-gift programs (dollar-for-dollar, no breadth weighting)
Crowdfunding (raises the base amount but has no matching-pool mechanic)
important_distinctions: Quadratic funding (a matching-pool allocation formula, requires a sponsor-funded pool) vs. quadratic voting (a governance-decision mechanism using a personal credit budget) — related math, different use case; see the governance-mechanism-design article's treatment of quadratic voting.
tensions: Rewards breadth of donors, which can be gamed by Sybil attacks (many fake small donors); the article does not discuss Gitcoin's anti-Sybil safeguards.
data.risks_of_flattening: Presenting "100 people giving $1 can out-earn one person giving $100" as a simple rule risks obscuring that the actual match depends on the specific round's formula, pool size, and anti-Sybil adjustments in effect at the time (the article itself flags that Gitcoin's rounds mix QF with other allocation mechanisms by domain).

data.title: M-of-N Multisig Treasury Management
data.short_description: A treasury control scheme requiring a threshold M of N designated signers to approve any transaction before it executes, instead of a single controller — e.g. 3-of-5 signers must agree.
source_traditions: traditional corporate board-of-directors approval structures
multi-signature cryptography (Bitcoin/Ethereum multisig wallets)
Gnosis Safe's productization of the pattern for DAOs
data.toolkit_usage: Presented in this article as the standard DAO treasury pattern, with concrete recommended thresholds by treasury size (3-of-5 under $10M, 4-of-7 for larger treasuries) and a hot/warm/cold storage split.
adjacent_meanings: multisig as a governance-decision mechanism (DAO Governance Models article's "Multi-Signature Governance" model)
multisig as a pure treasury-security control (this article's framing)
important_distinctions: multisig-governance-model-vs-multisig-treasury-control — the same underlying M-of-N mechanism can be used either to make general DAO decisions (governance) or narrowly to authorize fund movements (treasury security), and this article is specifically about the latter.
tensions: efficiency vs decentralization — a small signer set is fast to act but concentrates power if signers are not rotated or diversified.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "it's multisig, so it's decentralized" flattens that a 3-of-5 (or similar) scheme still concentrates authority in a small, named group of people; the article itself flags this as a real limitation elsewhere in the broader governance-models discussion.

data.title: What Is Decentralization?
data.summary: A plain-language guide to decentralization for community organizers and permaculturists new to crypto: what it means, why it matters for their existing work (local chapters, volunteer coordination, shared treasuries), how it's a spectrum rather than a binary, and how to spot genuine versus hyped decentralization using free/open/fair criteria plus concrete tools (Snapshot, quadratic voting).
data.audience: community organizers and permaculturists new to crypto
known_tensions: openness of infrastructure vs. concentration of day-to-day decision power

data.title: A Tools Directory for Knowledge That Outlives Turnover
data.summary: An opinionated, named-tool guide for building a team knowledge commons that survives contributor turnover. Organized around one governing principle ("infrastructure should follow function") and one portability test ("would your knowledge survive the tool dying?"), it maps tool choices to jobs (team knowledge base, individual notes, public site) and names a public/internal/private visibility-tier substrate mapping.
data.audience: small teams and local nodes choosing knowledge-commons tooling
known_tensions: Polished, collaboration-friendly tools (Notion) vs. durable, portable-in-plain-text tools (Markdown + Git) — the article resolves this as "own your source of truth in plain text and Git; use everything else as a publishing or collaboration layer on top."

Even historically file-based tools can drift away from portability — Logseq's 2025-2026 SQLite-backed "DB version" is cited as a caution that "file-on-disk" is a property to keep checking, not assume.

data.title: The Gatherings Pattern
data.summary: A five-element framework (Purpose, People, Place, Process, Practice) for designing intentional gatherings for local nodes, plus four ready-made gathering formats (Onboarding, Governance, Trust-Building, Learning) and five cross-cutting hosting principles. Framed as the primary way local nodes build the trust and shared understanding that community finance systems require.
data.audience: local node organizers / community hosts
known_tensions: "Don't default to everyone's invited" small-curated-group guidance vs. the inclusive, open-participation norms many decentralized communities hold as a default.
Generous authority (a single host holding structure) vs. anti-hierarchy instincts in horizontally-organized communities.

data.title: Federation and Portability: Building a Commons That Outlives Its Tools
data.summary: Argues that a knowledge commons needs both portability (moving your data between tools/people/orgs without rot) and federation (sharing across groups without merging into one database). Recommends a "portability floor" of plain Markdown in Git (readable, diffable, greppable, vendor-independent) with structure kept in frontmatter, then layers federation on top via named public/internal/private boundaries and stable references — from ad hoc shared folders up to protocols like KOI-net (RIDs) or ActivityPub (Mastodon).
data.audience: small-team leads who work in docs/GitHub but aren't ontologists
known_tensions: protocol-maturity-gap — ActivityPub/Mastodon federates social identity well but, as of 2025, doesn't yet portable-move actual post content

data.title: What Is a Crypto Wallet?
data.summary: A plain-language guide to crypto wallets for community organizers and permaculturists new to Web3: the "wallet holds keys, not money" distinction, public vs. private keys, recovery phrases and their single-point-of-failure risk, newer passkey/guardian-based smart-wallet recovery, hot vs. cold wallet trade-offs, energy-use context, and named scam patterns.
data.audience: community organisers and permaculturists new to Web3
known_tensions: convenience (hot wallet) vs. security (cold wallet)
classic recovery-phrase model (full user responsibility, no recourse) vs. smart-wallet guardian recovery (friendlier, newer, less battle-tested)
related_resources: Smart wallets with passkey/guardian recovery (Base App, Argent "Ready")

data.title: What Is ReFi?
data.summary: A plain-language introduction to Regenerative Finance for community organizers and growers new to crypto: the "money that builds soil instead of mining it" framing, three concrete problem/solution pairs (Silvi for proving impact, Gitcoin quadratic funding for community-driven grants, local tokens for keeping value circulating), the carbon-tokenization example with its Verra greenwashing caution, the proof-of-stake energy-use correction, and honest limitations.
data.audience: community organisers and growers new to crypto
known_tensions: pricing nature in vs. commodifying/greenwashing risk (the Verra episode)
crypto energy-use reputation (Bitcoin proof-of-work) vs. actual footprint of the Ethereum/Celo-based tools ReFi mostly uses

data.title: Gitcoin Grants and Quadratic Funding
data.summary: How quadratic funding distributes a matching pool by counting contributor count rather than dollar totals (sum-the-square-roots-then-square formula), illustrated with a real regen QF round (GG24's Bioregional Reforestation Round), the sybil-defense mechanisms rounds use (Human Passport proof-of-personhood, Connection-Oriented Cluster Matching), a walkthrough for running your own round on Grants Stack, and burnout guardrails for first-time round organizers.
data.audience: local node organizers considering running or joining a QF round
known_tensions: Live "estimated match" figures move after a round closes as Passport eligibility and COCM corrections are applied — organizers are warned not to promise applicants an exact payout in advance.
QF amplifies an existing community; it does not conjure one — a round run before relationships exist will underperform regardless of mechanism design.

data.title: Treasury Management for DAOs
data.summary: Practical guide to DAO treasury management: the "native token problem" (thin liquidity, extreme volatility, broken operational continuity when a treasury holds mostly its own governance token), the case for holding 2-3 years of operating expenses in stablecoins, four diversification methods (earning stablecoin revenue, strategic token sales, strategic partnerships, borrowing against tokens), and Maya Protocol as a transitioning-to-DAO-governance example.
data.audience: 🌱 Maya (beginner track, DAO governance/finance foundations)
known_tensions: diversification improves resilience but strategic token sales and borrowing both carry market-impact / liquidation risk
treasury management choices are framed as governance choices (who holds power), not purely financial ones

data.title: The Funding Landscape
data.summary: A map of web3 and ReFi-native funding mechanisms for local node builders, organized around one axis: prospective funding (grants, quadratic funding) that pays before the work happens, versus retrospective funding (RetroPGF / Retro Funding, hypercerts) that pays after impact is shown. Also surveys direct grants, streaming/recurring funding, yield-based ("evergreen") funding, and conviction voting, and closes on Sybil/collusion risk in QF and the case for blending funding sources so no single funder sets a node's direction.
data.audience: local node organizers evaluating funding mechanisms
known_tensions: Quadratic funding rewards breadth but is structurally vulnerable to Sybil attacks and collusion; every fix (e.g. identity verification via Gitcoin Passport/Human Passport) trades away some decentralization for integrity.
Retro funding rewards track record, which favors established nodes over brand-new ones with no visible output yet.
External/grant funding "often means external priorities entering your community space" — the article's own defense is blending sources, not avoiding funding.

data.title: Common Crypto Scams and How to Spot Them
data.summary: A plain-language field guide to the main crypto scam patterns — phishing, investment/"guaranteed returns" fraud, romance/"pig butchering" scams, and rug pulls — plus the psychological levers (urgency, authority, trust) scammers reuse, practical defenses (hardware wallets, 2FA, bookmarked URLs, multi-sig for shared funds), and what to do if you've been scammed (stop contact, document, report to IC3, alert your community).
data.audience: community organisers and newcomers to Web3
known_tensions: article notes AI is now used to generate convincing scam content/voices, which erodes "professional appearance" as a trust signal

data.title: Ontology vs Taxonomy: Which One Does Your Commons Need?
data.summary: A plain-language guide for teams building a knowledge commons: a taxonomy is a labelled filing cabinet (hierarchy of categories, preferred/alternate labels, broader/narrower/related relations) for browsing and finding things; an ontology adds typed classes, individuals, and named relationships that let software infer facts (e.g. flagging a missing report). The practical heuristic: taxonomy first, ontology only when a specific, recurring task needs machine reasoning over relationships. SKOS is offered as the bridge that keeps the door to an ontology open without wasted work.
data.audience: small-team leads building a knowledge commons who are comfortable in docs/GitHub but not ontologists
known_tensions: taxonomy-vs-ontology scope creep — promoting every useful tag to a structural type balloons the model (ontology sprawl)
classification (taxonomy) vs. machine-reasoning (ontology) are often conflated in practice

data.title: Source Systems: Knowledge That Outlives Turnover
data.summary: Defines a "source system" as a living knowledge environment (wiki, repo, forum, garden…) rather than a one-off link — one that has a steward, keeps getting new material added, and offers a return path to credit and trace claims back to their origin. Contrasts this with a static "link list" that rots. Ties provenance (recorded origin/history) to the principle "inclusion does not mean endorsement," gives real named tools (Obsidian, Logseq, TiddlyWiki, CITATION.cff, ADR/MADR) that already encode these properties, and frames stewardship of a source system as a governance problem (Ostrom's commons-design principles), not just tidying.
data.audience: small-team leads maintaining wikis/repos/knowledge bases who want them to survive contributor turnover
known_tensions: add-broadly-classify-lightly (low friction intake) vs. mark-maturity-honestly (don't let raw material pass as endorsed)
a link list is easy to start and cheap to maintain; a source system requires an actual steward and return path, which is more work up front

data.title: Why Measurement Matters for Your Local Node
data.summary: A practical guide for local-node and chapter builders on measuring impact without bureaucracy or burnout: why measurement prevents burnout on non-compounding activity, the outputs/outcomes/impact distinction, why in Web3 measurement is the funding rail rather than after-the-fact paperwork (retroactive funding, attestation, hypercerts), why holding your own verified record supports node autonomy, and a start-small honest-reporting practice.
data.audience: local node and chapter builders
known_tensions: measurement rigor vs. burnout / bureaucracy risk
node autonomy from a parent DAO/umbrella org vs. needing to report up to the network

data.title: Case Studies: How Nonprofits Are Using Web3
data.summary: Surveys real-world nonprofit adoption of crypto: Ukraine's 2022 emergency crypto fundraising after banks froze, Mercy Corps Ventures cutting delivery costs 60% with stablecoins in Syria, and the fast growth of crypto donations reported by The Giving Block. Frames web3 tools as practical infrastructure (fast settlement, transparency, lower cross-border fees) rather than a speculative novelty, and gives small nonprofits a low-effort on-ramp (accept crypto donations, use stablecoins for cross-border payments, use blockchain records for transparent reporting).
data.audience: nonprofit staff and small charity operators new to crypto
known_tensions: article leans on cited statistics from interested parties (The Giving Block, CryptoAltruists) without independent verification

data.title: What Is a Blockchain?
data.summary: Plain-language, no-hype introduction to blockchains via a "village notebook" analogy: many computers (nodes) keep identical copies of a record, batched into blocks that hash-chain to make history tamper-evident ("immutable"), removing the need to trust any single keeper ("trustless") and solving double-spending without a referee. Covers real regenerative/community examples (Grassroots Economics' Sarafu Network, Regen Network), an enterprise comparison (Walmart on Hyperledger Fabric), and an honest costs section (energy use differences between proof-of-work and proof-of-stake, permanence cutting both ways, and that blockchains record agreement but don't create it).
data.audience: community organisers and growers new to crypto
known_tensions: immutability is good for trust but unforgiving for mistakes (wrong entries/payments usually can't be undone)
'blockchain wastes energy' is true of proof-of-work chains like Bitcoin but false of proof-of-stake chains most regenerative projects actually use

data.title: Your First 90 Days Running a Local Node
data.summary: A paced playbook for standing up a ReFi local node without burnout: convene before you build (days 1-30), distribute the work early (days 31-60), and only fund the thing once there's a track record (days 61-90). Draws on ReFi Medellín's founding story (Tereza Bízková) and Commons Social Change Library burnout research, and points to existing networks (ReFi DAO, Greenpill Network, Regen Coordination) so organizers don't have to invent the whole stack.
data.audience: people starting a new place-based ReFi/regenerative-finance node
known_tensions: grant-payout-timing-vs-early-costs — Gitcoin-style grants can take up to three months to pay out, so early events must be funded some other way

data.title: Review and Maturity: Labelling What Your Knowledge Can Be Trusted To Do
data.summary: Guidance for labelling how trustworthy each page in a knowledge commons is, so trust survives founder/author turnover. Names the trap ("polished writing is not automatically reviewed knowledge"), borrows three proven maturity ladders (Wikipedia content assessment, ADR/MADR status field, Kubernetes Alpha/Beta/Stable), proposes a shippable four-rung ladder (Draft/Reviewed/Maintained/Deprecated) stored in frontmatter, ties review rigor to risk level, and treats maturity as an ongoing maintenance signal (expiry by date, compost instead of delete) rather than a one-time label.
data.audience: small-team leads building docs/wikis that must outlive their authors
known_tensions: self-claimed states (draft/proposed/alpha) vs. granted states (reviewed/accepted/stable) — the promotion gate only belongs on granted tiers
review-everything-equally burns teams out vs. review-scaled-to-risk leaves gaps if risk is misjudged

data.title: The Decentralization Spectrum
data.summary: Frames decentralization as a spectrum rather than a binary. Covers three network-architecture types (centralized, decentralized, distributed), four governance forms (deconcentration, delegation, devolution, privatization), and two cross-cutting dimensions (technological vs. sociopolitical decentralization) that must both be evaluated to judge how decentralized a system really is. Argues decentralization is a design tool to be tuned to context, not an ideology to maximize.
data.audience: individuals building or participating in regenerative systems (beginner level)
known_tensions: technological-vs-sociopolitical — a system can be technically decentralized (many nodes) while power/token concentration keeps real control narrow
resilience-vs-decision-speed — fully distributed systems maximize resilience but can struggle to make timely decisions

data.title: Wallet Comparison Guide
data.summary: A beginner-oriented comparison of four Android crypto wallets (Coinbase Wallet, MetaMask, Trust Wallet, Rainbow) on ease of use, feature breadth, and blockchain support, plus core wallet concepts (public address vs secret/seed phrase), safety tips, and step-by-step first-wallet setup instructions tied to a specific program's onboarding flow.
data.audience: complete beginners setting up their first crypto wallet on Android, within a specific program's onboarding
known_tensions: ease-of-use (Coinbase Wallet) vs feature breadth/Web3-app-compatibility (MetaMask)
simplicity for beginners vs the safety burden of self-custody (no bank to call if the seed phrase is lost or stolen)

data.title: How Blockchain Transactions Work
data.summary: Walks through the seven-step life cycle of a blockchain transaction — creation, signing (with a private key), broadcasting to the mempool, node verification, block inclusion, network consensus, and confirmation — and connects it to why transparent, permanent, no-single-entity records matter for community economies.
data.audience: beginners with no prior blockchain background
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: the article's "Try This" permaculture-notebook analogies and blockchain-explorer exercise were left as narrative exercises, not extracted as separate typed objects. "Bankless Academy - Blockchain Basics" is not re-created as a new resource object — an identically-titled resource already exists in data/kb/resource.yaml from a prior ingestion slice.

data.title: Building Trust in Community Finance
data.summary: A guide to building and protecting the trust a local node's community finance (timebank, local currency, shared treasury) runs on, for organizers already working in regen/web3. Distinguishes verification (proof of what happened) from trust (belief people will do what they say), names three kinds of trust to build deliberately (competence, integrity, benevolence), lists concrete trust-building practices (transparency by default, consistency, owning mistakes, keeping commitments, inclusion, celebrating trustworthy behavior), addresses the "trust velocity" bootstrapping paradox, names early warning signs of trust breakdown, and gives a five-step repair process after a breach. Cites Fukuyama's social-trust thesis and Grassroots Economics' Sarafu Network as worked evidence.
data.audience: organizers running community treasuries, timebanks, or local currencies
known_tensions: technology gives verification, not trust — the article treats a smart contract as able to enforce a rule but not make people want to show up, arguing nodes must build social trust rather than substitute technology for trust not yet earned.
trust velocity paradox — you need trust to run community finance, but you need to run community finance together to build trust; resolved by starting low-stakes and graduating trust over time.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No individual community members named; no exact locations, TEK, or

  public-use-boundary object.

data.title: Types of Gatherings for Local Nodes
data.summary: A practical guide for regen local-node organizers to a repertoire of gathering formats — informal (community meal, walk-and-talk, open house), educational (workshop, learning circle, demonstration day), decision-making (town hall using consent-based decision-making, retrospective), and celebration (milestone party, open celebration) — matched to a node's stage of development (pre-formation through renewal), with a sustainable weekly/monthly/quarterly rhythm and named real-world examples from ReFi Cape Town, ReFi Barcelona, and ReFi DAO's global cadence.
data.audience: people starting or running a regen local node (ReFi DAO / GreenPill Network chapter organizers)

known_tensions.format-choice-determines-outcome vs topi: same topic, different container, opposite result)

known_tensions: high-effort/ambitious-calendar vs low-effort/sustainable-rhythm (burnout risk)
central-facilitator-driven decisions vs genuinely-shared decision-making (why the guide pushes consent-based process)

data.title: What Is Ethereum?
data.summary: A beginner explainer for regenerative community builders (written for a Somaliland/East Africa audience) framing Ethereum not as "another cryptocurrency" but as a shared, tamper-proof digital notebook run by thousands of computers with no single controller. Explains smart contracts via a vending-machine metaphor (set conditions, code executes automatically, no middleman), sketches concrete regen use cases (DAO decision-making, transparent fundraising, automatic crop insurance via oracles), and addresses the energy-use objection head-on (Ethereum's 2022 "Merge" cut energy use ~99%).
data.audience: individual community builders new to Web3, East Africa / Somaliland
known_tensions: Ethereum-as-money vs. Ethereum-as-platform — the article's central reframing is that Ethereum's differentiator from Bitcoin is programmable smart contracts, not just being "digital cash."

data.title: What is dMRV and Why Should You Care?
data.summary: A beginner-friendly introduction to Digital Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (dMRV) — proving that regenerative work (tree planting, water conservation, grazing-land recovery) really happened, using phones/apps for data collection and either automated (satellite) or human verification. Walks through worked examples from Hargeisa and Berbera, a simple four-step process, and a five-step getting-started guide using tools like KoboToolbox, ODK, or Google Forms.
data.audience: Researcher / grassroots practitioners (beginner)
known_tensions: simple-phone-based-data-collection vs the technical/carbon-market expectations of formal MRV standards — the article deliberately keeps the bar low ("you don't need expensive equipment") while still connecting to "carbon markets and environmental programs" that require verified data.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- "Fatima's group in Hargeisa" and "a women's cooperative in Berbera" are

  person-nodes. The named locations (Hargeisa, Berbera) combined with
  specific project outcomes are a high-risk trigger (exact locations +

  public-use-boundary objects below.

data.title: Documentation for Local Nodes
data.summary: A practical guide to community documentation: why it builds institutional memory, the four types a node needs (governance, process, historical, knowledge-base), tool choices by tier (Google Docs/Drive, Notion/Coda, GitHub/GitBook), a priority guide (must-have/should-have/nice-to-have), maintenance practices (assign ownership, review schedule), a two-track documentation workflow (event-driven and ongoing), best practices (clear, concise, current, accessible), and common mistakes to avoid.
data.audience: Local-Organizer
known_tensions: over-documentation-risk vs the core argument that documentation prevents knowledge loss — the article explicitly warns "do not try to document everything," in tension with its own case for documenting thoroughly.
accessible-familiar-tools (Google Docs) vs durable-technical-tools (GitHub/GitBook) — the article frames this as a real trade-off between ease of adoption and long-term platform survival.

  mega-objects" while avoiding a near-complete tool-list dump for

data.title: Planning Web3 Events for Your Local Node
data.summary: A practitioner playbook for running local-node events without burning out organizers. Core moves: pick one job per event (educational, social, working, or celebration — never all four at once); tie web3 tooling to a concrete local question rather than leading with tokenomics; follow a five-phase repeatable plan (define the job, set logistics, promote, run the day, follow up within 24 hours); budget for the tier you can repeat monthly rather than a heroic one-off; and rotate hosting/roles so no single person becomes the node. Includes a current (mid-2026) survey of event tooling costs and status changes (Luma, Meetup, Eventbrite, Gather, POAP, Galxe OAT).
data.audience: local node stewards / community organizers
known_tensions: Attendance-badge collections (POAP/Galxe OAT) are framed as a nice touch, but the article also notes they "quietly become your node's on-chain history of who showed up," which "can later inform who gets a vote, a role, or a share of a grant" — a governance-relevant use the article flags but does not fully work through.

data.title: Common Pitfalls When Starting a Local Node
data.summary: Eight recurring failure patterns that sink new local regen nodes/chapters — designing in a vacuum, chasing on-chain tooling before the coordination problem is proven, premature governance theatre, founder burnout, confusing motion with progress, over-isolating or over-attaching to a parent network, and giving up during a natural low-participation dip — each paired with a concrete fix drawn from real projects (Greenpill Network, Grassroots Economics/Sarafu, Compound DAO's Proposal 289, hOurworld).
data.audience: people starting or stewarding a new local regen node/chapter
known_tensions: move-fast-with-a-token vs prove-the-coordination-problem-manually-first
autonomous-node vs connected-to-the-wider-network
sophisticated-governance-tooling vs actual-voter-participation

data.title: DAOs vs Traditional Organizations: A New Way to Coordinate
data.summary: Contrasts DAOs with traditional hierarchical firms across four dimensions — how decisions get made, organizational structure (flat vs pyramid), and how capital is raised (token issuance vs venture capital/loans/IPOs) — then lists benefits (reduced overhead, transparency, global access, aligned incentives) and honest challenges (voter fatigue, token concentration, legal uncertainty), with East-Africa-specific framing around cooperatives and cross-border participation.

data.title: Human Review Boundaries for a Knowledge Commons
data.summary: Argues that a knowledge commons needs an explicit, written "review boundary" — sorted by the consequence of an entry being wrong, not by its volume or length — so it neither buries reviewers under every edit nor lets unreviewed content masquerade as agreed truth. Proposes a three-tier model (ephemeral/personal, working/shared, canonical/load-bearing), grounds it in Elinor Ostrom's commons-governance principles, and shows how a Git/PR workflow (or a Notion Status property) can make the tool enforce the gate instead of a person policing it.
data.audience: small teams stewarding a wiki, digital garden, or knowledge base who need it to survive staff/volunteer turnover
known_tensions: reviewing-everything-bottlenecks-the-steward-vs-reviewing-nothing-lets-the-commons-rot
git-PR-audit-trail-rigor-vs-Notion's-lower-learning-curve-for-non-technical-teams

Ostrom's design principles were not re-asserted as a duplicate claim-evidence object — a near-identical claim ("Commons governance principles (Ostrom) apply to source-system stewardship") already exists in data/kb/claim-evidence.yaml; a more specific SuperBenefit-tiering claim was captured instead.

data.title: Is Your Community Ready for a Local Node?
data.summary: A readiness check for organizers standing up a local ReFi node, arguing that the technology is the easy part and the gap between imagined and actual participation is what kills these projects. Uses the nine-stage Community Readiness Model to set "stage 5, preparation" as the honest launch cutoff, lists green/red flags, gives a three-part readiness test (organize one small thing, handle one small conflict, sustain effort three months), and warns against single-founder dependency using the collapse of Ithaca Hours, the Bristol Pound, and the Brixton Pound as cautionary examples, contrasted with the resilient, multi-stakeholder Sarafu Network.
data.audience: organizers preparing to launch a local ReFi node/chapter
known_tensions: this-isnt-gatekeeping-framing-vs-the-real-effect-of-telling-a-community-it-isnt-ready-yet
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: "Grassroots Economics / Sarafu Network" is not re-created as a new resource object — it already exists in data/kb/resource.yaml from a prior ingestion slice. data.title: Common Concerns About Web3, Answered Honestly
data.summary: A myth-by-myth response to the standard newcomer worries about web3 for permaculturists and community organisers: is it a scam, is it only for the rich, is it just gambling, what about the environment, do I need to understand the tech, and what happens when I make mistakes. Distinguishes fraud (a human problem) from the tool, separates the volatile token from the underlying technology, and gives a precise (not hand-wavy) answer on energy use by contrasting proof-of-work and proof-of-stake networks.
data.audience: permaculturists and community organisers new to Web3, weighing whether to look closer
known_tensions: transparency-as-scam-fighter vs transparency-does-not-stop-fraud
token-price-speculation vs the-underlying-coordination-technology

data.title: What Is Cryptocurrency?
data.summary: A plain-language introduction to cryptocurrency for community organizers and growers, using a "shared notebook" analogy for blockchain, drawing the coin/token distinction, and grounding the "why should I care" question in four concrete cases (Sarafu Network local currency, Regen Network ecological credits, Glo Dollar's donation-funding stablecoin, and cheap cross-border remittances), before addressing head-on the three standard fears: environmental impact, scams, and hype.
data.audience: community organisers and growers new to crypto (gardens, tool libraries, seed swaps)
known_tensions: decentralisation-as-no-single-boss vs the practical need for someone to still write good software and maintain it
crypto's real environmental cost is chain-specific (proof-of-work vs proof-of-stake), not a single verdict
the honest "you almost certainly don't need crypto" framing vs the four cases presented as genuinely useful
