data.title: NFTs Beyond Art: Practical Applications of Digital Ownership
data.summary: Surveys non-collectible uses of NFTs (blockchain records of unique-item ownership): gaming/virtual-economy asset ownership, digital credentials/attestations for informally-trained skills, real-estate fractional ownership, supply-chain/product-provenance tracking, fraud-proof event ticketing with enforced resale rules, and direct-to-fan music releases with automatic royalty splits. Frames the value as permanent, verifiable, hard-to-forge ownership records rather than the speculative art/collectible use case.
data.audience: community organizers / individuals exploring web3 tools
known_tensions: Gaming section raises "who captures the value" of in-game digital labor once assets are player-owned and tradeable, without resolving it.

Real-estate fractionalization is framed as opening property investment access, but the article itself flags open questions about what fractionalizing collective/community-trust property would mean in practice.

data.title: Leadership Development for Community Finance
data.summary: How to identify, develop, and distribute leadership within a local node so community finance survives the departure of any single person. Names the "leadership paradox" (need coordination, but concentrated leadership recreates hierarchy), the "founder trap," qualities to look for in emerging leaders (initiative, reliability, relational skill, learning orientation, long-term thinking), a five-part development model, three distribution structures (role rotation, nested leadership, federated structure), five common mistakes, and a five-stage pathway from Observer to Elder. Frames leadership in East African / Somaliland contexts as already relational and contextual (clan elders, women's group leaders, mosque committee members) rather than importing a single-founder model.
data.audience: local-node organizers and community stewards, East Africa / Somaliland-focused track
known_tensions: the "leadership paradox" itself — enough leadership to coordinate collective action vs. too much leadership recreating the hierarchies community finance is meant to escape

data.title: An Editorial Workflow Your Commons Won't Outgrow
data.summary: A concrete editorial workflow for knowledge commons: five stages (Draft, Review, Approve, Publish, Maintain); making trust-state visible on every page (status field or growth labels like seedling/budding/evergreen); separating claims from evidence with a Wikipedia Good-Article-style citation spot-check; using pull requests (and GitBook's change-request equivalent for non-coders) as the review container, with CODEOWNERS auto-assigning reviewers; sorting pages by Diátaxis type (tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation) so reviewers know what "good" means for that page; treating maintenance as an owned, scheduled stage rather than an afterthought; and handling disagreement as a normal, non-violent part of the review process.
data.audience: small knowledge-commons/documentation teams
known_tensions: polished-writing vs reviewed-knowledge — "a well-written page can still be wrong," the article's core justification for separate Review/Approve stages.

friendly-non-technical-tooling (GitBook) vs rigorous-technical-tooling (GitHub pull requests + CODEOWNERS) — presented as the same underlying container with a friendlier door, not a real trade-off in outcome.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded

  conflict-management approach are all cited with named sources but treated

  objects rather than separate resource cards, since the article uses them
  as evidentiary references rather than tools this commons would adopt
  directly (unlike GitBook and Vale, which are actionable recommendations).
- No people/community profiles, exact locations, or MRV/ecological/funding
  claims — this is meta-level guidance about documentation process; no
  public-use-boundary object created.

data.title: Seed Phrases
data.summary: A plain-language explainer of seed phrases (Secret Recovery Phrase / mnemonic phrase) for community organisers and regenerative practitioners new to crypto: what the 12-24 word BIP39 phrase is, why it works across wallets and chains, how to store it safely, the phishing/social-engineering scams that target it, and multisig (Safe) as the group-treasury alternative to a single point of failure.
data.audience: community organisers and regenerative practitioners new to crypto
known_tensions: Full personal responsibility for the phrase (no password reset, no support line) is presented as empowering self-custody, but is also a real single-point-of-failure risk for individuals and treasuries.
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: no high-risk personal/location/TEK/MRV content in this article; no public person-nodes to create. The "For Community Treasuries" section's succession-planning questions are general governance prompts, not specific funding/legal advice, so not flagged high_risk.

data.title: How to Get Your First Crypto
data.summary: A scam-aware, "start tiny" guide for community organizers acquiring their first cryptocurrency, covering three ways in (centralized exchange, peer-to-peer with escrow, earning through paid work/bounties/staking), the energy objection (Bitcoin proof-of-work vs. Ethereum's post-Merge proof-of-stake), and a set of non-negotiable scam-avoidance habits.
data.audience: community organizers and growers with no prior crypto experience, especially those weighing crypto for cross-border grant/donation receipt
known_tensions: convenience-of-a-centralized-exchange-vs-custody-risk-of-trusting-a-company
earning-crypto-through-real-work-vs-chasing-free-airdrops
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: Greenpill Network is not re-created as a new source-system object here — it already exists in data/kb/source-system.yaml from a prior ingestion slice. The Ethereum Merge ~99.95% energy-reduction claim and the "no legitimate service asks for your seed phrase" warning are not re-created as new claim-evidence objects — near-identical claims already exist in data/kb/claim-evidence.yaml. Coinbase/Kraken are not created as new resource objects (generic, well-known centralized exchanges named only in passing); LocalCoinSwap and Bisq were chosen as the more novel P2P-specific resources worth capturing.

data.title: Funding Your Local Node
data.summary: A staged funding framework for local regen nodes: start free on purpose (free tools, learn real costs), move to member contributions and sweat equity, add earned revenue (workshops, goods, service fees) that stays local, manage money transparently via a fiscal host (Open Collective) or on-chain multisig (Safe) before scaling, then pursue external funding (Gitcoin Grants, Greenpill Network chapter rounds + hypercerts, ReFi DAO's Local Node program) only once the model is proven. Names concrete pitfalls (taking big money too early, over-funding, no Year-2 plan, letting the funding model reshape community values) and a realistic month-by-month sequence.
data.audience: local regen node builders deciding how to fund the node
known_tensions: The "funding model shapes your community" table names real trade-offs (member fees risk excluding lower-income members; grants drift toward funder priorities; earned revenue pulls toward what sells; sweat equity risks burnout) without resolving them — presented as an honest choice, not a solved problem.

data.title: Writing Grant Proposals
data.summary: A practical guide for local node builders writing Web3 grant proposals. Distinguishes prospective grants (fund a promise of future work) from retroactive grants (reward already-delivered impact, e.g. Optimism's Retro Funding), explains quadratic funding (QF) math and its implication that "your job isn't only to impress a panel, it's to turn out a lot of real people," lists what a working proposal contains per Gitcoin's own guidance (lead with a TL;DR including how the money will be spent, metrics over promises, show your team, iterate in public), argues that for a local node in a QF round the proposal IS the fundraising campaign (anchored on ReFi DAO's GG18 Local Node round case study), and closes with an explicit warning against single-source grant dependency as a burnout/turnover trap, recommending diversified funding.
data.audience: local node builders writing their first Web3 grant proposal
known_tensions: Grant as finish line vs. grant as one input — the article's central argument is that single-source grant dependency is a burnout/turnover risk, not that grants are bad.
Impressing a panel vs. turning out real people — in QF specifically, the article reframes proposal-writing as a community-organizing task, not a persuasive-writing task.

data.title: Onboarding New Members to Your Local Node
data.summary: A practical playbook for local-node stewards on welcoming and integrating new members without becoming the bottleneck. Reframes onboarding as a "trellis, not a funnel" — a pre-built structure newcomers climb rather than a conversion pipeline. Centers the first-90-days retention window, a one-buddy-per-newcomer system, a repeatable first-week structure, using web3 tooling (POAP, USSD access) as a welcome mat rather than a gate, and graduating members into roles (observe → first contribution → real role) so onboarding becomes self-sustaining and steward burnout is addressed as part of the onboarding design itself.
data.audience: local node stewards / community organizers
known_tensions: Token-gating as a filtering instinct ("prove you belong before we let you in") vs. the article's explicit recommendation to use web3 tools (POAP, phone-first access) to lower barriers instead.

Leaning on network-level support (ReFi DAO incubator, shared guides) framed as "mutual aid, not central overreach" — the article draws this line but flags it as something a steward must actively guard.

data.title: Which Chain Is Right for Your Project?
data.summary: A decision-framework guide (Somaliland/East Africa audience, Community- Steward level) for choosing a blockchain among 1,000+ options. Frames the choice around the "blockchain trilemma" (scalability, security, decentralization), maps use cases to chains (Ethereum L1 for high-value DeFi, Layer 2s like Base/Optimism/Arbitrum for general apps, Solana for high-volume consumer apps, Polygon for gaming), gives a TPS/fee comparison table, covers ecosystem/composability, developer-language fit (Solidity vs Rust vs Move), EVM-compatibility, consensus-mechanism energy tradeoffs (PoS vs PoW), and cross-chain bridge risk, closing with a six-question decision framework.
data.audience: community-steward-level project builders choosing a blockchain
known_tensions: The blockchain trilemma itself — the article states plainly that optimizing for one of scalability/security/decentralization typically means compromising on another; there is no chain that maximizes all three.

data.title: Smart Contracts Explained
data.summary: An accessible explainer of smart contracts (self-executing, transparent, immutable, decentralized programs on a blockchain), how they work (write -> deploy -> monitor -> execute -> record), their permissionless and composability properties, multisig contracts, the oracle problem (why they can't see the real world), and their limits (bugs are permanent, size limits, no legal recognition yet) — framed for East African regenerative communities.
data.audience: East African regenerative/community practitioners new to smart contracts
known_tensions: "Code is law" is presented as both a strength (no one can secretly alter the rules) and a risk (bugs execute exactly as written, with no undo).
Oracles are named as the mechanism that connects contracts to real-world data, and also as one of the most common failure points in practice.
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: no people/location/TEK/MRV high-risk content; the Hargeisa/Djibouti/sesame-trader scenario and sorghum-farmer/NGO examples are illustrative hypotheticals, not real named individuals, so no public-use-boundary or person-node created.

data.title: Multisig Setup for Community Treasuries
data.summary: A step-by-step guide to multi-signature wallets for community treasuries: what a multisig is and why it eliminates single points of failure, threshold configurations (2-of-3, 3-of-5, 4-of-7) and how to choose signers (geographic spread, role diversity, technical capacity), timelocks for large transactions, a five-step setup process on Gnosis Safe, ongoing operations (proposing/approving transactions), security best practices, common mistakes, and social recovery (Argent, SoulWallet) as an alternative for individual (not community) wallets.
data.audience: DAO operators and community treasurers
known_tensions: lower threshold (2-of-3: faster, but "if you lose any two signers, you lose access to the funds") vs. higher threshold (3-of-5 or 4-of-7: more resilient, but requires more coordination)
data.notes: Flagged high_risk: true — treasury/security guidance where getting the configuration wrong has direct financial consequences for a community; see paired public-use-boundary object (05-).

data.title: Finding Support and Mentorship
data.summary: A short guide for local-node builders on finding mentors, peer networks, technical support, and funding support. Names four support types (mentorship via other node leaders/cooperative-development orgs/community foundations/social-enterprise mentors; peer networks of similarly-staged nodes; technical support via developer communities and protocol teams; funding support via Gitcoin Grants, Giveth, and local funds), four ways to find mentors, and norms for being a good mentee.
data.audience: local regen node builders

data.title: Why Regens Are Interested in Blockchain
data.summary: An entry-level explainer for permaculturists and community organizers brand new to crypto, framing blockchain as plumbing, not magic, and asking why a "regen" (regenerative practitioner) would care. Names the fears first (scams, energy use, wasting time/looking foolish) and answers each honestly. Covers three concrete draws: funding without a gatekeeper (quadratic funding via Gitcoin), deciding things together in the open (DAOs, Snapshot voting), and ownership that stays local (self-custody, tokens as membership/voting markers, Sarafu as the grounded example). Closes by citing Greenpill Network's "tool-first honesty" stance: start with the community's actual problem, then ask whether blockchain helps.
data.audience: permaculturists and community organizers brand new to crypto
known_tensions: Tool-first honesty vs. crypto evangelism — the article explicitly distances the "regen corner" from broader crypto speculation/scam culture, framing usefulness-to-the-work as the only relevant test.

data.title: ReFi vs. DeFi vs. TradFi: Three Ways to Move Money
data.summary: A plain-language comparison of three financial systems for community organizers: TradFi (centralized institutions — banks, credit unions, grant foundations), DeFi (no-gatekeeper smart-contract finance, mostly speculative in practice), and ReFi (DeFi's machinery redirected at ecological/social repair, illustrated with Regen Network's ecocredit registry, Gitcoin's quadratic funding, and Grassroots Economics' Sarafu community currency). Addresses the "doesn't crypto boil the planet" objection via Ethereum's 2022 proof-of-stake switch, and closes with a task-to-tool matching table rather than an either/or framing.
data.audience: community organisers and permaculturists new to web3 finance concepts
known_tensions: DeFi is described as genuinely powerful infrastructure ("$150 billion... on any given day") but "usually just 'more money'" with no connection to anything growing in the ground — the article holds both points at once rather than resolving them.

data.title: Why Local Matters
data.summary: Argues that place-based nodes do work global protocols structurally cannot: capital is light and can flow anywhere, but trust is heavy and must be built face-to-face over time (the "Ethereum Localism" framing: "what is heavy should be local, what is light should be global and shared" — i.e. subsidiarity). Covers what a node does that a protocol can't (onboarding, deciding which local projects are real, custody/ accountability, the "eight forms of capital" beyond money), the standing network infrastructure a new node can plug into (Greenpill Network, quadratic funding via Gitcoin Grants), the "start small" pattern against building something nobody uses, designing against founder burnout from day one, and concrete tools a node can borrow (Mento/Celo local stablecoins, impactMarket UBI rails, the Regen Coordination Local ReFi Toolkit, BioFi Project templates).
data.audience: people who already know web3 and are ready to stand up a local node
known_tensions: Local autonomy vs. central overreach — the article frames subsidiarity and distributed local ownership as the defence against both a global DAO/funder steering local work and against founder burnout.
Starting small vs. building infrastructure — explicitly warns against setting up a DAO/token/five-tier governance model before the group has the coordination problems those solve.

data.title: Building in Public
data.summary: A short practice guide for local nodes on sharing progress, failures, and learnings openly as they build: posting updates, sharing decisions, and being transparent about challenges. Lists why it works (attracts supporters, creates accountability, builds trust, generates content, helps other nodes), what to share (progress updates, lessons learned, behind-the-scenes decision-making and financial transparency), where to share (Twitter/X, Farcaster, blog, newsletter, Discord/Telegram), and four best practices: be consistent, be honest, be specific, engage with responses.
data.audience: local node organizers deciding how to communicate publicly
known_tensions: consistency vs polish — the article's closing line, "consistency matters more than polish," treats frequent small updates as more valuable than infrequent, highly produced ones.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No people/community profiles, exact locations, TEK, MRV/carbon claims,
  or funding/legal/governance recommendations — no high-risk trigger.
  "Financial transparency" is listed only as a category of content to
  share, not a specific recommendation about treasury structure.
- The article names no specific tools, orgs, or external sources beyond
  generic platform categories (Twitter/X, Farcaster, Discord/Telegram) —
  too generic to warrant dedicated resource objects.

data.title: Donor Stewardship in Web3
data.summary: A short guide on stewarding crypto donors: thank donors within 24 hours (including the transaction ID as blockchain proof), provide ongoing impact updates (photos, stories, crypto-to-impact conversions), understand crypto donor motivations (transparency, global access, innovation), consider publishing onchain proof of fund usage, and build community around major crypto donors.
data.audience: nonprofit/regenerative-project fundraisers (grounded-regen)
known_tensions: crypto-native donor expectation of onchain transparency vs traditional nonprofit donor-communication norms — the article frames this gap as an opportunity ("builds trust in a way traditional finance can't match") rather than a problem.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- Article's own frontmatter marks research_done: false and gives a single
  source ("CryptoAltruists Web3 Impact Toolkit") with no link — no
  resource object created for it since the article gives no URL and no
  further descriptive detail to responsibly build a resource card without
  inventing facts.
- No people/community profiles, exact locations, or MRV/ecological claims
  in this short article. The suggestion to "publish onchain proof of how
  funds are used" / a donor address is a lightweight operational
  suggestion, not a funding/legal/governance recommendation about a
  specific organization — judged not to cross the high-risk threshold, but
  flagged here for reviewer judgment call given it touches financial
  transparency practice.

data.title: Crypto Donation Platforms: What You Need to Know
data.summary: Orients a nonprofit to what crypto-donation platforms do (donor landing page, handling blockchain transactions, optional conversion to dollars, payout, tax receipts), surveys named options (The Giving Block, Infinite Giving, CryptoAltruists, plus Causes/Facebook giving, Binance Charity, Alchemy Pay), gives a what-to-look-for checklist (fees, supported coins, instant conversion, integration, support), and a getting-started flow (verify 501(c)(3) status, customize page, publish, promote).
data.audience: nonprofit staff choosing a crypto-donation platform to onboard
known_tensions: holding-crypto-for-appreciation vs instant-conversion-to-avoid-volatility
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- no independent verification of platform fee levels, supported-coin counts,
  or nonprofit-verification requirements beyond what the article itself
  states; treated as a directory-style overview, not fact-checked pricing.

data.title: Key Terms A-Z
data.summary: An A-Z glossary of beginner web3 and Regen terms (Airdrop through Yield Farming) — wallets and keys, DeFi mechanics (APR, liquidity, staking), DAOs and governance tokens, and crypto slang (FOMO, rug pull, moon). Ends with a security reminder never to share a seed phrase or private key.
data.audience: beginners new to web3 and regenerative finance
known_tensions: glossary brevity vs. accuracy — each term is a one- or two-sentence simplification of concepts (e.g. Proof of Stake, oracles) that have much deeper technical and economic nuance elsewhere in the toolkit
data.notes: Source is a flat A-Z glossary (~80 terms) authored by Tej Pipeline for the "Sarreya programs" cohort; captured whole as one encyclopedia entry rather than one object per term.

data.title: The History of Bitcoin
data.summary: A chronological explainer of Bitcoin's origins, foundations-track intro article: the pre-Bitcoin digital-cash experiments (Chaum's ecash, Back's hashcash, Dai's b-money, Szabo's bit gold, Finney's RPOW), Satoshi Nakamoto's October 2008 whitepaper solving the double-spend problem without a central authority, the January 2009 genesis block, the 2010 Bitcoin Pizza Day transaction and the August 2010 value-overflow bug and its fix, Bitcoin's 2011-2012 mainstream milestones, and Satoshi's disappearance. Frames Bitcoin as the culmination of 30+ years of attempts to build money that doesn't depend on central authorities.
data.audience: newcomers to crypto/web3 in a foundations learning track
known_tensions: each pioneer (Chaum, Back, Dai, Szabo, Finney) solved one piece of the digital-cash puzzle but needed a central authority or never launched; the article frames Bitcoin's contribution as synthesis, not any single novel idea.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- Named individuals (Satoshi Nakamoto, Hal Finney, Wei Dai, Nick Szabo,
  Adam Back, David Chaum, Laszlo Hanyecz, Gavin Andresen) are treated as
  already-public, extensively documented historical/crypto-history
  figures rather than community members whose profiles need protecting —
  no public-person-node created and no high_risk flag set, since this is
  canonical, widely-published history rather than a community identity
  disclosure.
- No exact locations, TEK/Indigenous knowledge, MRV/carbon claims, or
  funding/legal/governance recommendations present.

data.title: Delegation and Representation in DAOs
data.summary: A design guide for DAO delegation systems, covering four delegation types (full, topic-based, liquid, time-limited), key design questions, concrete recommendations for local nodes (optional delegation, power caps of 20-30%, transparency, accountability, always-available direct voting), accountability mechanisms (delegate reports, recall, term limits, conflict disclosure), and common mistakes to avoid.
data.audience: DAO-Operator / Local-Node governance designers
known_tensions: reducing-voter-fatigue-via-delegation vs concentrating-power-in-delegates — the whole article is an argument for building delegation carefully so it solves the first problem without causing the second.
flexibility-of-liquid-delegation vs complexity-requiring-sophisticated- tooling.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No named tools/platforms are cited in this article (unlike dao-tooling.md
  or dao-governance-models.md) — no resource objects created; this is a
  pure governance-design guide with generic "on-chain/off-chain/hybrid"
  language rather than named implementations.
- No people/community profiles, exact locations, or high-risk triggers
  identified. Note: the article does make a governance-design
  recommendation (cap delegate power at 20-30%) — this is generic best-
  practice advice, not a claim about a specific real DAO's funding/legal
  status, so it was not treated as a high-risk governance recommendation
  requiring a public-use-boundary; flagged here for reviewer judgment call.

data.title: DAO Governance Models
data.summary: Surveys five DAO governance models — token-weighted voting, quadratic voting, reputation-based governance, multi-signature governance, and hybrid governance — with pros/cons and a named example DAO for each, then gives guidance on choosing a model based on purpose, size, desired decentralization, speed-vs-fairness, and scalability.
data.audience: DAO-Operator
known_tensions: simplicity-and-investment-alignment (token voting) vs whale-dominance-risk — wealth translating directly into decision power.
efficiency-of-multi-sig vs centralization-risk-if-signers-are-not-rotated.
flexibility-of-hybrid-models vs complexity-and-communication-overhead.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- CityDAO, MakerDAO, and Decentraland DAO are named as one-line examples for
  quadratic/reputation/hybrid models respectively; not built out as separate
  resource objects since the article gives no more than a single sentence
  about each beyond "uses this model" — kept ENS DAO and SafeDAO (the two
  given the most concrete operational detail: ENS name-service governance,
  SafeDAO's treasury/upgrade coordination) as resources instead.
- Soulbound Tokens and conviction voting are mentioned as "emerging

  article; left as a mention inside the encyclopedia entry rather than a

- No people/community profiles, exact locations, or high-risk triggers

data.title: Voting Mechanisms in DAOs
data.summary: Compares six DAO decision-making mechanisms — token-based quorum voting, quadratic voting, conviction voting, holographic consensus, multi-sig voting, and off-chain voting via Snapshot — on the trade-offs of speed vs inclusivity, simplicity vs manipulation-resistance, and participation vs scalability, and notes that most mature DAOs combine several mechanisms rather than relying on one.
data.audience: DAO operators choosing or designing a governance/voting process
known_tensions: speed vs inclusivity (multi-sig fast-but-concentrated vs conviction-voting open-but-slow)
simplicity vs manipulation-resistance (quorum voting easy-to-understand but vulnerable)
participation vs scalability (everyone-votes-on-everything does not scale)
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- the "Try This" reflection on cooperative/savings-group decision-making
  is folded into the encyclopedia summary framing rather than a
  separate object; it's an exercise prompt, not a distinct typed fact.
- no people/community profiles, exact locations, TEK, or funding/legal
  recommendations named; the Somaliland/East-Africa aside is a general,
  unattributed comparison (cooperative boards facing similar low-turnout
  dynamics), not a specific claim with a named source — captured only as
  an adjacent note in the concept-lineage object.

data.title: Knowledge Gardens
data.summary: How to build a community knowledge garden that survives contributor turnover: linking over filing, openly-marked growth stages (seedling/budding/evergreen), and active tending by a named gardener. Uses SuperBenefit's public Knowledge Garden as a worked model (Docs, Lexicon, Links, Patterns) and recommends plain markdown + Git (Obsidian + Quartz + GitHub) as the durable, non-lock-in tool stack.
data.audience: community organizers and local-node stewards building a team knowledge commons
known_tensions: polished, collaboration-friendly tools (Notion) vs. durable, portable-in-plain-text tools (Markdown + Git) — the article resolves this as "own your source of truth in plain text and Git; use anything prettier as a window onto it, not the vault itself"

data.title: Credentials and Certifications (Web3 verifiable credentials)
data.summary: Explains web3 credentials as records tied to a wallet address and signed by an issuer's private key, independently verifiable without contacting the issuer — Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and Soulbound Tokens (SBTs); the trust problem they solve especially where institutions are weak or hard to reach at a distance; active issuers (Gitcoin Passport, Karma, Lens, Galxe, Open Badges); use in grant/DAO gating; and practical setup via MetaMask, Ceramic/IDX, and Disco.xyz. High-risk: this whole topic is identity/reputation infrastructure — see paired public-use-boundary.
data.audience: individuals (e.g. in East Africa) building a portable, verifiable track record via web3
known_tensions: portability-and-verifiability vs wallet-linked-identity-and-reputation-being-inherently-trackable/doxable
credential-gating-as-sybil-resistance vs credential-gating-as-gatekeeping
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- "Sarreya itself issues credentials on completion of path milestones" —
  appears to reference a specific platform/product by name not otherwise
  described in this batch; kept as prose context, not spun into its own
  resource object since the article gives no further detail to verify against.

data.title: Why Accept Crypto Donations?
data.summary: A beginner guide for local organizers (Somaliland/East Africa audience) making the case for accepting cryptocurrency donations: the tax advantage to donors (avoiding capital-gains tax by donating appreciated crypto directly), lower cross-border processing costs than bank wires or card fees, access to a younger/values-aligned donor community, quadratic funding as an amplifier for small donations (via Gitcoin Grants), and honest treatment of concerns (price volatility, security, energy footprint). Recommends four donor-facing platforms (The Giving Block, Endaoment, Every.org, Givepact) that convert crypto to fiat automatically so the receiving organization never has to hold volatile crypto.
data.audience: local organizers/nonprofits in East Africa/Somaliland considering crypto donations
known_tensions: Donor tax benefit vs. organizational risk — the article's tax-advantage argument is aimed at the donor's incentive, while separately acknowledging the receiving organization's own volatility/security risk, which it resolves by recommending instant fiat-conversion platforms.

data.title: Social Tokens for Creators
data.summary: A short guide to social tokens (community-specific tokens for membership, access, or reputation) covering the three main types (creator, community, reputation tokens), use cases for local regen nodes (event access, governance weight, incentive alignment, community identity), and pitfalls (over-financializing relationships, designing for speculation, securities-law exposure).
data.audience: creators and local-node community organisers considering social tokens
known_tensions: The guide encourages using tokens to "track and reward contribution" while simultaneously warning against financializing community relationships and against designing for speculation — a tension it names but does not resolve with concrete guardrails.
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: article is short (60 lines) with no named external tools, no people/location/TEK/MRV content, and no specific funding/legal recommendation beyond a generic pointer to consult securities-law considerations — not treated as high_risk since it is a caution flag, not advice given. No resource-schema candidate produced; the article names no specific external tool/platform to register as a resource.

data.title: How Web3 Relates to Your Existing Work
data.summary: A short orientation piece framing web3 as an addition to an organization's existing mission-driven work (community relationships, program delivery, physical presence), not a replacement for it. Offers a pain-point-matching exercise across four areas (fundraising, transparency, coordination, community building) mapping each to a corresponding web3 tool category (crypto donations, blockchain transparency, DAOs/governance tools, tokens/credentials), and recommends starting with one small, reversible use case (a crypto-donate button, a Snapshot vote, a POAP, an on-chain published budget) rather than rebuilding everything.
data.audience: mission-driven organizations and community groups new to web3

data.title: Building Momentum for Your Local Node
data.summary: A guide to sustaining a local node's energy past initial launch excitement, aimed at organizers in East African contexts. Covers a rhythm model (weekly/monthly/quarterly/annual cadences), a celebration strategy for small and large wins, a four-stage newcomer pathway (awareness, first interaction, first action, ownership), an engagement loop that turns contributors into recruiters, common pitfalls (founder bottleneck, expertise trap, evening-only meetings, insider circles), how to manage low-momentum "dips," leadership rotation, and a growth-vs- sustainability framing that favors 20 engaged people over 100 on a mailing list. The article explicitly builds its rhythm/celebration model on existing East African community traditions (saving circles, inter-clan coordination, community meals after jumu'ah prayers) rather than inventing new ones.
data.audience: local-organizer (East African regen/ReFi context)
known_tensions: growth vs sustainability — the article's rule of thumb: "if you're sacrificing sustainability for growth, you're on borrowed time," favoring 20 actively engaged people over 100 on a mailing list.
communication cadence — too little communication and momentum dies, too much and people tune out; the article prescribes a specific weekly/ monthly/as-needed rhythm as the resolution.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No individual community members are named (no public-person-node
  risk); high_risk is set here because the article makes broad-strokes
  cultural attributions ("in many East African traditions...", "already
  deeply embedded in how people relate, through saving circles, through
  inter-clan coordination, through community meals after jumu'ah
  prayers") without citing a specific community or community-authored
  source — the same TEK/cultural-attribution trigger pattern already
  flagged in this framework's prior ingestion of gatherings-pattern.md.
  See the companion public-use-boundary object.
- The article's frontmatter lists generic sources ("Greenpill Local Regen
  Guide," "Community building literature," "DAO governance") with no
  inline citations or References section — see the companion signal
  object.

data.title: What You Can Do on Ethereum
data.summary: A narrowly-scoped beginner guide, written for participants in "the Sarreya programs," that deliberately limits Ethereum's relevance to three concrete uses: (1) sending/receiving digital money (e.g. USDC stablecoin transfers, low "gas" fees), (2) earning verifiable digital credentials for completed trainings/skills, and (3) tracking and proving real-world impact (photo + location submitted and recorded on-chain), which the article names as digital measurement, reporting, and verification (dMRV), citing Silvi as an example program. Explicitly tells readers NOT to worry about NFTs, DeFi lending, staking, or app development.
data.audience: participants in the Sarreya program(s); general audience individuals new to Ethereum
known_tensions: Simplicity vs. completeness — the article deliberately narrows scope to 3 uses and tells the reader to ignore the rest of the Ethereum ecosystem, trading completeness for actionability.
data.notes: Source-article frontmatter flags this piece itself as still in-progress: factcheck_done: false, review_done: false, critique_done: false, published_flag: false, stage: draft. This does not change our own maturity: raw / ai_assisted: true rating (that reflects THIS extraction), but a human reviewer should weigh that the underlying article has not yet been fact-checked by its own authors, particularly the dMRV/Silvi claim below.

data.title: Inclusive Practices for Community Finance
data.summary: Argues that community finance systems default to excluding the same people banks already exclude unless designed otherwise, and lays out five dimensions of inclusion (economic, technical, temporal, social, accessibility), practical strategies (plain language, multiple on-ramps, rotating what gets centered, explicit invitation, accountability), common mistakes (tokenism, one-size-fits-all design, uncompensated burden on marginalized groups), and community-finance-specific barriers (financial literacy, technical barriers, time poverty, trust barriers) with matched solutions.
data.audience: community stewards designing or running a community finance system
known_tensions: counting-participation-is-easy-vs-measuring-whether-people-feel-valued-and-influence-decisions-is-the-actual-goal
rewarding-time-and-care-contributions-equally-to-money-vs-avoiding-uncompensated-inclusion-labor-falling-on-marginalized-members
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: the article's References section lists only generic topic labels ("Inclusive community design principles", "Equity in economic systems and community finance", "Accessibility guidelines for community organizations") with no actual sources/links — not turned into resource objects since they name no identifiable, findable source. The "Try This" self-audit exercise was left as a narrative prompt, not extracted as a separate object.

data.title: Stablecoins: Digital Dollars That Hold Their Value
data.summary: A plain-language explainer of stablecoins for community organisers: what a peg is, why dollar-stable digital money is useful for cross-border payments and grants, the energy-use difference between Bitcoin and proof-of-stake chains, the three stablecoin designs (fiat-backed, crypto-backed, algorithmic), where stablecoins actually break (USDC's 2023 depeg, Terra/UST's 2022 collapse), and a caution on "earning interest" yield offers.
data.audience: community organisers and regenerative practitioners new to crypto
known_tensions: Fiat-backed stablecoins are framed as the safer, auditable choice, but the article also notes issuers can freeze balances under law enforcement order — safety and censorship-resistance trade off against each other.
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: no people/location/TEK content requiring a public-use-boundary; market-size and depeg-event figures are captured separately as claim-evidence objects with uncertainty noted rather than asserted as flat fact here.

data.title: The Promise: Coordination, Transparency, and New Economic Models
data.summary: A high-level orientation to why web3 excites regens beyond money: DAOs, quadratic voting, and futarchy as coordination-without-central-control tools; blockchain transparency as verifiable (not "transparency theater") accountability; and new economic models (credentialing via POAPs/Gitcoin/ retroactive funding, community value capture, and impact-aligned instruments like regenerative tokens and outcome-based bonds).
data.audience: regens evaluating whether web3 coordination tools are worth exploring
known_tensions: experimental-and-imperfect-tools vs genuinely-new-coordination-possibilities
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- article is thin on citations (mostly definitional/promotional claims about
  web3 capabilities with no sourcing); treated as concept overview rather
  than claim-evidence since there is no specific verifiable figure to
  isolate as a claim.

data.title: Legal Structures for Your Local Node
data.summary: How to choose a legal wrapper (co-op, nonprofit, LLC, DAO-specific structure) for a local ReFi node so the entity, not individual members, holds liability. Walks through risk-sizing (low/medium/high), staying informal, cooperatives, 501(c)(3) nonprofits, LLCs, and DAO-specific wrappers (Wyoming DUNA, DAO LLC, Marshall Islands DAO LLC, Cayman Islands foundation), with 2026 costs, a decision path, three common mistakes, and where to get free help.
data.audience: local-node organizers ready to hold funds, sign contracts, or run public events
known_tensions: protection vs. overhead — "over-wrapping too early" (e.g. a Cayman foundation for a $3,000 treasury) is named as one of the three mistakes that actually hurt people
data.notes: High-risk trigger: legal/governance recommendations (Principle from skills/ingest and skills/capture-and-route). This is jurisdiction- and time-specific (2026 fee figures, a 2024-effective statute) guidance, not legal advice — see the paired public-use-boundary object (05-).

data.title: What Web3 Can and Can't Do
data.summary: An honest capability/limits comparison for community and regenerative work. What Web3 does well, moving value across borders without a gatekeeper, permissionless building, public/hard-to-fake records, and censorship resistance, illustrated with Grassroots Economics' Sarafu network. What it cannot do (yet): cheap high-volume transactions on the main chain (though Layer 2s help), replacing a normal spreadsheet/database, verifying real-world facts (the Toucan/Verra carbon-credit case as the cautionary tale), and keeping activity private by default. Ends with a single screening question ("do multiple parties who don't fully trust each other need to share one record none of them can secretly change?") as the decision rule.
data.audience: community organizers deciding whether to use blockchain tools
known_tensions: Hype vs. honest fit — the article explicitly positions itself against "put it on the blockchain" as an unexamined buzzword answer.
On-chain code correctness vs. off-chain reality — the Toucan/Verra case shows a smart contract can work exactly as coded while the real-world facts and rules around it still fail to cooperate.

data.title: Proposal Writing for DAOs
data.summary: A short guide to writing DAO governance proposals that pass and get implemented. Lays out a seven-part proposal anatomy (title, summary, background/context, specification, budget, success criteria, risks), recommends informal pre-proposal steps (temperature check, coalition building, preemptively addressing objections), and lists five common mistakes (vague language, no budget, no success criteria, no timeline, surprising the community with an undiscussed proposal).
data.audience: DAO members / grounded-regen practitioners drafting governance proposals

data.title: Centralized vs. Decentralized Systems: What It Means for Your Garden and Community
data.summary: A foundations-track explainer contrasting centralized systems (one authority in charge — banks, concentrated food-processing, single- telecom mobile money) against decentralized systems (control spread across many independent parts — cooperatives, rotating savings circles, community seed banks, Bitcoin), aimed at community gardeners and permaculturists new to crypto. Argues most real systems are hybrids on a spectrum, ties the distinction to permaculture's resilience-through- diversity principle, and cites a 2022 food-systems resilience study as supporting evidence while noting the same study found centralization can help during labor shortages.
data.audience: individual community gardeners/permaculturists new to web3
known_tensions: centralized systems are easier to manage and can produce more cheaply (a single large farm vs many small ones) but carry a single point of failure; decentralized systems trade some efficiency for resilience.

the article's own cited study found decentralization improves resilience under supply-chain disruption but centralization can be favored when responding to labor shortages — presented as evidence that neither approach is categorically better.

data.title: Stories: Regens Who Made the Leap
data.summary: Three illustrative adoption stories (a community garden receiving a crypto donation, an environmental-nonprofit coalition moving its treasury to a multisig, and a from-scratch African ReFi community using Discord/Gitcoin/Snapshot/POAPs) used to show that starting small, finding one knowledgeable ally, and staying mission-focused is enough to begin using web3 tools without deep technical expertise.
data.audience: regenerative practitioners considering their first step into web3

data.title: Communicating with Stakeholders About Crypto
data.summary: A guide for nonprofits on talking to board, staff, and donors before/while adopting crypto donations: educate first, prepare the board on legality, tax, risk and asset-management questions, address volatility/security/ complexity concerns openly, communicate the new option across channels once ready, and build reusable templates.
data.audience: nonprofit leaders preparing to introduce crypto donations to their org
known_tensions: honesty-about-risk vs not-scaring-off-a-skeptical-board

data.title: Creating, Buying, and Earning Tokens & NFTs
data.summary: A practical how-to for getting started with digital assets: minting NFTs (OpenSea/Blur) and fungible ERC-20 tokens, buying crypto via CEX/DEX/ onramps (with a Layer-2-first tip for low fees), and earning tokens through staking, DeFi lending, governance-token rewards, and learning modules (Bankless Academy) — plus security basics on token allowances and seed phrases.
data.audience: newcomers wanting a hands-on first step into creating/buying/earning digital assets
known_tensions: permissionless-token-creation vs quality-and-scam-risk-that-comes-with-it

data.title: Is a DAO Right for Your Community?
data.summary: A plain-language decision guide for permaculture/grassroots communities weighing DAO structure, using a community-garden analogy to explain decentralized/autonomous/organization, listing when a DAO fits (everyone wants a voice, global participation, transparency, rewarding contribution) and when it doesn't (fast emergency decisions, need for legal protection, low tech comfort, governance-attack risk), a five- question discussion guide, and cooperative/sociocracy/simple-voting-tool alternatives.
data.audience: permaculture and grassroots community organizers evaluating governance structures
known_tensions: radical-transparency-and-global-participation-vs-no-legal-protection-and-real-technical-learning-curve

data.title: Identity Verification in Web3
data.summary: Explains wallet-based identity verification as proving attributes about yourself (age, membership, location) without handing over documents to every counterparty, using zero-knowledge proofs and wallet-held credentials, framed for community members considering web3 grants, DAOs, or reputation-building in a Somaliland/East Africa context.
data.audience: community members and stewards new to web3, evaluating whether/how to engage with verification-gated programs
known_tensions: access-to-verification-gated-opportunities-vs-privacy-cost-of-any-identity-linkage
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: the article has no References/sources section (its frontmatter sources: [] is empty) and names no specific verification protocol, product, or platform, so no resource object was created — the content is purely conceptual/explanatory. No public person-nodes or location-specific individual data were created; the Somaliland/Sarreya programs reference is kept general (audience framing only, no named individuals).

data.title: Understanding Gas Fees in Cryptocurrency
data.summary: A quick, plain-language explainer of blockchain gas fees: what gas is and why it exists (pay validators, prevent spam, allocate block space), the EIP-1559 base-fee + tip fee model (base fee auto-adjusts with demand and is burned; priority fee/tip jumps the queue), typical gas costs by transaction type, what drives fees up or down (network demand, time of day, transaction complexity), and five ways to save (time transactions, avoid volatility spikes, use fee estimators, use Layer 2, set max fees).
data.audience: newcomers doing their first crypto transactions

data.title: AI Tools for Community Knowledge
data.summary: An opinionated guide to the AI tools that help a small team build a knowledge commons that survives contributor turnover. Organized around one governing rule, "infrastructure should serve the work, not define it" — ask what job needs doing (capture, synthesize, search) before picking a tool. Walks through transcription (Otter.ai) for capture, retrieval-augmented generation (Google NotebookLM) for grounded synthesis, and local-first search (Obsidian + Smart Connections) for private, durable ownership, then closes on three guardrails: privacy, attribution, and naming one steward.
data.audience: small community teams building a durable, AI-assisted knowledge base
known_tensions: cloud convenience (NotebookLM, Otter.ai) vs local ownership (Obsidian + Smart Connections) — article resolves this by routing sensitive or long-lived material to local tools and using cloud tools for lower-stakes synthesis and search.

polished AI writing reads as trustworthy whether or not it is accurate — the article treats this as more dangerous than a messy human note, not less, and insists AI drafts be marked distinctly from human-confirmed knowledge.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No people/community profiles or exact locations named in this article;
  privacy/consent is discussed as general advice about handling
  transcripts, not itself sensitive material — no high-risk trigger on
  the entry itself.
- GravityDAO is mentioned only as an analogy ("the kind of practice
  GravityDAO has built its work around") rather than described in enough
  detail to warrant its own resource object; folded into this entry's
  summary instead.

data.title: Trust and Transparency in Decentralized Systems
data.summary: Argues decentralization does not eliminate trust but relocates it — from institutions (banks, platforms) to open-source code, consensus mechanisms, and public verifiability. Explains how blockchain properties (immutability, transparency, cryptographic security) enable this, walks through Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake as the "trust engine," then names a "transparency paradox": the same public visibility that enables accountability (detecting insider trading, concentrated ownership) also creates attack surfaces (sophisticated actors planning attacks on visible positions). Closes on decentralized identity (DIDs) as returning ownership of one's digital self.
data.audience: general readers evaluating whether/why decentralized trust models matter
known_tensions: trust-in-institutions vs trust-in-code/math/consensus
transparency-enables-accountability vs transparency-enables-attack-planning
individual-control-of-identity vs currently-scattered-centralized-identity-databases

data.title: Stewardship Roles for a Knowledge Commons That Outlives You
data.summary: A guide on naming, assigning, and handing off the five stewardship roles (Editor, Curator, Facilitator, Maintainer, Onboarder) a knowledge commons needs, how to measure fragility via the Contributor Absence Factor (Bus Factor), and how to wire roles into existing tooling (CODEOWNERS, all-contributors, GOVERNANCE.md) so succession survives turnover.
data.audience: small teams running a docs/GitHub-based knowledge commons
known_tensions: Roles "written in a Notion page nobody opens are decoration"; the article argues roles only become real when enforced by tooling (CODEOWNERS, bots) rather than documented as intent.
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: the article addresses a reader named "Sol" directly ("Sol, this is where it gets concrete") — this reads as an audience persona / direct-address device, not a real private individual's personal information being exposed, so no person-node or public-use-boundary created for it. No ecological/MRV/funding-decision content triggering high_risk.

data.title: Building Internal Capacity
data.summary: A guide on developing the skills and systems a community needs to sustain web3 operations independently, without relying on external experts or consultants. Names four capacity areas (technical: wallet management, smart contract interaction, treasury operations, security; governance: facilitation, proposal writing, conflict resolution, decision-making; communication: writing, social media, community management, outreach; financial: bookkeeping, grant writing, budgeting, fundraising) and a five-step process to build it: identify gaps, map existing skills, create learning pathways, practice with low stakes, and document everything.
data.audience: local node organizers investing in member skill development
data.notes:

data.title: On-Chain Attestations: Your Digital Proof Record
data.summary: A beginner-level explainer of on-chain attestations as permanent, verifiable, tamper-proof digital proof records for skills, training completion, volunteering, and community impact — framed as a replacement for paper certificates that can be lost, damaged, or forged. Explains the mechanism in three steps (someone vouches for you → it's recorded permanently on a blockchain → anyone can verify it) and lists use cases: proving skills for scholarships/jobs, building a portable reputation, showing community impact, and accessing opportunity programs that require verifiable proof.
data.audience: Written directly for young women participants in "Sarreya programs" (a named training/mentorship context referenced in the source article, apparently East Africa / Somaliland-adjacent based on sibling articles in this batch); beginner, non-technical.
known_tensions: The article asserts attestations are simply superior to paper certificates on every axis (permanent, verifiable, portable, trustworthy) without discussing failure modes (e.g. the vouching party itself being wrong, revoked, or unaccountable) — see accompanying claim-evidence entry.

data.audience: Community-Steward
known_tensions: local-autonomy vs global-coordination — "isolation breeds fragility; dependence on a single external power breeds capture."

data.title: Find Your Community
data.summary: A plain-language guide for community organizers and permaculturists on finding a trustworthy, real-world ReFi (regenerative finance) community without getting scammed or wasting time. Frames ReFi DAO and Greenpill Network as the two established "front doors," recommends listening before committing (field notes, public Telegram, assessment, steward call), and gives concrete rules for telling a real community from a scam (never share a seed phrase, real teams don't DM first, always type the known URL yourself, never send money first, big member counts aren't proof, slow is safe).
data.audience: community organizers and permaculturists new to ReFi/web3, wary of scams
known_tensions: Encourages joining named, centralized-looking "front doors" (ReFi DAO, Greenpill) as the safe path, which is itself a form of gatekeeping — worth naming that "established" is being used as a proxy for "safe," not a guarantee.

data.title: The Ethereum Ecosystem
data.summary: A grounded, hype-free tour of Ethereum for regenerative communities in East Africa and Somaliland: what Ethereum is (a shared, permissionless compute platform, not just a currency), Layer 2 networks as a cost/speed fix, DeFi (swaps, lending, stablecoins), NFTs as provable digital ownership, and DAOs as a new organizational form. Closes with practical low-risk starter steps (wallet, L2 browsing, block explorer, browsing a DAO's governance).
data.audience: beginner community members and organizers in East Africa / Somaliland exploring web3 for the first time
known_tensions: The article frames the technology as neutral ("can serve extractive finance or regenerative purposes") while also actively encouraging exploration of DeFi/DAOs — readers should weigh real risk (smart contract bugs, volatility, hacks) against the framed opportunity.

data.title: Security Best Practices for Organizations Using Crypto Wallets
data.summary: Security guidance for regenerative organizations holding crypto assets: the core rule is no single point of failure, achieved via multi-sig wallets (e.g. Safe) with configurations from 2-of-3 to 4-of-7 depending on org size; layered role-based access control (operations/managers/ executives/board); separation of hot wallets (2-4 weeks of operating funds) from cold-storage treasury reserves; a written policy framework (digital-asset management, security protocols, emergency response, smart-contract vetting); and ongoing team training on phishing and safe transaction practices. Includes a practical security checklist and an explicit warning against using personal wallets for organizational funds.
data.audience: DAO operators / regenerative organizations managing crypto treasuries

data.title: Local Currency Design for Community Finance
data.summary: A practical guide to designing and launching a community currency: what unit to use (time-based, value-based, points-based), what backs it (nothing/fiat, labour, goods, national currency), who issues it (member-issued, system-issued, hybrid), what rules to set (earning, spending, expiry, fees), and technical implementation choices (paper ledgers, shared digital ledger, blockchain). Covers a three-phase launch process (design, pilot, scale), common mistakes, and named case studies (Ithaca Hours, Brixton Pound, Sardex, BerkShares, and East African chamas/ROSCAs as an existing informal precedent to build on).
data.audience: local-node organizers, East Africa-focused track (Somaliland, Kenya, Tanzania context)
known_tensions: keeping value local (the core purpose of a local currency) vs. tying the unit to a national currency (value-based backing), which re-imports the inflation/instability the currency is meant to buffer against

data.title: Real Examples of Impact DAOs
data.summary: Introduces Impact DAOs (DAOs organized specifically for positive change) to a permaculture/regenerative-community audience through three named cases — ReFi DAO's global network of place-based Local Nodes, Greenpill's "degens to regens" chapter model with tiered participation, and Klima DAO's approach to bringing verified carbon credits on-chain — and draws an explicit analogy to permaculture principles (working with natural systems, local resilience connected to broader networks, sharing over hoarding, regenerative over extractive economies).
data.audience: permaculture practitioners and regenerative-community members new to web3/DAOs
known_tensions: Frames DAOs as "trust built into the system rather than relying on one person," which risks overstating how automatic trust is in practice — DAO participation, accountability, and decision quality are named elsewhere in the site as real, unresolved challenges.

Klima DAO's premise (bringing carbon credits on-chain for a liquid, accessible market) assumes the underlying off-chain carbon verification is sound; the article does not examine that layer's integrity.

data.title: Is Web3 Right for Your Community?
data.summary: A short decision-framing guide arguing web3 isn't for everyone: it lists when web3 adds value (transparent/verifiable finance, programmable governance, cross-border coordination, connecting to the wider web3 ecosystem, immutable records) versus when it doesn't (small high-trust groups, minimal financial activity, low tech comfort, "a spreadsheet does everything you need"), five questions to ask before adopting it, and recommends a hybrid approach — web3 where it adds clear value, traditional tools elsewhere.
data.audience: community groups deciding whether to adopt web3 tools at all
known_tensions: web3-genuinely-solving-a-coordination-problem-vs-adopting-it-out-of-curiosity-or-hype
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: no resource/source-system objects were created — the article names no specific tool, platform, or protocol, only generic categories ("Web3 tools," "spreadsheets," "group chats"). See accompanying signal noting the article's frontmatter sources field is a placeholder ("Community building") rather than an actual citation.

data.title: Layer 2 Solutions
data.summary: Explains how Layer 2 networks (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, zkSync Era, Starknet, Scroll) scale Ethereum by processing transactions off the main chain and settling compressed batches back to it, cutting fees from several dollars to fractions of a cent. Covers Optimistic vs. ZK rollup designs, why this matters for regenerative-finance projects running micro-transactions or community token systems, and how to get started (MetaMask, bridging, using L2 dApps).
data.audience: regen project builders new to Ethereum scaling, East Africa / Somaliland-focused track
known_tensions: Optimistic Rollups (accessible, widely compatible, ~7-day challenge window) vs. ZK Rollups (faster finality, no challenge window, more technically complex, "still maturing")

data.title: Custodial vs Non-Custodial Wallets: Understanding Who Holds the Keys
data.summary: Compares custodial wallets (a third party like an exchange holds your private keys, similar to a bank) against non-custodial wallets (you hold your own keys/seed phrase, no intermediary). Walks through the trade-offs of each — recovery, ease of use, DeFi access, privacy, counterparty risk — then gives East-Africa-specific framing (mobile money precedents like M-Pesa, Eva, Telesom ZAAD) and decision guidance for when to choose which.
data.audience: Individual (beginner, East African communities)
known_tensions: ease-of-use-and-recoverability (custodial) vs full-ownership-and-no-safety-net (non-custodial) — the article frames this as situational, not a universal "better" choice.
convenience of built-in recovery vs the "not your keys, not your crypto" principle of true ownership.

data.title: Local Nodes and DAOs: When (and Whether) to Formalize
data.summary: Distinguishes a local node (a community concept — people in a place, organized around shared purpose) from a DAO (a legal-and-technical form). Argues for "minimum viable coordination" (SuperBenefit's term) rather than building governance machinery pre-emptively. Names the three concrete things formalizing actually gives you (a treasury no one person controls, decisions anyone can verify, roles that survive people leaving), surveys which DAO tools are actually still standing as of mid-2026 (Safe, Snapshot/Snapshot X, Hats Protocol — with Tally and Coordinape flagged as having wound down), and recommends a hybrid model: informal/human for the social layer, onchain only for the parts that need a trust backstop.
data.audience: local-node organizers deciding whether/how to formalize governance
known_tensions: formalizing to gain trust/legitimacy vs. formalizing as maintenance burden that "exhausts founders and quietly kills nodes" — the article argues structure should be added only in response to a named, current problem
related_concepts: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) vs. Local Node

data.title: Hot Wallets vs. Cold Storage
data.summary: Contrasts internet-connected "hot" wallets (fast, convenient, higher theft risk) with fully offline "cold storage" (hardware or paper, slower to access, much lower theft risk), and recommends a layered custody model — hot for operational funds, hardware cold storage for reserves/grants, multi-signature for organizational decisions.
data.audience: community organizers or treasurers deciding where to keep organizational or personal crypto holdings
known_tensions: convenience-of-hot-wallets-vs-security-of-cold-storage
upfront-hardware-wallet-cost-vs-perceived-affordability-for-small-holdings
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: the article's "Try This" self-audit checklist (identify holdings, classify hot/cold, check seed-phrase storage, rate exposure 1-10) was excluded as a standalone object — it is an exercise prompt, not a typed knowledge object, and is preserved in full in the source file. MetaMask, Ledger, Trezor, and Safe/Gnosis Safe were not re-created as new resource objects: equivalent resources ("MetaMask", "Hardware / cold wallets (Ledger, Trezor)", "Safe (Wallet)") already exist in data/kb/resource.yaml from a prior ingestion slice.

data.title: What Is a Local Node?
data.summary: A practical guide for people ready to build, defining a "local node" as a place-based community group using Web3 tools and regenerative principles to coordinate real-world action in one specific area — simultaneously self-governing and network-connected. Covers what nodes do (pool resources, fund public goods, onboard newcomers, run a steady meetup cadence, connect outward), when Web3 tooling actually earns its place vs. a spreadsheet, the Localism Fund / quadratic-funding network-funding picture, common structural patterns, a three-stage Seed/Sapling/Canopy maturity model (ReFi DAO), and the single biggest failure mode: bus-factor- of-one burnout.
data.audience: people ready to build a place-based Web3-enabled regen community group
known_tensions: Node autonomy vs. central overreach — the article frames "subsidiarity" (decisions at the most local level able to make them) as the design answer to the fear that a network could swallow a local project.
Technology-first vs. relationships-first — "a node with strong relationships and a Google Sheet beats a node with flawless tokenomics and no trust."

data.title: Archive or Compost: Handling Outdated Knowledge Without Losing the Plot
data.summary: A practical framework for retiring stale documents in a knowledge commons without deleting institutional memory or confusing readers. Names four moves — archive (preserve as labeled history), compost (harvest the still -good parts into living pages, retire the husk), deprecate (mark obsolete with a warning and a pointer), and remove (rare; last resort) — against the Regen Knowledge Commons Toolkit's Evolution Layer and cross-cutting principle #17, "compost, archive, and memory." Closes on the governance rule that keeps this from becoming chaos: a staleness flag is a signal, not a conclusion — a named steward decides which move applies and does it on the record.
data.audience: teams stewarding docs/wikis that must outlive contributor turnover
known_tensions: most teams only know two verbs, keep and delete — keeping lets the wiki silently rot, deleting erases the memory of why a decision was made; the article's four-move framework is presented as the fix.

composting requires human judgment (deciding what's worth keeping) while archiving and deprecating are described as "near-mechanical" — the article treats this as why composting is the most valuable and least practiced of the four moves.
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- No people/community profiles, exact locations, TEK, MRV/carbon claims,
  or funding/legal/governance recommendations in this article — no
  high-risk trigger identified. It is a general documentation-hygiene
  practice guide.
- GravityDAO is mentioned only as an analogy for tending trust on purpose,
  not described in enough detail here to warrant its own resource object
  (a fuller GravityDAO resource object already exists from other
  ingestions of articles that describe it directly).

data.title: Cooperative Economics and Digital Commons
data.summary: Explains cooperative economics (worker, consumer, savings-and-loan, and multi-stakeholder cooperatives) grounded in Somaliland/East African traditions (coffee cooperatives, savings circles), extends the idea to the digital commons and DAOs, walks through Elinor Ostrom's eight principles for governing shared resources, and lists funding paths (member contributions, savings-group formalization, grants, quadratic funding, community currencies).
data.audience: community stewards in Somaliland/East Africa building cooperative or commons-based projects
known_tensions: informal-savings-circles-already-work vs formalizing-them-into-registered-cooperatives-with-broader-reach
data.notes:
# assessed-but-excluded
- "target_audience: Somaliland / East Africa" in the source frontmatter names a
  region, not an exact location or individual/community profile, so no
  high-risk flag; kept as general geographic/cultural framing only.

data.title: What Is a Knowledge Commons?
data.summary: A plain-language guide for small teams comfortable with docs/GitHub on building a shared knowledge base that survives team turnover. Distinguishes a "commons" from a plain wiki by governance (drawing on Elinor Ostrom's commons-governance principles and her later "knowledge as a commons" work with Charlotte Hess), argues turnover is the real test of a knowledge base, profiles three real working examples at different scales (Wikipedia, SuperBenefit Knowledge Garden, GravityDAO), introduces the "digital garden" posture (rough/unfinished notes published openly rather than perfected before publishing), and warns against building an ontology before content exists.
data.audience: small teams and local nodes new to knowledge-commons practice
known_tensions: Perfectionism vs. "digital garden" posture — the article argues pages must be allowed to be rough/unfinished and openly marked as such, rather than withheld until polished.
Structure-first vs. content-first — explicitly argues against designing a full ontology before a real pile of notes exists to inform it.

data.title: Token Standards: The Building Blocks of Digital Assets
data.summary: Compares the three main Ethereum token standards — ERC-20 (fungible), ERC-721 (unique/non-fungible), and ERC-1155 (flexible multi-token) — explaining what each is used for and how a community project (savings tokens, impact credits, marketplaces) should pick between them, framed for East African/Somaliland community and cooperative use cases.
data.audience: community organisers/cooperatives choosing a token standard for their project
data.notes: assessed-but-excluded: no people/location/TEK/MRV high-risk content; the "Hargesa Savings Token" example is a generic illustrative name, not a real identifiable entity.

data.title: Metadata That Matters
data.summary: How to design a small, durable set of metadata fields (title, type, status, owner, source, updated, tags) so a knowledge commons stays findable and trustworthy after the people who built it move on. Draws the type-vs-tag distinction (one type per document, many tags, a controlled vocabulary to prevent sprawl), recommends borrowing established field names (Dublin Core, Murmurations) rather than inventing new ones, and shows how to make the schema machine-enforced (Astro/Zod content collections, remark-lint-frontmatter-schema) so consistency does not depend on memory. Names status, owner, and source as the three non-negotiable "trust fields."
data.audience: knowledge-commons builders and stewards (any team, not local-node-specific)
known_tensions: minimal metadata (fast to fill in, low friction) vs. rich metadata (more useful for trust/findability) — resolved as "spend the field budget carefully," six or seven fields as a starting default

data.title: Tokens as Coordination Tools
data.summary: Explains how tokens function as coordination mechanisms for distributed groups: signaling (temperature checks before formal votes), on-chain vs off-chain voting, reputation-based alternatives to pure token wealth, and incentive/penalty design. Walks through MakerDAO, Gitcoin DAO, and KlimaDAO as real examples, then names the recurring failure modes (low participation, wealth concentration, hidden multisig hierarchies, short-termism) and points to the SuperBenefit anticapture framework as a design response.
data.audience: regenerative community members and DAO organizers weighing whether/how to use tokens for governance
known_tensions: token-weighted-voting vs one-person-one-voice ideals
decentralization-as-stated-value vs multisig-concentrated-power-in-practice
short-term-price-speculation vs long-term-ecosystem-health
data.notes:

data.title: Other Chains and Ecosystems
data.summary: A comparison of five blockchain ecosystems beyond Ethereum — Solana, Cosmos, Polkadot, Avalanche, and Near — covering each chain's core mechanism, tradeoffs, and relevance to regenerative-finance projects (micro-donation/carbon-credit throughput, sovereign community-currency chains, shared-security launches, custom subnets, and accessibility/ climate focus respectively). Closes with a four-factor decision framework for choosing where to build (team skills, transaction needs, community location, project type).
data.audience: individuals evaluating which blockchain ecosystem fits a regenerative project

data.title: Tokens for Real-World Assets
data.summary: Introduces real-world-asset (RWA) tokenization: turning off-chain valuable things (real estate, gold, bonds, art, carbon credits) into blockchain tokens that prove ownership and can be fractionally traded. Covers the claimed benefits (liquidity, fractional access, transparency, lower cost, global access), the real challenges (legal complexity across borders, valuation/oracle dependence, custody of the physical asset, scalability), the actors involved (issuers, platforms, liquidity providers, service providers), and beginner action items.
data.audience: newcomers exploring what asset tokenization is and whether to look closer (per source, "target learner Maya")
known_tensions: blockchain-token-portability vs national-legal-jurisdiction-over-the-underlying-asset
claimed-transparency-and-lower-fraud vs continued-dependence-on-a-human-custodian-for-the-physical-asset

data.title: AI-Assisted Classification for Your Knowledge Commons
data.summary: An opinionated guide for small teams on using AI to sort and tag a growing document pile without letting it silently invent its own taxonomy. Distinguishes typing (what kind of thing) from tagging (what it's about), contrasts unsupervised discovery (BERTopic) with supervised bucketing (LLMs against a fixed category list), and argues for running discovery once to design a taxonomy then constraining all later AI output to an enum so the categories stay stable. Closes with a human-in-the-loop discipline: store model confidence, stamp provenance on every tag, and never let an AI suggestion pass as a settled decision.
data.audience: small teams and local nodes running a shared docs/GitHub knowledge base
known_tensions: discovery (let the data surprise you) vs bucketing (force answers into a fixed list) — article resolves this as "discovery once to design the taxonomy, bucketing for everything after."

constrained output (schema/enum-locked classification) prevents taxonomy sprawl but also means a genuinely new category needs a deliberate, reviewed "new tag" escape hatch rather than silent invention.

data.title: What Is a DAO?
data.summary: A plain-language DAO primer for regenerative community organizers, using a "community garden bank account, made visible and rule-bound" analogy. Breaks down the acronym (Decentralized / Autonomous / Organization), contrasts it with a familiar savings circle, names the four core parts of any DAO (treasury, proposals, voting, smart contracts), and walks through the standard tooling (Snapshot for gasless voting, Safe for multi-sig treasury custody, Aragon for no-code DAO creation), plus real regen-space examples (ReFi DAO, Greenpill Network).
data.audience: community organisers and regenerative practitioners new to crypto, evaluating whether a DAO would help their group

data.title: Finding Your People
data.summary: A member-attraction framework for local regen node builders: define your ideal member (values, skills, contribution, needs) and your non-ideal member before looking; look in named online spaces (Discord, Twitter/X, Reddit, LinkedIn) and offline spaces (local meetups, co-working spaces, community events, university groups); attract people through content marketing, community presence, events, and one-on-one relationships; and move them through a four-stage funnel (Awareness, Interest, Visit, Join) toward what ultimately attracts people to stay — authenticity, belonging, purpose, and value.
data.audience: local regen node builders/organizers

data.title: Conflict Resolution for Local Nodes

data.audience: people stewarding or organizing a local regen node/chapter
known_tensions: reaching-for-a-mechanism-to-end-discomfort vs protecting-the-relationship-first
rewarding-contribution-algorithmically vs agreeing-on-values-before-metrics

data.title: Crypto Wallet Recovery Planning: Ensuring Access for the Long Term
data.summary: A guide to crypto wallet recovery methods for individuals and regenerative organizations: seed-phrase backups (paper, metal, geographic distribution), social recovery wallets (guardian-based, e.g. Argent), multi-signature wallets (e.g. Safe, 2-of-3 through 4-of-7 configurations), Shamir Secret Sharing, and inheritance/succession planning. Gives context-specific best practices for individuals, organizations, and DAOs, plus common mistakes (single point of failure, improvised secret-splitting, undocumented passphrases, no written procedures, unavailable guardians). Includes region-specific guidance for Somaliland/East Africa (trusted community storage locations where bank deposit boxes are scarce).
data.audience: individuals and regenerative organizations managing crypto treasuries

data.title: Setting Up Your First Wallet
data.summary: A calm, step-by-step guide to creating a first self-custody crypto wallet (MetaMask) safely: what a wallet is, hot vs cold wallets, guarding the Secret Recovery Phrase, the wallet address vs phrase distinction, the setup steps, gas on layer-2 networks, and beginner safety habits.
data.audience: community organisers and growers brand new to Web3

data.title: Building Your Founding Team
data.summary: A guide for organizers standing up a local ReFi node on assembling a small, durable founding team. Argues to start with two or three committed people rather than a crowd, fill roles (convener, builder/doer, treasurer/ops) rather than titles, bring people in through real work rather than abstract membership, and design against burnout from day one (no single point of failure, legitimate rest). Cites named real-world nodes (ReFi Medellín, ReFi Cartagena) and their named founders as worked examples, plus research on founder conflict and DAO burnout.
data.audience: organizers standing up a local ReFi/regen node
known_tensions: recruiting a crowd feels like momentum but the article argues small, trust-bonded founding teams (2-3 people) outperform larger, looser ones that "attended one call."
one person can hold two of the three core roles at the start, but the article warns against any one person holding all three for long — tension between fast bootstrapping and burnout risk.
